2.0.oldText: “Faith,” muttered Passepartout, somewhat flustered, “I’ve seen people at Madame Tussaud’s as lively as my new master!”

2.1.oldText: Madame Tussaud’s “people,” it should be said, are made of wax, and are much visited in London; only speech is wanting to make them human.

2.2.oldText: During his brief interview with Mr. Fogg, Passepartout had observed his new master carefully. He appeared to be a man of about forty, with fine, handsome features and a tall, well-built figure; his hair and whiskers were light, his forehead smooth and unwrinkled, his face rather pale, his teeth magnificent. His countenance possessed in the highest degree what physiognomists call “repose in action,” the quality of those who act rather than talk. Calm and phlegmatic, with a clear eye, Mr. Fogg seemed a perfect specimen of that English composure which Angelica Kauffmann has rendered so skilfully on canvas. Seen in the various phases of his daily life, he gave the impression of being perfectly balanced, as exactly regulated as a Leroy chronometer. Phileas Fogg was, indeed, exactitude personified, and the quality showed itself even in the expression of his hands and feet; for in men, as in animals, the limbs themselves express the passions.

2.3.oldText: He was so exact that he was never in a hurry, was always ready, and was economical alike of his steps and his motions. He never took one step too many, and always reached his destination by the shortest route; he made no superfluous gestures, and was never seen moved or agitated. He was the most deliberate man in the world, and yet he always arrived at the exact moment.

2.4.oldText: He lived alone, and, so to speak, outside every social relation; and since he knew that in this world account must be taken of friction, and that friction retards, he never rubbed against anybody.

2.5.oldText: As for Passepartout, he was a true Parisian of Paris. Since leaving his own country for England to take service as a valet, he had searched in vain for a master after his own heart. Passepartout was by no means one of those pert dunces depicted by Molière, with a bold stare and a nose held high; he was an honest fellow with a pleasant face, lips a trifle protruding, soft-mannered and obliging, with a good round head of the kind one likes to see on the shoulders of a friend. His eyes were blue, his complexion ruddy, his figure almost portly and well-built, his body muscular, and his physical powers fully developed by the exercises of his younger days. His brown hair was rather tumbled; for while the ancient sculptors are said to have known eighteen methods of arranging Minerva’s tresses, Passepartout was familiar with only one for dressing his own: three strokes of a large-toothed comb completed his toilet.

2.6.oldText: It would be rash to predict how Passepartout’s lively nature would agree with Mr. Fogg. It was impossible to tell whether the new servant would turn out as absolutely methodical as his master required; only experience could settle the question. Passepartout had been something of a vagrant in his early years, and now longed for repose; but so far he had failed to find it, though he had already served in ten English houses. He could not put down roots in any of them; to his chagrin, his masters were invariably whimsical and irregular, constantly running about the country or on the look-out for adventure. His last master, young Lord Longferry, Member of Parliament, after spending his nights in the Haymarket taverns, was too often brought home in the morning on policemen’s shoulders. Passepartout, anxious to respect the gentleman he served, ventured a mild remonstrance on such conduct; it was poorly received, and he took his leave. Hearing that Mr. Phileas Fogg was looking for a servant, and that his life was one of unbroken regularity—that he neither travelled nor stayed away from home overnight—he felt sure this was the place he was after. He presented himself, and was accepted, as we have seen.

2.7.oldText: At half-past eleven, then, Passepartout found himself alone in the house in Saville Row. He began his inspection without delay, scouring it from cellar to garret. So clean, so well-arranged, so solemn a mansion pleased him; it seemed to him like a snail’s shell, lit and warmed by gas, which sufficed for both purposes. When Passepartout reached the second floor he recognised at once the room he was to occupy, and was well satisfied with it. Electric bells and speaking-tubes provided communication with the lower stories; while on the mantel stood an electric clock, exactly like the one in Mr. Fogg’s bedroom, both beating the same second at the same instant. “That’s good, that’ll do,” said Passepartout to himself.

2.8.oldText: Then he noticed, hung over the clock, a card which on inspection proved to be a programme of the daily routine of the house. It comprised everything required of the servant, from eight in the morning—the exact hour at which Phileas Fogg rose—until half-past eleven, when he left for the Reform Club: all the details of service, the tea and toast at twenty-three minutes past eight, the shaving-water at thirty-seven minutes past nine, the toilet at twenty minutes before ten. Everything from half-past eleven a.m. until midnight, when the methodical gentleman retired, was regulated and foreseen.

2.9.oldText: Mr. Fogg’s wardrobe was amply stocked and in the best taste. Each pair of trousers, each coat and vest, bore a number indicating the time of year and season at which it was to be laid out for wearing; and the same system was applied to the master’s shoes. In short, the house in Saville Row—which must have been a very temple of disorder and unrest under the illustrious but dissipated Sheridan—was cosiness, comfort, and method idealised. There was no study and no books, which would have been quite useless to Mr. Fogg; for at the Reform two libraries, one of general literature, the other of law and politics, were at his service. A moderate-sized safe stood in his bedroom, built to defy both fire and burglars; but Passepartout found no weapons anywhere, no hunting gear; everything betrayed the most tranquil and peaceable habits.

2.10.oldText: Having scrutinised the house from top to bottom, he rubbed his hands, a broad smile spread across his features, and he said joyfully: “This is just what I wanted! Ah, we shall get on together, Mr. Fogg and I! What a domestic and regular gentleman! A real machine—well, I don’t mind serving a machine.”

3.0.oldText: Phileas Fogg, having closed the door of his house at half-past eleven, and having placed his right foot before his left five hundred and seventy-five times, and his left foot before his right five hundred and seventy-six times, reached the Reform Club—an imposing building in Pall Mall which cannot have cost less than three millions. He went straight to the dining-room, whose nine windows open upon a tasteful garden where the trees were already gilded with autumn colour, and took his place at the usual table, the cover already laid for him. His breakfast consisted of a side-dish, a broiled fish with Reading sauce, a scarlet slice of roast beef garnished with mushrooms, a rhubarb and gooseberry tart, and a morsel of Cheshire cheese, the whole washed down with several cups of tea, for which the Reform is famous. He rose at thirteen minutes to one and made his way to the large hall, a sumptuous room hung with lavishly framed paintings. A flunkey handed him an uncut _Times_, which he proceeded to cut with the skill of long familiarity. The reading of this paper absorbed Phileas Fogg until a quarter before four, while the _Standard_, his next task, occupied him until the dinner hour. Dinner passed as breakfast had done, and Mr. Fogg reappeared in the reading-room and sat down to the _Pall Mall_ at twenty minutes before six. Half an hour later several members of the Reform came in and drew up to the fireplace, where a coal fire was steadily burning. They were Mr. Fogg’s usual partners at whist: Andrew Stuart, an engineer; John Sullivan and Samuel Fallentin, bankers; Thomas Flanagan, a brewer; and Gauthier Ralph, one of the directors of the Bank of England—all wealthy and highly respectable men, even in a club that included the princes of English trade and finance.

3.1.oldText: “Well, Ralph,” said Thomas Flanagan, “what about that robbery?”

3.2.oldText: “Oh,” replied Stuart, “the Bank will lose the money.”

3.3.oldText: “On the contrary,” broke in Ralph, “I hope we may yet lay hands on the robber. Skilful detectives have been sent to every principal port in America and on the Continent, and he’ll be a clever fellow if he slips through their fingers.”

3.4.oldText: “But have you got a description of the robber?” asked Stuart.

3.5.oldText: “In the first place, he is no robber at all,” returned Ralph, positively.

3.6.oldText: “What! A fellow who makes off with fifty-five thousand pounds, no robber?”

3.9.oldText: “The _Daily Telegraph_ says he is a gentleman.”

3.10.oldText: It was Phileas Fogg, whose head now emerged from behind his newspapers, who made this remark. He bowed to his friends and joined the conversation. The affair which formed its subject, and which was the talk of the town, had occurred three days before at the Bank of England. A package of banknotes, to the value of fifty-five thousand pounds, had been taken from the principal cashier’s table, that official being at the moment engaged in registering the receipt of three shillings and sixpence. Of course he could not have his eyes everywhere. Let it be noted that the Bank of England reposes a touching confidence in the honesty of the public. There are neither guards nor gratings to protect its treasures; gold, silver, banknotes lie freely exposed, at the mercy of the first comer. A keen observer of English customs relates that one day, finding himself in one of the rooms of the Bank, he had the curiosity to examine a gold ingot weighing some seven or eight pounds. He picked it up, scrutinised it, passed it to his neighbour, who passed it to the next man, and so on, until the ingot, going from hand to hand, was carried down to the end of a dark entry; nor did it return to its place for half an hour. All the while the cashier had not so much as raised his head. But in the present case things had not gone so smoothly. The package of notes not being found when five o’clock sounded from the ponderous clock in the “drawing office,” the amount was passed to the account of profit and loss. As soon as the robbery was discovered, picked detectives hurried off to Liverpool, Glasgow, Havre, Suez, Brindisi, New York, and other ports, inspired by the reward offered—two thousand pounds, and five per cent. on the sum that might be recovered. Detectives were also charged with closely watching all who arrived at or left London by rail, and a judicial inquiry was at once begun.

3.11.oldText: There were real grounds for supposing, as the _Daily Telegraph_ said, that the thief did not belong to any professional band. On the day of the robbery a well-dressed gentleman of polished manners, with a well-to-do air, had been noticed coming and going in the paying room where the crime had taken place. A description of him was easily obtained and circulated to the detectives; and some hopeful spirits, of whom Ralph was one, did not despair of catching him. The papers and the clubs were full of the affair, and everywhere people were debating the prospects of a successful pursuit. The Reform Club was particularly stirred up, several of its members being officials of the Bank.

3.12.oldText: Ralph would not concede that the work of the detectives was likely to be in vain; he thought the prize offered would greatly stimulate their zeal and activity. But Stuart was far from sharing this confidence; and as they placed themselves at the whist-table, they continued to argue the matter. Stuart and Flanagan played together, while Phileas Fogg had Fallentin for his partner. As the game went on, the conversation ceased, except between rubbers, when it revived.

3.13.oldText: “I maintain,” said Stuart, “that the chances are with the thief, who must be a shrewd fellow.”

3.14.oldText: “Well, but where can he fly to?” asked Ralph. “No country is safe for him.”

3.17.oldText: “Oh, I don’t know about that. The world is big enough.”

3.18.oldText: “It was once,” said Phileas Fogg, in a low tone. “Cut, sir,” he added, handing the cards to Thomas Flanagan.

3.19.oldText: The discussion died during the rubber; afterwards Stuart picked up its thread again.

3.20.oldText: “What do you mean by ‘once’? Has the world grown smaller?”

3.21.oldText: “Certainly,” returned Ralph. “I agree with Mr. Fogg. The world has grown smaller, since a man can now go round it ten times more quickly than a hundred years ago. And that is why the search for this thief is the more likely to succeed.”

3.22.oldText: “And also why the thief can get away more easily.”

3.23.oldText: “Be so good as to play, Mr. Stuart,” said Phileas Fogg.

3.24.oldText: But the sceptical Stuart was not convinced, and when the hand was finished he said eagerly: “You have a strange way, Ralph, of proving that the world has grown smaller. So, because you can go round it in three months—”

3.26.oldText: “That is true, gentlemen,” added John Sullivan. “Only eighty days, now that the section between Rothal and Allahabad, on the Great Indian Peninsula Railway, has been opened. Here is the estimate made by the _Daily Telegraph:_—

3.27.oldText: From London to Suez _viâ_ Mont Cenis and Brindisi, by rail and steamboats ................. 7 days From Suez to Bombay, by steamer .................... 13 ” From Bombay to Calcutta, by rail ................... 3 ” From Calcutta to Hong Kong, by steamer ............. 13 ” From Hong Kong to Yokohama (Japan), by steamer ..... 6 ” From Yokohama to San Francisco, by steamer ......... 22 ” From San Francisco to New York, by rail ............. 7 ” From New York to London, by steamer and rail ........ 9 ” ------- Total ............................................ 80 days.”

3.28.oldText: “Yes, in eighty days!” exclaimed Stuart, who in his excitement made a false deal. “But that doesn’t account for bad weather, contrary winds, shipwrecks, railway accidents, and so on.”

3.29.oldText: “All included,” returned Phileas Fogg, continuing to play despite the discussion.

3.30.oldText: “But suppose the Hindoos or Indians pull up the rails,” said Stuart; “suppose they stop the trains, pillage the luggage-vans, and scalp the passengers!”

3.31.oldText: “All included,” Fogg calmly retorted, adding, as he threw down his cards, “Two trumps.”

3.32.oldText: Stuart, whose turn it was to deal, gathered them up and went on: “You are right, theoretically, Mr. Fogg, but practically—”

3.34.oldText: “I’d like to see you do it in eighty days.”

3.35.oldText: “It depends on you. Shall we go?”

3.36.oldText: “Heaven preserve me! But I would wager four thousand pounds that such a journey, made under these conditions, is impossible.”

3.37.oldText: “Quite possible, on the contrary,” returned Mr. Fogg.

3.39.oldText: “The journey round the world in eighty days?”

3.43.oldText: “At once. Only I warn you that I shall do it at your expense.”

3.44.oldText: “It’s absurd!” cried Stuart, who was beginning to be annoyed at his friend’s persistence. “Come, let’s get on with the game.”

3.45.oldText: “Deal again, then,” said Phileas Fogg. “There’s a false deal.”

3.46.oldText: Stuart took up the pack with a feverish hand; then suddenly set it down again.

3.47.oldText: “Well, Mr. Fogg,” he said, “so be it: I will wager the four thousand on it.”

3.48.oldText: “Calm yourself, my dear Stuart,” said Fallentin. “It’s only a joke.”

3.49.oldText: “When I say I’ll wager,” returned Stuart, “I mean it.”

3.50.oldText: “All right,” said Mr. Fogg; and turning to the others he went on: “I have a deposit of twenty thousand at Baring’s which I will willingly risk on it.”

3.51.oldText: “Twenty thousand pounds!” cried Sullivan. “Twenty thousand pounds, which you might lose by a single accidental delay!”

3.52.oldText: “The unforeseen does not exist,” Phileas Fogg quietly replied.

3.53.oldText: “But, Mr. Fogg, eighty days are only the estimate of the least possible time in which the journey can be made.”

3.55.oldText: “But, in order not to exceed it, you must jump mathematically from the trains to the steamers, and from the steamers back onto the trains.”

3.58.oldText: “A true Englishman does not joke when he is talking about so serious a thing as a wager,” Phileas Fogg replied solemnly. “I will bet twenty thousand pounds against anyone who wishes that I will make the tour of the world in eighty days or less; in nineteen hundred and twenty hours, or a hundred and fifteen thousand two hundred minutes. Do you accept?”

3.59.oldText: “We accept,” replied Messrs. Stuart, Fallentin, Sullivan, Flanagan, and Ralph, after consulting one another.

3.60.oldText: “Good,” said Mr. Fogg. “The train leaves for Dover at a quarter before nine. I shall take it.”

3.62.oldText: “This very evening,” returned Phileas Fogg. He took out and consulted a pocket almanac, and added: “As today is Wednesday, the 2nd of October, I shall be due in London, in this very room of the Reform Club, on Saturday, the 21st of December, at a quarter before nine p.m.; or else the twenty thousand pounds, now deposited in my name at Baring’s, will belong to you, in fact and in right, gentlemen. Here is a cheque for the amount.”

3.63.oldText: A memorandum of the wager was drawn up at once and signed by all six parties, during which Phileas Fogg preserved a stoical composure. He certainly did not bet to win, and had only staked the twenty thousand pounds—half his fortune—because he foresaw that he might have to spend the other half to carry out this difficult, not to say impossible, project. His opponents, for their part, seemed much agitated; not so much by the value of their stake as because they had some scruples about betting on terms so unfavourable to their friend.

3.64.oldText: The clock struck seven, and the party offered to suspend the game so that Mr. Fogg might make his preparations for departure.

3.65.oldText: “I am quite ready now,” was his tranquil reply. “Diamonds are trumps: be so good as to play, gentlemen.”

4.0.oldText: Having won twenty guineas at whist, and having taken leave of his friends, Phileas Fogg left the Reform Club at twenty-five minutes past seven.

4.1.oldText: Passepartout, who had conscientiously studied the programme of his duties, was more than surprised to see his master commit the inexactness of appearing at this unaccustomed hour; for, according to the rule, he was not due in Saville Row until precisely midnight.

4.2.oldText: Mr. Fogg went up to his bedroom and called out, “Passepartout!”

4.3.oldText: Passepartout did not reply. It could not be him being called; it was not the right hour.

4.4.oldText: “Passepartout!” repeated Mr. Fogg, without raising his voice.

4.6.oldText: “I’ve called you twice,” observed his master.

4.7.oldText: “But it is not midnight,” replied the other, showing his watch.

4.8.oldText: “I know; I don’t blame you. We start for Dover and Calais in ten minutes.”

4.9.oldText: A puzzled grin spread across Passepartout’s round face; clearly he had not grasped what his master meant.

4.11.oldText: “Yes,” returned Phileas Fogg. “We are going round the world.”

4.12.oldText: Passepartout opened his eyes wide, raised his eyebrows, held up his hands, and seemed about to collapse, so overcome was he with stupefied astonishment.

4.14.oldText: “In eighty days,” returned Mr. Fogg. “So we haven’t a moment to lose.”

4.15.oldText: “But the trunks?” gasped Passepartout, unconsciously swaying his head from side to side.

4.16.oldText: “We’ll have no trunks; only a carpet-bag, with two shirts and three pairs of stockings for me, and the same for you. We’ll buy our clothes on the way. Bring down my mackintosh and travelling-cloak, and some stout shoes, though we shall do little walking. Make haste!”

4.17.oldText: Passepartout tried to reply, but could not. He went out, climbed to his own room, dropped into a chair, and muttered: “That’s good, that is! And I, who wanted to remain quiet!”

4.18.oldText: He mechanically set about making the preparations for departure. Around the world in eighty days! Was his master a fool? No. Was it a joke, then? They were going to Dover; good! To Calais; good again! After all, Passepartout, who had been away from France for five years, would not be sorry to set foot on his native soil once more. Perhaps they would go as far as Paris, and it would do his eyes good to see Paris again. But surely a gentleman so sparing of his steps would stop there—no doubt; and yet it was none the less true that he was going away, this most domestic of men!

4.19.oldText: By eight o’clock Passepartout had packed the modest carpet-bag, which held the wardrobes of both his master and himself; then, still troubled in mind, he carefully shut the door of his room and went down to Mr. Fogg.

4.20.oldText: Mr. Fogg was quite ready. Under his arm could be seen a red-bound copy of Bradshaw’s Continental Railway Steam Transit and General Guide, with its timetables showing the arrival and departure of steamers and railways. He took the carpet-bag, opened it, and slipped into it a goodly roll of Bank of England notes, which would pass wherever he might go.

4.25.oldText: “Good. Take this carpet-bag,” he said, handing it to Passepartout. “Take good care of it, for there are twenty thousand pounds in it.”

4.26.oldText: Passepartout nearly dropped the bag, as if the twenty thousand pounds had been in gold and were weighing him down.

4.27.oldText: Master and man then went downstairs, the street-door was double-locked, and at the end of Saville Row they took a cab and drove rapidly to Charing Cross. The cab stopped at the railway station at twenty minutes past eight. Passepartout jumped down from the box and followed his master, who, having paid the cabman, was about to enter the station when a poor beggar-woman, with a child in her arms, her bare feet smeared with mud, her head covered with a wretched bonnet from which hung a tattered feather, and her shoulders wrapped in a ragged shawl, approached and mournfully asked for alms.

4.28.oldText: Mr. Fogg drew out the twenty guineas he had just won at whist and handed them to the beggar, saying: “Here, my good woman. I’m glad I met you”; and passed on.

4.29.oldText: Passepartout felt a moist sensation about the eyes; his master’s action had touched his susceptible heart.

4.30.oldText: Two first-class tickets for Paris having been quickly purchased, Mr. Fogg was crossing the station towards the train when he caught sight of his five friends from the Reform.

4.31.oldText: “Well, gentlemen,” he said, “I’m off, you see; and, if you will examine my passport when I get back, you will be able to judge whether I have accomplished the journey agreed upon.”

4.32.oldText: “Oh, that would be quite unnecessary, Mr. Fogg,” said Ralph politely. “We will trust your word, as a gentleman of honour.”

4.33.oldText: “You do not forget when you are due in London again?” asked Stuart.

4.34.oldText: “In eighty days; on Saturday, the 21st of December, 1872, at a quarter before nine p.m. Good-bye, gentlemen.”

4.35.oldText: Phileas Fogg and his servant took their seats in a first-class carriage at twenty minutes before nine; five minutes later the whistle screamed, and the train slowly glided out of the station.

4.36.oldText: The night was dark, and a fine, steady rain was falling. Phileas Fogg, snugly settled in his corner, did not open his lips. Passepartout, not yet recovered from his stupefaction, clung mechanically to the carpet-bag with its enormous treasure.

4.37.oldText: Just as the train was whirling through Sydenham, Passepartout suddenly uttered a cry of despair.

4.41.oldText: “To turn off the gas in my room!”

4.42.oldText: “Very well, young man,” returned Mr. Fogg coolly; “it will burn—at your expense.”

5.0.oldText: Phileas Fogg rightly suspected that his departure from London would create a lively sensation at the West End. The news of the bet spread through the Reform Club and gave its members an exciting topic of conversation. From the club it soon got into the papers throughout England. The boasted “tour of the world” was talked about, disputed, argued over with as much warmth as if the subject were another Alabama claim. Some took the side of Phileas Fogg, but the great majority shook their heads and declared against him; it was absurd, impossible, they said, that the tour of the world could be made, except theoretically and on paper, in this minimum of time, and with the existing means of travel. The _Times, Standard, Morning Post_, and _Daily News_, and twenty other highly respectable newspapers dismissed Mr. Fogg’s project as madness; the _Daily Telegraph_ alone hesitantly supported him. People generally thought him a lunatic, and blamed his Reform Club friends for having accepted a wager that betrayed the mental aberration of its proposer.

5.1.oldText: Articles no less passionate than logical appeared on the question, for geography is one of the pet subjects of the English; and the columns devoted to Phileas Fogg’s venture were eagerly devoured by all classes of readers. At first a few rash individuals, principally of the gentler sex, took up his cause, which became still more popular when the _Illustrated London News_ came out with his portrait, copied from a photograph in the Reform Club. A few readers of the _Daily Telegraph_ even dared to say, “Why not, after all? Stranger things have come to pass.”

5.2.oldText: At last a long article appeared, on the 7th of October, in the bulletin of the Royal Geographical Society, which treated the question from every angle and demonstrated the utter folly of the enterprise.

5.3.oldText: Everything, it said, was against the travellers, every obstacle imposed by both man and nature. A miraculous coincidence in the times of departure and arrival, which was impossible, was absolutely necessary to his success. He might, perhaps, count on the arrival of trains at the appointed hours in Europe, where the distances were relatively moderate; but when he reckoned on crossing India in three days, and the United States in seven, could he rely without misgiving on accomplishing his task? There were accidents to machinery, the risk of trains running off the line, collisions, bad weather, blocking by snow—were not all these against Phileas Fogg? Would he not find himself, when travelling by steamer in winter, at the mercy of the winds and fogs? Is it uncommon for the best ocean steamers to be two or three days behind time? But a single delay would be enough to fatally break the chain of communication; should Phileas Fogg once miss, even by an hour, a steamer, he would have to wait for the next, and that would irrevocably ruin his attempt.

5.4.oldText: This article caused a great deal of noise, and, being reprinted in all the papers, seriously depressed the supporters of the rash tourist.

5.5.oldText: Everybody knows that England is the world of betting men, who rank rather higher than mere gamblers; to bet is in the English temperament. Not only the members of the Reform but the general public made heavy wagers for or against Phileas Fogg, who was set down in the betting books as if he were a race-horse. Bonds were issued and appeared on ’Change; “Phileas Fogg bonds” were offered at par or at a premium, and a great business was done in them. But five days after the article in the bulletin of the Geographical Society appeared, the demand began to fall: “Phileas Fogg” declined. They were offered in packages, first of five, then of ten, until at last nobody would take less than twenty, fifty, a hundred!

5.6.oldText: Lord Albemarle, an elderly paralytic gentleman, was now the only advocate of Phileas Fogg left. This noble lord, fastened to his chair, would have given his fortune to be able to make the tour of the world, even if it took ten years; and he bet five thousand pounds on Phileas Fogg. When the folly, as well as the uselessness, of the adventure was pointed out to him, he contented himself with replying, “If the thing is feasible, the first to do it ought to be an Englishman.”

5.7.oldText: The Fogg party dwindled steadily, everybody was going against him, and the bets stood at a hundred and fifty to one and two hundred to one; and a week after his departure an incident occurred that deprived him of backers at any price.

5.8.oldText: The commissioner of police was sitting in his office at nine o’clock one evening when the following telegraphic dispatch was put into his hands:

5.10.oldText: ROWAN, COMMISSIONER OF POLICE, SCOTLAND YARD: I’ve found the bank robber, Phileas Fogg. Send without delay warrant of arrest to Bombay.

5.12.oldText: The effect of this dispatch was instantaneous. The polished gentleman disappeared, replaced by the bank robber. His photograph, which hung with those of the other members at the Reform Club, was examined in detail, and it betrayed, feature by feature, the description of the robber that had been given to the police. The mysterious habits of Phileas Fogg were recalled; his solitary ways, his sudden departure; and it seemed clear that, in undertaking a tour round the world on the pretext of a wager, he had had no other end in view than to elude the detectives and throw them off his track.

6.0.oldText: The circumstances under which this telegraphic dispatch about Phileas Fogg was sent were as follows:

6.1.oldText: The steamer “Mongolia,” belonging to the Peninsular and Oriental Company, built of iron, of two thousand eight hundred tons burden and five hundred horse-power, was due at eleven o’clock a.m. on Wednesday, the 9th of October, at Suez. The “Mongolia” plied regularly between Brindisi and Bombay _viâ_ the Suez Canal, and was one of the fastest steamers belonging to the company, always making more than ten knots an hour between Brindisi and Suez, and nine and a half between Suez and Bombay.

6.2.oldText: Two men were walking up and down the wharves, among the crowd of natives and strangers who were staying in this once-straggling village—now, thanks to the enterprise of M. Lesseps, a fast-growing town. One was the British consul at Suez, who, despite the prophecies of the English Government and the unfavourable predictions of Stephenson, was in the habit of watching, from his office window, English ships pass daily to and fro on the great canal, by which the old roundabout route from England to India by the Cape of Good Hope was shortened by at least a half. The other was a small, slight-built personage, with a nervous, intelligent face and bright eyes peering out from under eyebrows he was incessantly twitching. He was just now showing unmistakable signs of impatience, nervously pacing up and down, unable to stand still for a moment. This was Fix, one of the detectives sent out from England in search of the bank robber; it was his task to watch every passenger arriving at Suez closely, and to follow up anyone who seemed a suspicious character or resembled the description of the criminal he had received two days before from police headquarters in London. The detective was evidently inspired by the hope of obtaining the splendid reward that would be the prize of success, and he awaited, with an easily understandable feverish impatience, the arrival of the steamer “Mongolia.”

6.3.oldText: “So you say, consul,” he asked for the twentieth time, “that this steamer is never behind time?”

6.4.oldText: “No, Mr. Fix,” replied the consul. “She was signalled yesterday at Port Said, and the rest of the way is nothing to such a craft. I repeat that the ‘Mongolia’ has been ahead of the time required by the company’s regulations, and gained the prize awarded for excess of speed.”

6.6.oldText: “Directly from Brindisi; she takes on the Indian mails there, and she left there Saturday at five p.m. Have patience, Mr. Fix; she will not be late. But really, I don’t see how, from the description you have, you will be able to recognise your man, even if he is on board the ‘Mongolia.’”

6.7.oldText: “A man rather feels the presence of these fellows, consul, than recognises them. You must have a scent for them, and a scent is like a sixth sense that combines hearing, seeing, and smelling. I’ve arrested more than one of these gentlemen in my time, and if my thief is on board, I’ll answer for it; he won’t slip through my fingers.”

6.8.oldText: “I hope so, Mr. Fix, for it was a heavy robbery.”

6.9.oldText: “A magnificent robbery, consul; fifty-five thousand pounds! We don’t often have such windfalls. Burglars are becoming so contemptible these days! A fellow gets hanged for a handful of shillings!”

6.10.oldText: “Mr. Fix,” said the consul, “I like your way of talking, and I hope you’ll succeed; but I fear you’ll find it far from easy. Don’t you see, the description you have there bears a singular resemblance to an honest man?”

6.11.oldText: “Consul,” remarked the detective dogmatically, “great robbers always resemble honest folks. Fellows with rascally faces have only one course to take, and that’s to remain honest; otherwise they’d be arrested out of hand. The artistic thing is to unmask honest countenances; it’s no light task, I admit, but a real art.”

6.12.oldText: Mr. Fix was evidently not without his share of self-conceit.

6.13.oldText: Little by little the scene on the quay grew more animated; sailors of various nations, merchants, ship-brokers, porters, fellahs bustled to and fro as if the steamer were expected at any moment. The weather was clear and slightly chilly. The minarets of the town loomed above the houses in the pale rays of the sun. A jetty pier, some two thousand yards long, stretched out into the roadstead. A number of fishing-smacks and coasting boats, some still keeping the fantastic shape of ancient galleys, could be seen on the Red Sea.

6.14.oldText: As he made his way through the busy crowd, Fix scrutinised the passers-by, as was his habit, with a keen, rapid glance.

6.16.oldText: “The steamer doesn’t come!” he exclaimed, as the port clock struck.

6.17.oldText: “She can’t be far off now,” returned his companion.

6.18.oldText: “How long will she stop at Suez?”

6.19.oldText: “Four hours; long enough to take on coal. It is thirteen hundred and ten miles from Suez to Aden, at the other end of the Red Sea, and she has to take on a fresh coal supply.”

6.20.oldText: “And does she go from Suez directly to Bombay?”

6.22.oldText: “Good,” said Fix. “If the robber is on board, he will no doubt get off at Suez, so as to reach the Dutch or French colonies in Asia by some other route. He ought to know that he would not be safe an hour in India, which is English soil.”

6.23.oldText: “Unless,” objected the consul, “he is exceptionally shrewd. An English criminal, you know, is always better concealed in London than anywhere else.”

6.24.oldText: This observation gave the detective food for thought, and meanwhile the consul went away to his office. Fix, left alone, was more impatient than ever, having a presentiment that the robber was on board the “Mongolia.” If he had indeed left London intending to reach the New World, he would naturally take the route _viâ_ India, which was less watched—and harder to watch—than the Atlantic. But Fix’s reflections were soon interrupted by a succession of sharp whistles, which announced the arrival of the “Mongolia.” The porters and fellahs rushed down the quay, and a dozen boats pushed off from the shore to go and meet the steamer. Soon her gigantic hull appeared, gliding between the banks, and eleven o’clock struck as she anchored in the roadstead. She brought an unusual number of passengers, some of whom remained on deck to scan the picturesque panorama of the town, while the greater part disembarked into the boats and landed on the quay.

6.25.oldText: Fix took up a position and carefully examined each face and figure that appeared. Presently one of the passengers, after vigorously pushing his way through the importunate crowd of porters, came up to him and politely asked if he could point out the English consulate, at the same time showing a passport which he wished to have _visaed_. Fix instinctively took the passport, and with a rapid glance read the description of its bearer. An involuntary motion of surprise nearly escaped him, for the description in the passport was identical with that of the bank robber he had received from Scotland Yard.

6.30.oldText: “But he must come to the consul’s in person, so as to establish his identity.”

6.34.oldText: “There, on the corner of the square,” said Fix, pointing to a house two hundred steps off.

6.35.oldText: “I’ll go and fetch my master, who won’t be much pleased, however, at being disturbed.”

6.36.oldText: The passenger bowed to Fix and returned to the steamer.

7.0.oldText: The detective passed down the quay and made his way rapidly to the consul’s office, where he was at once admitted to the presence of that official.

7.1.oldText: “Consul,” he said, without preamble, “I have strong reasons to believe that my man is a passenger on the ‘Mongolia.’” And he related what had just passed concerning the passport.

7.2.oldText: “Well, Mr. Fix,” replied the consul, “I shall not be sorry to see the rascal’s face; but perhaps he won’t come here—that is, if he is the person you suppose him to be. A robber doesn’t much like to leave traces of his flight behind him; and besides, he is not obliged to have his passport countersigned.”

7.3.oldText: “If he is as shrewd as I think he is, consul, he will come.”

7.5.oldText: “Yes. Passports are only good for annoying honest folks and helping rogues in their flight. I assure you it will be quite the thing for him to do; but I hope you will not _visa_ the passport.”

7.6.oldText: “Why not? If the passport is genuine, I have no right to refuse.”

7.7.oldText: “Still, I must keep this man here until I can get a warrant to arrest him from London.”

7.8.oldText: “Ah, that’s your look-out. But I cannot—”

7.9.oldText: The consul did not finish his sentence, for as he spoke a knock was heard at the door, and two strangers entered, one of them the servant Fix had met on the quay. The other, his master, held out his passport with the request that the consul would do him the favour of _visaing_ it. The consul took the document and read it carefully, while Fix observed, or rather devoured, the stranger with his eyes from a corner of the room.

7.10.oldText: “You are Mr. Phileas Fogg?” said the consul, after reading the passport.

7.18.oldText: “Very good, sir. You know that a _visa_ is useless, and that no passport is required?”

7.19.oldText: “I know it, sir,” replied Phileas Fogg; “but I wish to prove, by your _visa_, that I came by way of Suez.”

7.21.oldText: The consul proceeded to sign and date the passport, after which he added his official seal. Mr. Fogg paid the customary fee, bowed coldly, and went out, followed by his servant.

7.23.oldText: “Well, he looks and acts like a perfectly honest man,” replied the consul.

7.24.oldText: “Possibly; but that is not the question. Do you think, consul, that this phlegmatic gentleman resembles, feature by feature, the robber whose description I have received?”

7.25.oldText: “I grant that; but then, you know, all descriptions—”

7.26.oldText: “I’ll make certain of it,” interrupted Fix. “The servant seems to me less mysterious than the master; besides, he’s a Frenchman, and can’t help talking. Excuse me for a little while, consul.”

7.27.oldText: Fix set off in search of Passepartout.

7.28.oldText: Meanwhile Mr. Fogg, after leaving the consulate, went to the quay, gave some orders to Passepartout, then took a boat out to the “Mongolia” and went down to his cabin. He took up his notebook, which contained the following memoranda:

7.32.oldText: “Reached Turin by Mont Cenis, Friday, October 4th, at 6.35 a.m.

7.34.oldText: “Arrived at Brindisi, Saturday, October 5th, at 4 p.m.

7.37.oldText: “Total hours spent, 158½; or, in days, six days and a half.”

7.38.oldText: These dates were entered in an itinerary divided into columns, indicating the month, the day of the month, and the day for the stipulated and actual arrivals at each principal point—Paris, Brindisi, Suez, Bombay, Calcutta, Singapore, Hong Kong, Yokohama, San Francisco, New York, and London—from the 2nd of October to the 21st of December; with a space for setting down the gain made or the loss suffered on arrival at each locality. This methodical record contained an account of everything needed, and Mr. Fogg always knew whether he was behind or ahead of his time. On this Friday, October 9th, he noted his arrival at Suez, and observed that he had as yet neither gained nor lost. He sat down quietly to breakfast in his cabin, never once thinking of inspecting the town, being one of those Englishmen who are accustomed to see foreign countries through the eyes of their servants.

8.0.oldText: Fix soon rejoined Passepartout, who was lounging and looking about on the quay, as though he didn’t feel that he, at least, was obliged not to see anything.

8.1.oldText: “Well, my friend,” said the detective, coming up with him, “is your passport _visaed?_”

8.2.oldText: “Ah, it’s you, is it, monsieur?” responded Passepartout. “Thanks, yes, the passport is all right.”

8.4.oldText: “Yes; but we travel so fast that I seem to be journeying in a dream. So this is Suez?”

8.10.oldText: “In Africa!” repeated Passepartout. “Just think, monsieur, I had no idea we should go farther than Paris; and all I saw of Paris was between twenty minutes past seven and twenty minutes before nine in the morning, between the Northern and Lyons stations, through the windows of a railway carriage, and in a driving rain! How I regret not having seen Père la Chaise once more, and the circus in the Champs-Élysées!”

8.11.oldText: “You are in a great hurry, then?”

8.12.oldText: “I am not, but my master is. By the way, I must buy some shoes and shirts. We came away without trunks, only with a carpet-bag.”

8.13.oldText: “I will show you an excellent shop for getting what you want.”

8.15.oldText: And they walked off together, Passepartout chatting volubly as they went.

8.16.oldText: “Above all,” he said, “don’t let me lose the steamer.”

8.17.oldText: “You have plenty of time; it’s only twelve o’clock.”

8.18.oldText: Passepartout pulled out his big watch. “Twelve!” he exclaimed; “why, it’s only eight minutes before ten.”

8.20.oldText: “My watch? A family watch, monsieur, that has come down from my great-grandfather! It doesn’t vary five minutes in the year. It’s a perfect chronometer, look you.”

8.21.oldText: “I see how it is,” said Fix. “You have kept London time, which is two hours behind that of Suez. You ought to regulate your watch at noon in each country.”

8.23.oldText: “Well, then, it won’t agree with the sun.”

8.24.oldText: “So much the worse for the sun, monsieur. The sun will be wrong, then!”

8.25.oldText: And the worthy fellow returned the watch to its fob with a defiant gesture. After a few minutes’ silence, Fix resumed: “You left London hastily, then?”

8.26.oldText: “I rather think so! Last Friday at eight o’clock in the evening, Monsieur Fogg came home from his club, and three-quarters of an hour afterwards we were off.”

8.28.oldText: “Always straight ahead. He is going round the world.”

8.30.oldText: “Yes, and in eighty days! He says it’s on a wager; but, between us, I don’t believe a word of it. That wouldn’t be common sense. There’s something else in the wind.”

8.31.oldText: “Ah! Mr. Fogg is a character, is he?”

8.34.oldText: “No doubt, for he is carrying an enormous sum in brand new banknotes with him. And he doesn’t spare the money on the way, either: he has offered a large reward to the engineer of the ‘Mongolia’ if he gets us to Bombay well ahead of time.”

8.35.oldText: “And you have known your master a long time?”

8.36.oldText: “Why, no; I entered his service the very day we left London.”

8.37.oldText: The effect of these replies on the already suspicious and excited detective can be imagined. The hasty departure from London soon after the robbery; the large sum carried by Mr. Fogg; his eagerness to reach distant countries; the pretext of an eccentric and foolhardy bet—all confirmed Fix in his theory. He continued to pump poor Passepartout, and learned that he really knew little or nothing of his master, who lived a solitary existence in London, was said to be rich though no one knew where his riches came from, and was mysterious and impenetrable in his affairs and habits. Fix felt sure that Phileas Fogg would not land at Suez, but was really going on to Bombay.

8.38.oldText: “Is Bombay far from here?” asked Passepartout.

8.39.oldText: “Pretty far. It’s a ten days’ voyage by sea.”

8.44.oldText: “The deuce! I was going to tell you—there’s one thing that worries me—my burner!”

8.46.oldText: “My gas-burner, which I forgot to turn off, and which is burning at this moment at my expense. I have calculated, monsieur, that I lose two shillings every twenty-four hours, exactly sixpence more than I earn; and you will understand that the longer our journey—”

8.47.oldText: Did Fix pay any attention to Passepartout’s trouble about the gas? It is not likely. He was not listening, but turning a project over in his mind. Passepartout and he had now reached the shop, where Fix left his companion to make his purchases, after telling him not to miss the steamer, and hurried back to the consulate. Now that he was fully convinced, Fix had quite recovered his equanimity.

8.48.oldText: “Consul,” he said, “I have no longer any doubt. I have spotted my man. He passes himself off as an odd stick who is going round the world in eighty days.”

8.49.oldText: “Then he’s a sharp fellow,” returned the consul, “and counts on returning to London after putting the police of the two countries off his track.”

8.53.oldText: “Why was this robber so anxious to prove, by the _visa_, that he had passed through Suez?”

8.54.oldText: “Why? I have no idea; but listen to me.”

8.55.oldText: He reported in a few words the most important parts of his conversation with Passepartout.

8.56.oldText: “In short,” said the consul, “appearances are wholly against this man. And what are you going to do?”

8.57.oldText: “Send a dispatch to London for a warrant of arrest to be dispatched instantly to Bombay, take passage on board the ‘Mongolia,’ follow my rogue to India, and there, on English ground, arrest him politely, with my warrant in my hand and my hand on his shoulder.”

8.58.oldText: Having uttered these words with a cool, careless air, the detective took leave of the consul and went to the telegraph office, from which he sent the dispatch we have already seen to the London police office. A quarter of an hour later Fix, with a small bag in his hand, was making his way on board the “Mongolia”; and a few moments later the noble steamer rode out at full steam upon the waters of the Red Sea.

9.0.oldText: The distance between Suez and Aden is precisely thirteen hundred and ten miles, and the company’s regulations allow the steamers one hundred and thirty-eight hours in which to traverse it. The “Mongolia,” thanks to the vigorous exertions of the engineer, seemed likely—so rapid was her speed—to reach her destination considerably within that time. The greater part of the passengers from Brindisi were bound for India: some for Bombay, others for Calcutta by way of Bombay, which is now the nearest route thither, since a railway crosses the Indian peninsula. Among the passengers was a number of officials and military officers of various grades, the latter either attached to the regular British forces or commanding the Sepoy troops, and receiving high salaries ever since the central government took over the powers of the East India Company: sub-lieutenants get £280, brigadiers £2,400, and generals of divisions £4,000. What with the military men, a number of rich young Englishmen on their travels, and the hospitable efforts of the purser, the time passed quickly on the “Mongolia.” The best of fare was set out on the cabin tables at breakfast, lunch, dinner, and the eight o’clock supper; the ladies scrupulously changed their toilets twice a day; and the hours flew by, when the sea was tranquil, in music, dancing, and games.

9.1.oldText: But the Red Sea is full of caprice, and often boisterous, like most long, narrow gulfs. When the wind came from the African or Asian coast, the “Mongolia,” with her long hull, rolled fearfully. Then the ladies quickly disappeared below; the pianos were silent; singing and dancing suddenly ceased. Yet the good ship ploughed straight on, unhindered by wind or wave, towards the Strait of Bab-el-Mandeb. What was Phileas Fogg doing all this time? It might be thought that, in his anxiety, he would be constantly watching the changes of the wind, the unruly raging of the billows—every chance, in short, which might force the “Mongolia” to slacken her speed and so interrupt his journey. But if he thought of these possibilities, he did not betray it by any outward sign.

9.2.oldText: Always the same impassive member of the Reform Club, whom no incident could surprise, as unvarying as the ship’s chronometers, seldom even curious enough to go on deck, he passed through the memorable scenes of the Red Sea with cold indifference; did not care to recognise the historic towns and villages whose picturesque outlines rose against the sky along its shores; and betrayed no fear of the dangers of the Arabian Gulf, of which the old historians always spoke with horror, and upon which the ancient navigators never ventured without propitiating the gods with ample sacrifices. How did this eccentric personage pass his time on the “Mongolia”? He took his four hearty meals every day, regardless of the most persistent rolling and pitching on the part of the steamer; and he played whist indefatigably, for he had found partners as enthusiastic about the game as himself. A tax-collector on the way to his post at Goa; the Rev. Decimus Smith, returning to his parish at Bombay; and a brigadier-general of the English army, who was about to rejoin his brigade at Benares, made up the party, and together with Mr. Fogg played whist by the hour in absorbing silence.

9.3.oldText: As for Passepartout, he too had escaped sea-sickness, and took his meals conscientiously in the forward cabin. He rather enjoyed the voyage, for he was well fed and well lodged, took a great interest in the scenes through which they were passing, and consoled himself with the delusion that his master’s whim would end at Bombay. He was pleased, the day after leaving Suez, to find on deck the obliging person with whom he had walked and chatted on the quays.

9.4.oldText: “If I am not mistaken,” he said, approaching this person with his most amiable smile, “you are the gentleman who so kindly volunteered to guide me at Suez?”

9.5.oldText: “Ah! I quite recognise you. You are the servant of the strange Englishman—”

9.8.oldText: “Monsieur Fix,” resumed Passepartout, “I’m charmed to find you on board. Where are you bound?”

9.10.oldText: “That’s capital! Have you made this trip before?”

9.11.oldText: “Several times. I am one of the agents of the Peninsular Company.”

9.13.oldText: “Why yes,” replied Fix, who spoke cautiously.

9.15.oldText: “Oh, very curious. Mosques, minarets, temples, fakirs, pagodas, tigers, snakes, elephants! I hope you will have ample time to see the sights.”

9.16.oldText: “I hope so, Monsieur Fix. You see, a man of sound sense ought not to spend his life jumping from a steamer onto a railway train, and from a railway train onto a steamer again, pretending to make the tour of the world in eighty days! No; all these gymnastics, you may be sure, will cease at Bombay.”

9.17.oldText: “And Mr. Fogg is getting on well?” asked Fix, in the most natural tone in the world.

9.18.oldText: “Quite well, and I too. I eat like a famished ogre; it’s the sea air.”

9.19.oldText: “But I never see your master on deck.”

9.21.oldText: “Do you know, Mr. Passepartout, that this pretended tour in eighty days may conceal some secret errand—perhaps a diplomatic mission?”

9.22.oldText: “Faith, Monsieur Fix, I assure you I know nothing about it, nor would I give half a crown to find out.”

9.23.oldText: After this meeting, Passepartout and Fix got into the habit of chatting together, the latter making it a point to gain the worthy fellow’s confidence. He frequently offered him a glass of whiskey or pale ale in the steamer’s bar-room, which Passepartout never failed to accept with graceful alacrity, mentally pronouncing Fix the best of good fellows.

9.24.oldText: Meanwhile the “Mongolia” was pushing forward rapidly; on the 13th, Mocha, surrounded by its ruined walls on which date-trees were growing, came into sight, and on the mountains beyond vast coffee-fields could be made out. Passepartout was enchanted to behold this celebrated place, and thought that, with its circular walls and dismantled fort, it looked like an immense coffee-cup and saucer. The following night they passed through the Strait of Bab-el-Mandeb, which means in Arabic “The Bridge of Tears,” and the next day they put in at Steamer Point, north-west of Aden harbour, to take on coal. This matter of fuelling steamers is a serious one at such distances from the coal-mines; it costs the Peninsular Company some eight hundred thousand pounds a year. In these distant seas, coal is worth three or four pounds sterling a ton.

9.25.oldText: The “Mongolia” still had sixteen hundred and fifty miles to traverse before reaching Bombay, and had to remain four hours at Steamer Point to coal up. But this delay, as it had been foreseen, did not affect Phileas Fogg’s programme; besides, the “Mongolia,” instead of reaching Aden on the morning of the 15th as she was due, arrived there on the evening of the 14th, a gain of fifteen hours.

9.26.oldText: Mr. Fogg and his servant went ashore at Aden to have the passport _visaed_ again; Fix, unobserved, followed them. The _visa_ procured, Mr. Fogg returned on board to resume his former habits; while Passepartout, as usual, sauntered about among the mixed population of Somalis, Banyans, Parsees, Jews, Arabs, and Europeans who make up the twenty-five thousand inhabitants of Aden. He gazed with wonder at the fortifications which make this place the Gibraltar of the Indian Ocean, and at the vast cisterns where the English engineers were still at work, two thousand years after the engineers of Solomon.

9.27.oldText: “Very curious, _very_ curious,” said Passepartout to himself on returning to the steamer. “I see that it is by no means useless to travel, if a man wants to see something new.” At six p.m. the “Mongolia” slowly moved out of the roadstead, and was soon once more on the Indian Ocean. She had a hundred and sixty-eight hours in which to reach Bombay, and the sea was favourable, the wind being in the north-west, and all sails aiding the engine. The steamer rolled but little; the ladies, in fresh toilets, reappeared on deck; and the singing and dancing were resumed. The trip was being accomplished most successfully, and Passepartout was enchanted with the congenial companion chance had secured him in the person of the delightful Fix. On Sunday, October 20th, towards noon, they came in sight of the Indian coast: two hours later the pilot came on board. A range of hills lay against the sky on the horizon, and soon the rows of palms which adorn Bombay came distinctly into view. The steamer entered the road formed by the islands in the bay, and at half-past four she hauled up at the quays of Bombay.

9.28.oldText: Phileas Fogg was in the act of finishing the thirty-third rubber of the voyage, and his partner and himself, having by a bold stroke captured all thirteen of the tricks, concluded this fine campaign with a brilliant victory.

9.29.oldText: The “Mongolia” was due at Bombay on the 22nd; she arrived on the 20th. This was a gain to Phileas Fogg of two days since his departure from London, and he calmly entered the fact in the itinerary, in the column of gains.

10.0.oldText: Everybody knows that the great reversed triangle of land, with its base in the north and its apex in the south, which is called India, takes in fourteen hundred thousand square miles, on which is spread, unevenly, a population of one hundred and eighty million souls. The British Crown exercises a real and despotic dominion over the larger portion of this vast country, and has a governor-general stationed at Calcutta, governors at Madras, Bombay, and in Bengal, and a lieutenant-governor at Agra.

10.1.oldText: But British India proper takes in only seven hundred thousand square miles, with a population of from one hundred to one hundred and ten million inhabitants. A considerable portion of India is still free from British authority; and there are certain ferocious rajahs in the interior who are absolutely independent. The celebrated East India Company was all-powerful from 1756, when the English first gained a foothold on the spot where the city of Madras now stands, down to the time of the great Sepoy insurrection. It gradually annexed province after province, purchasing them from the native chiefs, whom it seldom paid, and appointed the governor-general and his subordinates, civil and military. But the East India Company has now passed away, leaving the British possessions in India directly under the control of the Crown. The aspect of the country, as well as the manners and racial distinctions, is daily changing.

10.2.oldText: Formerly one was obliged to travel in India by the old cumbrous methods—going on foot or on horseback, in palanquins or unwieldy coaches; now fast steamboats ply on the Indus and the Ganges, and a great railway, with branch lines joining the main line at many points along its route, traverses the peninsula from Bombay to Calcutta in three days. This railway does not run in a direct line across India. The distance between Bombay and Calcutta, as the bird flies, is only from one thousand to eleven hundred miles; but the deflections of the road increase this distance by more than a third.

10.3.oldText: The general route of the Great Indian Peninsula Railway is as follows: leaving Bombay, it passes through Salcette, crossing to the continent opposite Tannah, goes over the chain of the Western Ghauts, runs thence north-east as far as Burhampoor, skirts the nearly independent territory of Bundelcund, ascends to Allahabad, turns thence eastward, meeting the Ganges at Benares, then departs from the river a little, and, descending south-eastward by Burdivan and the French town of Chandernagor, has its terminus at Calcutta.

10.4.oldText: The passengers of the “Mongolia” went ashore at half-past four p.m.; at exactly eight the train would start for Calcutta.

10.5.oldText: Mr. Fogg, after bidding good-bye to his whist partners, left the steamer, gave his servant several errands to do, urged him to be at the station promptly at eight, and, with his regular step which beat to the second like an astronomical clock, made his way to the passport office. As for the wonders of Bombay—its famous city hall, its splendid library, its forts and docks, its bazaars, mosques, synagogues, its Armenian churches, and the noble pagoda on Malabar Hill, with its two polygonal towers—he did not care a straw to see them. He would not deign to examine even the masterpieces of Elephanta, or the mysterious hypogea concealed south-east of the docks, or those fine remains of Buddhist architecture, the Kanherian grottoes of the island of Salcette.

10.6.oldText: Having transacted his business at the passport office, Phileas Fogg went quietly to the railway station, where he ordered dinner. Among the dishes served up to him, the landlord especially recommended a certain giblet of “native rabbit,” on which he prided himself.

10.7.oldText: Mr. Fogg accordingly tasted the dish, but, despite its spiced sauce, found it far from palatable. He rang for the landlord, and, when he appeared, said, fixing his clear eyes on him: “Is this rabbit, sir?”

10.8.oldText: “Yes, my lord,” the rogue boldly replied, “rabbit from the jungles.”

10.9.oldText: “And this rabbit did not mew when he was killed?”

10.10.oldText: “Mew, my lord! What, a rabbit mew! I swear to you—”

10.11.oldText: “Be so good, landlord, as not to swear, but remember this: cats were formerly considered, in India, as sacred animals. That was a good time.”

10.14.oldText: After which Mr. Fogg quietly continued his dinner. Fix had gone ashore shortly after Mr. Fogg, and his first destination was the headquarters of the Bombay police. He made himself known as a London detective, told his business at Bombay and the position of affairs concerning the supposed robber, and nervously asked whether a warrant had arrived from London. It had not reached the office; indeed, there had not yet been time for it to arrive. Fix was sorely disappointed, and tried to obtain an order of arrest from the director of the Bombay police. This the director refused, since the matter concerned the London office, which alone could legally deliver the warrant. Fix did not insist, and had to resign himself to wait for the arrival of the important document; but he was determined not to lose sight of the mysterious rogue as long as he stayed in Bombay. He did not doubt for a moment, any more than Passepartout did, that Phileas Fogg would remain there, at least until it was time for the warrant to arrive.

10.15.oldText: Passepartout, however, had no sooner heard his master’s orders on leaving the “Mongolia” than he saw at once that they were to leave Bombay as they had left Suez and Paris, and that the journey would be extended at least as far as Calcutta, and perhaps beyond. He began to ask himself whether this bet that Mr. Fogg talked about wasn’t really in good earnest, and whether his fate wasn’t truly forcing him, despite his love of repose, round the world in eighty days!

10.16.oldText: Having bought the usual quota of shirts and shoes, he took a leisurely stroll about the streets, where crowds of people of many nationalities—Europeans, Persians with pointed caps, Banyas with round turbans, Sindes with square bonnets, Parsees with black mitres, and long-robed Armenians—were gathered. It happened to be the day of a Parsee festival. These descendants of the sect of Zoroaster—the most thrifty, civilised, intelligent, and austere of the East Indians, among whom are counted the richest native merchants of Bombay—were celebrating a sort of religious carnival, with processions and shows, in the midst of which Indian dancing-girls, clothed in rose-coloured gauze, looped up with gold and silver, danced airily, but with perfect modesty, to the sound of viols and the clanging of tambourines. Needless to say, Passepartout watched these curious ceremonies with staring eyes and gaping mouth, and his countenance was that of the greenest booby imaginable.

10.17.oldText: Unhappily for his master, as well as for himself, his curiosity drew him unconsciously farther off than he had meant to go. At last, having seen the Parsee carnival wind away into the distance, he was turning his steps towards the station when he happened to catch sight of the splendid pagoda on Malabar Hill, and was seized with an irresistible desire to see its interior. He was quite ignorant that it is forbidden to Christians to enter certain Indian temples, and that even the faithful must not go in without first leaving their shoes outside the door. It may be said here that the wise policy of the British Government severely punishes any disregard of the practices of the native religions.

10.18.oldText: Passepartout, however, thinking no harm, went in like a simple tourist, and was soon lost in admiration of the splendid Brahmin ornamentation that met his eyes on every side, when of a sudden he found himself sprawling on the sacred flagging. He looked up to see three enraged priests, who at once fell upon him, tore off his shoes, and began to beat him with loud, savage exclamations. The agile Frenchman was soon on his feet again, and lost no time in knocking down two of his long-gowned adversaries with his fists and a vigorous application of his toes; then, rushing out of the pagoda as fast as his legs could carry him, he soon escaped the third priest by mingling with the crowd in the streets.

10.19.oldText: At five minutes before eight, Passepartout, hatless, shoeless, and having in the squabble lost his package of shirts and shoes, rushed breathlessly into the station.

10.20.oldText: Fix, who had followed Mr. Fogg to the station and saw that he was really going to leave Bombay, was there, on the platform. He had resolved to follow the supposed robber to Calcutta, and farther, if necessary. Passepartout did not notice the detective, who stood in an obscure corner; but Fix heard him relate his adventures in a few words to Mr. Fogg.

10.21.oldText: “I hope this will not happen again,” said Phileas Fogg coldly, as he got into the train. Poor Passepartout, quite crestfallen, followed his master without a word. Fix was on the point of entering another carriage when an idea struck him which made him change his plan.

10.22.oldText: “No, I’ll stay,” he muttered. “An offence has been committed on Indian soil. I’ve got my man.”

10.23.oldText: Just then the locomotive gave a sharp screech, and the train passed out into the darkness of the night.

11.0.oldText: The train had left on time. Among the passengers were a number of officers, government officials, and opium and indigo merchants whose business called them to the eastern coast. Passepartout rode in the same carriage as his master, and a third passenger sat in the seat opposite them. This was Sir Francis Cromarty, one of Mr. Fogg's whist partners on the "Mongolia," now on his way to rejoin his corps at Benares. Sir Francis was a tall, fair man of fifty who had distinguished himself greatly in the last Sepoy revolt. He made India his home, paying only brief visits to England at rare intervals, and was nearly as familiar as a native with the customs, history, and character of India and its people. But Phileas Fogg, who was not traveling but only tracing a circumference, took no pains to inquire into such matters. He was a solid body, moving along an orbit around the terrestrial globe according to the laws of rational mechanics. At that very moment he was calculating in his head the number of hours that had passed since his departure from London, and, had it been in his nature to make a useless display, he would have rubbed his hands in satisfaction. Sir Francis Cromarty had observed the oddity of his traveling companion—though his only chance to study him had come while dealing the cards and between two rubbers—and he asked himself whether a human heart really beat beneath this cold exterior, and whether Phileas Fogg had any sense of the beauties of nature. The brigadier-general was free to admit privately that, of all the eccentric people he had ever met, none compared to this product of the exact sciences.

11.2.oldText: An hour after leaving Bombay the train had passed the viaducts and the Island of Salcette and had reached the open country. At Callyan they came to the junction of the branch line that descends toward south-eastern India by Kandallah and Pounah. Passing Pauwell, they entered the defiles of the mountains, with their basalt bases and summits crowned with thick, green forests. Phileas Fogg and Sir Francis Cromarty exchanged a few words from time to time, and now Sir Francis, picking up the conversation again, remarked, "Some years ago, Mr. Fogg, you would have run into a delay at this point that would probably have cost you your wager."

11.4.oldText: "Because the railway stopped at the foot of these mountains, and the passengers had to cross them in palanquins or on ponies to reach Kandallah on the other side."

11.5.oldText: "Such a delay would not have disrupted my plans in the least," said Mr. Fogg. "I have always foreseen the likelihood of certain obstacles."

11.6.oldText: "But, Mr. Fogg," Sir Francis continued, "you run the risk of having some trouble over this worthy fellow's adventure at the pagoda." Passepartout, his feet comfortably wrapped in his travelling blanket, was sound asleep and never dreamed that anyone was talking about him. "The Government is very severe on that kind of offense. It is especially careful that the religious customs of the Indians be respected, and if your servant had been caught—"

11.7.oldText: "Very well, Sir Francis," Mr. Fogg replied. "If he had been caught, he would have been convicted and punished, and then he would have quietly gone back to Europe. I don't see how this affair could have delayed his master."

11.11.oldText: Passepartout was now sunk in absorbing reverie. Up until their arrival at Bombay he had hoped that the journey would end there; but now that they were clearly tearing across India at full speed, the mood of his daydreams had suddenly changed. His old vagabond nature came back to him; the fantastic ideas of his youth once again took hold of him. He began to regard his master's project as serious in earnest, to believe in the reality of the bet, and therefore in the tour round the world and the necessity of completing it within the appointed time. He was already worrying about possible delays and accidents that might happen on the way. He felt himself personally invested in the wager and trembled at the thought that he might have been the cause of losing it through his unforgivable folly of the night before. Far less cool-headed than Mr. Fogg, he was far more restless, counting and recounting the days that had passed, cursing whenever the train stopped, accusing it of sluggishness, and silently blaming Mr. Fogg for not having bribed the engineer. The worthy fellow had no idea that, while such methods might speed up a steamer, they could not work on a railway.

11.12.oldText: Toward evening the train entered the defiles of the Sutpour Mountains, which separate the Khandeish from Bundelcund. The next day Sir Francis Cromarty asked Passepartout what time it was, and the latter, after consulting his watch, answered that it was three in the morning. This famous timepiece, always set to the Greenwich meridian—which was now some seventy-seven degrees to the westward—was at least four hours slow. Sir Francis corrected Passepartout's time, whereupon Passepartout made the same remark he had made to Fix. When the general insisted that the watch should be adjusted at each new meridian, since he was constantly traveling east, that is, into the face of the sun, and therefore the days were shorter by four minutes for every degree crossed, Passepartout stubbornly refused to alter his watch, which he kept on London time. It was a harmless delusion that could do no one any harm.

11.13.oldText: At eight o'clock the train stopped in the middle of a clearing some fifteen miles beyond Rothal, where there were several bungalows and workmen's cabins. The conductor, walking along the carriages, called out, "Passengers will get out here!"

11.15.oldText: Passepartout, no less surprised, rushed out and quickly came back, crying, "Monsieur, no more railway!"

11.16.oldText: "What do you mean?" asked Sir Francis.

11.17.oldText: "I mean that the train isn't going on."

11.24.oldText: "No. There are still a matter of fifty miles to be laid between here and Allahabad, where the line begins again."

11.25.oldText: "But the papers announced the opening of the railway throughout."

11.26.oldText: "What would you have, officer? The papers were wrong."

11.27.oldText: "Yet you sell tickets from Bombay to Calcutta," Sir Francis retorted, growing heated.

11.28.oldText: "No doubt," the conductor replied; "but the passengers know they must arrange their own transportation from Kholby to Allahabad."

11.30.oldText: "Sir Francis," Mr. Fogg said quietly, "we will, if you please, look around for some means of conveyance to Allahabad."

11.31.oldText: "Mr. Fogg, this is a delay very much to your disadvantage."

11.34.oldText: "Not at all; but I knew that some obstacle or other would sooner or later come up on my route. Nothing, therefore, is lost. I have two days, which I have already gained, to sacrifice. A steamer leaves Calcutta for Hong Kong at noon on the 25th. Today is the 22nd, and we shall reach Calcutta in time."

11.38.oldText: "I shall go on foot," said Phileas Fogg.

11.39.oldText: Passepartout, who had just rejoined his master, made a sour grimace as he thought of his magnificent but all-too-flimsy Indian shoes. Happily he too had been looking around, and after a moment's hesitation he said, "Monsieur, I think I have found a means of conveyance."

11.41.oldText: "An elephant! An elephant belonging to an Indian who lives only a hundred steps from here."

11.42.oldText: "Let's go and see the elephant," replied Mr. Fogg.

11.43.oldText: They soon reached a small hut, near which, enclosed within some high palings, stood the animal in question. An Indian came out of the hut and, at their request, led them inside the enclosure. The elephant, which its owner had raised not as a beast of burden but for warlike purposes, was half-tamed. The Indian had already begun, by frequently irritating him and feeding him every three months on sugar and butter, to give him a ferocity foreign to his nature—a method often used by those who train Indian elephants for battle. Fortunately for Mr. Fogg, however, the animal's training in that direction had not gone far, and the elephant still kept his natural gentleness. Kiouni—this was the name of the beast—could no doubt travel quickly for a long time, and, in the absence of any other means of conveyance, Mr. Fogg resolved to hire him. But elephants are far from cheap in India, where they are growing scarce. The males, which alone are fit for circus shows, are much sought after, especially since only a few of them are domesticated. So when Mr. Fogg proposed to hire Kiouni, the Indian flatly refused. Mr. Fogg persisted, offering the extravagant sum of ten pounds an hour for the loan of the animal to Allahabad. Refused. Twenty pounds? Refused as well. Forty pounds? Still refused. Passepartout jumped at each new offer; but the Indian would not be tempted. And yet the offer was a tempting one, for, supposing the elephant took fifteen hours to reach Allahabad, his owner would receive no less than six hundred pounds sterling.

11.47.oldText: "What a price, good heavens!" cried Passepartout, "for an elephant."

11.48.oldText: It only remained now to find a guide, which was comparatively easy. A young Parsee with an intelligent face offered his services, which Mr. Fogg accepted, promising so generous a reward as to substantially sharpen his zeal. The elephant was led out and equipped. The Parsee, an accomplished elephant driver, covered his back with a sort of saddle-cloth and attached to each of his flanks one of those curiously uncomfortable howdahs. Phileas Fogg paid the Indian with some banknotes that he drew from the famous carpet-bag, a proceeding that seemed to wring poor Passepartout's vitals out of him. Then he offered to carry Sir Francis to Allahabad, an invitation the brigadier gratefully accepted, since one traveler more would hardly tire the gigantic beast. Provisions were purchased at Kholby, and while Sir Francis and Mr. Fogg took the howdahs on either side, Passepartout got astride the saddle-cloth between them. The Parsee perched himself on the elephant's neck, and at nine o'clock they set out from the village, the animal striding off through the dense forest of palms by the shortest route.

12.1.oldText: Phileas Fogg and Sir Francis Cromarty, plunged up to the neck in the peculiar howdahs provided for them, were horribly jolted by the swift trot of the elephant, urged on as he was by the skillful Parsee; but they endured the discomfort with true British phlegm, speaking little and scarcely able to catch a glimpse of each other. As for Passepartout, who was mounted on the beast's back and took the direct force of each jolt as the elephant strode along, he was very careful, as his master had advised, to keep his tongue from between his teeth, as it would otherwise have been bitten clean off. The worthy fellow bounced from the elephant's neck to his rump and vaulted like a clown on a springboard; yet he laughed in the middle of his bouncing, and from time to time took a piece of sugar out of his pocket and slipped it into Kiouni's trunk, who took it without slackening his regular trot in the slightest.

12.2.oldText: After two hours the guide stopped the elephant and gave him an hour to rest, during which Kiouni, after quenching his thirst at a nearby spring, set about devouring the branches and shrubs around him. Neither Sir Francis nor Mr. Fogg regretted the delay, and both climbed down with a feeling of relief. "Why, he's made of iron!" exclaimed the general, gazing admiringly at Kiouni.

12.3.oldText: "Of forged iron," replied Passepartout, as he set about preparing a hasty breakfast.

12.9.oldText: At two o'clock the guide entered a thick forest that stretched for several miles; he preferred to travel under the cover of the woods. So far they had had no unpleasant encounters, and the journey seemed on the point of being completed successfully when the elephant, growing restless, suddenly stopped.

12.11.oldText: "What's the matter?" asked Sir Francis, putting out his head.

12.12.oldText: "I don't know, officer," replied the Parsee, listening attentively to a confused murmur that came through the thick branches.

12.14.oldText: "A procession of Brahmins is coming this way. We must keep them from seeing us, if possible."

12.15.oldText: The guide untied the elephant and led him into a thicket, at the same time asking the travelers not to stir. He held himself ready to mount the animal at a moment's notice should flight become necessary; but he plainly thought the procession of the faithful would pass without noticing them amid the thick foliage, in which they were entirely hidden.

12.17.oldText: Sir Francis, recognizing the statue, whispered, "The goddess Kali; the goddess of love and death."

12.18.oldText: "Of death, perhaps," muttered Passepartout in reply, "but of love—that ugly old hag? Never!"

12.22.oldText: Sir Francis watched the procession with a sad countenance, and, turning to the guide, said, "A suttee."

12.24.oldText: Phileas Fogg had heard what Sir Francis said, and, as soon as the procession had disappeared, asked: "What is a suttee?"

12.25.oldText: "A suttee," returned the general, "is a human sacrifice, but a voluntary one. The woman you have just seen will be burned tomorrow at break of day."

12.26.oldText: "Oh, the scoundrels!" cried Passepartout, who could not hold back his indignation.

12.28.oldText: "Is that of the prince, her husband," said the guide; "an independent rajah of Bundelcund."

12.29.oldText: "Is it possible," Phileas Fogg went on, his voice betraying not the least emotion, "that these barbarous customs still exist in India, and that the English have been unable to put a stop to them?"
