12.30.oldText: "These sacrifices do not occur over the greater part of India," Sir Francis replied; "but we have no power over these savage territories, and especially here in Bundelcund. The whole district north of the Vindhias is the scene of incessant murder and pillage."

12.31.oldText: "The poor wretch!" exclaimed Passepartout, "to be burned alive!"

12.32.oldText: "Yes," returned Sir Francis, "burned alive. And if she were not, you cannot imagine the kind of treatment she would have to submit to from her relatives. They would shave off her hair, feed her on a scanty allowance of rice, treat her with contempt; she would be looked upon as an unclean creature and would die in some corner like a mangy dog. The prospect of such a frightful existence drives these poor creatures to the sacrifice much more than love or religious fanaticism. Sometimes, however, the sacrifice is really voluntary, and it takes active interference from the Government to prevent it. Several years ago, when I was living at Bombay, a young widow asked the governor for permission to be burned with her husband's body; but, as you may imagine, he refused. The woman left the town, took refuge with an independent rajah, and there carried out her self-devoted purpose."

12.33.oldText: While Sir Francis was speaking, the guide shook his head several times, and now said, "The sacrifice that will take place tomorrow at dawn is not a voluntary one."

12.35.oldText: "Everybody in Bundelcund knows about this affair."

12.36.oldText: "But the wretched creature did not seem to be putting up any resistance," observed Sir Francis.

12.37.oldText: "That was because they had stupefied her with the fumes of hemp and opium."

12.39.oldText: "To the pagoda of Pillaji, two miles from here; she will pass the night there."

12.41.oldText: "Tomorrow, at the first light of dawn."

12.42.oldText: The guide now led the elephant out of the thicket and leapt upon his neck. Just as he was about to urge Kiouni forward with a peculiar whistle, Mr. Fogg stopped him, and, turning to Sir Francis Cromarty, said, "Suppose we save this woman."

12.44.oldText: "I still have twelve hours to spare; I can devote them to that."

12.45.oldText: "Why, you are a man of heart!"

12.46.oldText: "Sometimes," replied Phileas Fogg quietly; "when I have the time."

13.1.oldText: As for Passepartout, he was ready for anything that might be proposed. His master's idea charmed him; he sensed a heart, a soul, beneath that icy exterior. He was beginning to love Phileas Fogg.

13.4.oldText: "Officers," replied the guide, "I am a Parsee, and this woman is a Parsee. Command me as you will."

13.6.oldText: "However," the guide went on, "it is certain that we shall risk not only our lives, but horrible tortures, if we are caught."

13.7.oldText: "That is foreseen," replied Mr. Fogg. "I think we must wait till night before acting."

13.9.oldText: The worthy Indian then gave some account of the victim. She was, he said, a celebrated beauty of the Parsee race and the daughter of a wealthy Bombay merchant. She had received a thoroughly English education in that city, and from her manners and intelligence would be taken for a European. Her name was Aouda. Left an orphan, she had been married against her will to the old rajah of Bundelcund; and, knowing the fate that awaited her, she had escaped, been recaptured, and condemned by the rajah's relatives—who had an interest in her death—to the sacrifice from which it seemed she could not escape.

13.10.oldText: The Parsee's narrative only strengthened Mr. Fogg and his companions in their generous plan. It was decided that the guide should steer the elephant toward the pagoda of Pillaji, which he accordingly approached as quickly as possible. Half an hour later they halted in a copse some five hundred feet from the pagoda, where they were well concealed; but they could hear the groans and cries of the fakirs distinctly.

13.12.oldText: As soon as night fell, around six o'clock, they decided to make a reconnaissance around the pagoda. The cries of the fakirs were just ceasing; the Indians were in the act of sinking into the drunkenness produced by liquid opium mingled with hemp, and it might be possible to slip between them to the temple itself.

13.17.oldText: In the background, among the trees, the pagoda of Pillaji loomed distinctly. Much to the guide's disappointment, the rajah's guards, lit by torches, were watching at the doors and marching to and fro with bare sabres; and the priests, no doubt, were watching within as well.

13.19.oldText: "It is only eight now," said the brigadier, "and these guards may go to sleep too."

13.20.oldText: "It is not impossible," replied the Parsee.

13.29.oldText: "There is nothing for us to do but go away," whispered Sir Francis.

13.30.oldText: "Nothing but go away," echoed the guide.

13.31.oldText: "Stop," said Fogg. "I am not due at Allahabad until tomorrow before noon."

13.32.oldText: "But what can you hope to do?" asked Sir Francis. "In a few hours it will be daylight, and—"

13.33.oldText: "The chance that now seems lost may turn up at the last moment."

13.34.oldText: Sir Francis would have liked to read Phileas Fogg's eyes. What was this cool Englishman thinking? Was he planning to make a rush for the young woman at the very moment of the sacrifice and boldly snatch her from her executioners?

13.37.oldText: He had begun by saying to himself, "What folly!" and then repeated, "Why not, after all? It's a chance—perhaps the only one; and with such sots!" Thinking this, he slipped, with the suppleness of a serpent, down to the lowest branches, whose tips bent almost to the ground.

13.38.oldText: The hours passed, and the lighter tints in the sky now announced the approach of day, though it was not yet light. This was the moment. The slumbering crowd stirred to life, the tambourines sounded, songs and cries went up; the hour of the sacrifice had come. The doors of the pagoda swung open, and a bright light escaped from inside, in the midst of which Mr. Fogg and Sir Francis caught sight of the victim. Having shaken off the stupor of intoxication, she seemed to be struggling to escape from her executioner. Sir Francis's heart pounded; and, convulsively seizing Mr. Fogg's hand, he found an open knife in it. Just at that moment the crowd began to move. The young woman had again fallen into a stupor brought on by the fumes of hemp, and was carried among the fakirs, who escorted her with their wild religious cries.

13.39.oldText: Phileas Fogg and his companions, mingling with the rear ranks of the crowd, followed; and in two minutes they reached the banks of the stream and stopped fifty paces from the pyre, on which the rajah's corpse still lay. In the half-light they saw the victim, quite senseless, stretched out beside her husband's body. Then a torch was brought, and the wood, heavily soaked with oil, instantly caught fire.

13.44.oldText: The resurrected rajah approached Sir Francis and Mr. Fogg, and, in an abrupt tone, said, "Let us be off!"

13.46.oldText: A moment later all four of the party had vanished into the woods, and the elephant was bearing them away at a rapid pace. But the cries and noise, and a ball that whizzed through Phileas Fogg's hat, told them the trick had been discovered.

13.47.oldText: The old rajah's body did, indeed, now appear on the burning pyre; and the priests, recovering from their terror, realized that an abduction had taken place. They rushed into the forest, followed by the soldiers, who fired a volley after the fugitives; but the latter quickly increased the distance between them, and before long found themselves out of reach of bullets and arrows.

14.0.oldText: The rash exploit had been carried off; and for an hour Passepartout laughed cheerfully at his success. Sir Francis pressed the worthy fellow's hand, and his master said, "Well done!"—which, from him, was high praise. To which Passepartout replied that all the credit of the affair belonged to Mr. Fogg. As for himself, he had only been struck with a "queer" idea; and he laughed to think that for a few moments he, Passepartout, the ex-gymnast and ex-sergeant fireman, had been the spouse of a charming woman—a venerable, embalmed rajah! As for the young Indian woman, she had been unconscious all through what had passed, and now, wrapped in a travelling-blanket, was resting in one of the howdahs.

14.1.oldText: The elephant, thanks to the skillful guidance of the Parsee, was moving quickly through the still-dim forest, and an hour after leaving the pagoda had crossed a vast plain. They halted at seven o'clock, the young woman still in a state of complete prostration. The guide made her drink a little brandy and water, but the drowsiness that stupefied her could not yet be shaken off. Sir Francis, who knew the effects of the intoxication produced by the fumes of hemp, reassured his companions about her. But he was more worried about her future fate. He told Phileas Fogg that if Aouda remained in India, she would inevitably fall back into the hands of her executioners. These fanatics were scattered throughout the county, and, despite the English police, they would recover their victim at Madras, Bombay, or Calcutta. She would only be safe by leaving India forever.

14.2.oldText: Phileas Fogg replied that he would think the matter over.

14.3.oldText: The station at Allahabad was reached about ten o'clock, and the interrupted line of railway, now resumed, would let them reach Calcutta in less than twenty-four hours. Phileas Fogg would thus be able to arrive in time to catch the steamer that left Calcutta the next day, October 25th, at noon for Hong Kong.

14.4.oldText: The young woman was placed in one of the waiting rooms of the station, while Passepartout was charged with buying for her various articles of toilet—a dress, a shawl, and some furs; for which his master gave him unlimited credit. Passepartout set off at once and found himself in the streets of Allahabad—that is, the City of God, one of the most venerated in India, built at the junction of the two sacred rivers, the Ganges and the Jumna, whose waters draw pilgrims from every part of the peninsula. The Ganges, according to the legends of the Ramayana, rises in heaven, from which, through Brahma's agency, it descends to the earth.

14.5.oldText: Passepartout made a point, as he made his purchases, of taking a good look at the city. It had once been defended by a noble fort, which has since become a state prison; its commerce has dwindled, and Passepartout looked around in vain for the kind of bazaar he used to frequent in Regent Street. At last he came upon an elderly, crusty Jew, a dealer in second-hand articles, from whom he bought a dress of Scotch stuff, a large mantle, and a fine otter-skin pelisse, for which he did not hesitate to pay seventy-five pounds. He then returned triumphantly to the station.

14.6.oldText: The influence to which the priests of Pillaji had subjected Aouda began gradually to wear off, and she became more herself, so that her fine eyes recovered all their soft Indian expression.

14.7.oldText: When the poet-king Ucaf Uddaul celebrates the charms of the queen of Ahmehnagara, he speaks like this:

14.8.oldText: "Her shining tresses, divided in two parts, encircle the harmonious contour of her white and delicate cheeks, brilliant in their glow and freshness. Her ebony brows have the form and charm of the bow of Kama, the god of love, and beneath her long silken lashes the purest reflections and a celestial light swim, as in the sacred lakes of Himalaya, in the black pupils of her great clear eyes. Her teeth, fine, even, and white, glitter between her smiling lips like dewdrops in a passion-flower's half-enveloped breast. Her delicately formed ears, her vermilion hands, her little feet, curved and tender as the lotus-bud, glitter with the brilliancy of the loveliest pearls of Ceylon, the most dazzling diamonds of Golconda. Her narrow and supple waist, which a hand may clasp around, sets forth the outline of her rounded figure and the beauty of her bosom, where youth in its flower displays the wealth of its treasures; and beneath the silken folds of her tunic she seems to have been modelled in pure silver by the godlike hand of Vicvarcarma, the immortal sculptor."

14.9.oldText: It is enough to say, without applying this poetic rhapsody to Aouda, that she was a charming woman in every European sense of the phrase. She spoke English with great purity, and the guide had not exaggerated in saying that the young Parsee had been transformed by her upbringing.

14.10.oldText: The train was about to leave Allahabad, and Mr. Fogg proceeded to pay the guide the price agreed upon for his service, and not a farthing more—which astonished Passepartout, who remembered all that his master owed to the guide's devotion. The Parsee had, in fact, risked his life in the adventure at Pillaji, and if he were caught later by the Indians, he would hardly escape their vengeance. Kiouni, too, had to be dealt with. What was to be done with the elephant, who had been so dearly bought? Phileas Fogg had already settled this question.

14.11.oldText: "Parsee," he said to the guide, "you have been helpful and devoted. I have paid you for your service, but not for your devotion. Would you like to have this elephant? He is yours."

14.13.oldText: "Your honour is giving me a fortune!" he cried.

14.14.oldText: "Take him, guide," returned Mr. Fogg, "and I shall still be your debtor."

14.15.oldText: "Good!" exclaimed Passepartout. "Take him, friend. Kiouni is a brave and faithful beast." And, going up to the elephant, he gave him several lumps of sugar, saying, "Here, Kiouni, here, here."

14.16.oldText: The elephant grunted out his satisfaction and, clasping Passepartout around the waist with his trunk, lifted him as high as his head. Passepartout, not in the least alarmed, stroked the animal, which gently set him down on the ground.

14.17.oldText: Soon after, Phileas Fogg, Sir Francis Cromarty, and Passepartout, settled in a carriage with Aouda, who had the best seat, were tearing along at full speed toward Benares. It was a run of eighty miles, covered in two hours. During the journey the young woman fully recovered her senses. How astonished she was to find herself in this carriage, on the railway, dressed in European clothes, and with travelers who were complete strangers to her! Her companions first set about reviving her fully with a little liquor, and then Sir Francis told her what had happened, dwelling on the courage with which Phileas Fogg had not hesitated to risk his life to save her, and recounting the happy outcome of the venture—the result of Passepartout's rash idea. Mr. Fogg said nothing, while Passepartout, embarrassed, kept repeating that "it wasn't worth telling."

14.18.oldText: Aouda pathetically thanked her deliverers, more with tears than with words; her fine eyes spoke her gratitude better than her lips. Then, as her thoughts drifted back to the scene of the sacrifice and recalled the dangers that still threatened her, she shuddered with terror.

14.19.oldText: Phileas Fogg understood what was going on in Aouda's mind, and offered, in order to reassure her, to escort her to Hong Kong, where she might remain safely until the affair was hushed up—an offer which she eagerly and gratefully accepted. She had, it appeared, a Parsee relation who was one of the leading merchants of Hong Kong, which is entirely an English city, though on an island off the Chinese coast.

14.20.oldText: At half-past twelve the train stopped at Benares. The Brahmin legends maintain that this city is built on the site of the ancient Casi, which, like Mahomet's tomb, once hung suspended between heaven and earth; though the Benares of today, which the Orientalists call the Athens of India, stands quite unpoetically on solid ground. Passepartout caught glimpses of its brick houses and clay huts, giving the place a desolate look as the train entered it.

14.21.oldText: Benares was Sir Francis Cromarty's destination, the troops he was rejoining being encamped some miles north of the city. He bade farewell to Phileas Fogg, wishing him every success, and expressing the hope that he would come that way again in a less original but more profitable fashion. Mr. Fogg lightly pressed him by the hand. Aouda's parting, who did not forget what she owed to Sir Francis, was warmer; and, as for Passepartout, he received a hearty handshake from the gallant general.

14.22.oldText: The railway, on leaving Benares, ran for a while along the valley of the Ganges. Through the windows of their carriage the travelers caught glimpses of the varied landscape of Behar, with its mountains clothed in green, its fields of barley, wheat, and corn, its jungles peopled with green alligators, its neat villages, and its still thickly-leaved forests. Elephants were bathing in the waters of the sacred river, and groups of Indians, despite the late season and the chilly air, were solemnly performing their pious ablutions. These were fervent Brahmins, the bitterest foes of Buddhism—their deities being Vishnu, the solar god, Shiva, the divine impersonation of natural forces, and Brahma, the supreme ruler of priests and legislators. What would these divinities think of India, anglicised as it is today, with steamers whistling and scudding along the Ganges, frightening the gulls floating on its surface, the turtles swarming along its banks, and the faithful living along its shores?

14.23.oldText: The panorama swept past their eyes like a flash, except when the steam fitfully hid it from view; the travelers could scarcely make out the fort of Chupenie, twenty miles south-west of Benares, the ancient stronghold of the rajahs of Behar; or Ghazipur and its famous rose-water factories; or the tomb of Lord Cornwallis, rising on the left bank of the Ganges; the fortified town of Buxar, or Patna, a large manufacturing and trading place, where the principal opium market of India is held; or Monghir, a more than European town, for it is as English as Manchester or Birmingham, with its iron foundries, edge-tool factories, and high chimneys puffing clouds of black smoke heavenward.

14.24.oldText: Night came on; the train rushed on at full speed, in the midst of the roaring of the tigers, bears, and wolves that fled before the locomotive; and the marvels of Bengal—Golconda, ruined Gour, Murshedabad the ancient capital, Burdwan, Hugly, and the French town of Chandernagor, where Passepartout would have been proud to see his country's flag flying—were hidden from their view in the darkness.

14.25.oldText: Calcutta was reached at seven in the morning, and the packet left for Hong Kong at noon; so Phileas Fogg had five hours before him.

14.26.oldText: According to his journal he was due in Calcutta on the 25th of October, and that was the exact date of his actual arrival. He was therefore neither behind time nor ahead of it. The two days gained between London and Bombay had been lost, as we have seen, on the journey across India. But it is not to be supposed that Phileas Fogg regretted them.

15.1.oldText: Just as he was leaving the station, a policeman came up to him and said, "Mr. Phileas Fogg?"

15.3.oldText: "Is this man your servant?" added the policeman, pointing to Passepartout.

15.5.oldText: "Be so good, both of you, as to follow me."

15.7.oldText: "May this young lady go with us?" he asked.

15.9.oldText: Mr. Fogg, Aouda, and Passepartout were conducted to a palkigahri, a sort of four-wheeled carriage drawn by two horses, in which they took their places and were driven off. No one spoke during the twenty minutes that passed before they reached their destination. They first passed through the "black town," with its narrow streets, its wretched, dirty huts, and its squalid population; then through the "European town," which offered a relief in its bright brick mansions, shaded by coconut trees and bristling with masts, where, although it was early morning, elegantly dressed horsemen and handsome equipages were passing back and forth.

15.10.oldText: The carriage stopped before a modest-looking house, which, however, did not look like a private mansion. The policeman, having asked his prisoners—for so they might truly be called—to step down, led them into a room with barred windows, and said, "You will appear before Judge Obadiah at half-past eight."

15.12.oldText: "Why, we are prisoners!" exclaimed Passepartout, dropping into a chair.

15.13.oldText: Aouda, with an emotion she tried to conceal, said to Mr. Fogg, "Sir, you must leave me to my fate! It is on my account that you are being treated this way, it is for having saved me!"

15.15.oldText: "But the steamer leaves at noon!" Passepartout observed nervously.

15.16.oldText: "We shall be on board by noon," his master replied placidly.

15.17.oldText: It was said so firmly that Passepartout could not help muttering to himself, "Parbleu, that's certain! Before noon we shall be on board." But he was by no means reassured.

15.20.oldText: "The first case," he said. Then, putting his hand to his head, he exclaimed, "Eh! This is not my wig!"

15.21.oldText: "No, your worship," answered the clerk, "it is mine."

15.22.oldText: "My dear Mr. Oysterpuff, how can a judge give a wise sentence in a clerk's wig?"

15.30.oldText: "Good," said the judge. "You have been looked for, prisoners, for two days on the trains from Bombay."

15.31.oldText: "But what are we accused of?" asked Passepartout impatiently.

15.33.oldText: "I am an English subject, sir," said Mr. Fogg, "and I have the right—"

15.36.oldText: "Very well; let the complainants come in."

15.38.oldText: "That's it," muttered Passepartout; "these are the rogues who were going to burn our young lady."

15.40.oldText: "You hear the charge?" asked the judge.

15.41.oldText: "Yes, sir," replied Mr. Fogg, consulting his watch, "and I admit it."

15.43.oldText: "I admit it, and I wish to hear these priests admit, in their turn, what they were going to do at the pagoda of Pillaji."

15.45.oldText: "Yes," cried Passepartout warmly; "at the pagoda of Pillaji, where they were about to burn their victim."

15.47.oldText: "What victim?" said Judge Obadiah. "Burn whom? In Bombay itself?"

15.49.oldText: "Certainly. We are not speaking of the pagoda of Pillaji, but of the pagoda of Malabar Hill, at Bombay."

15.50.oldText: "And as proof," added the clerk, "here are the desecrator's very shoes, which he left behind him."

15.52.oldText: "My shoes!" cried Passepartout, in his surprise letting this imprudent exclamation slip out.

15.54.oldText: Fix the detective had foreseen the advantage Passepartout's escapade gave him, and, delaying his departure for twelve hours, had consulted the priests of Malabar Hill. Knowing that the English authorities dealt very severely with this kind of offense, he promised them a handsome sum in damages and sent them on to Calcutta by the next train. Owing to the delay caused by the rescue of the young widow, Fix and the priests reached the Indian capital before Mr. Fogg and his servant, the magistrates having already been warned by a dispatch to arrest them should they arrive. Fix's disappointment when he learned that Phileas Fogg had not turned up in Calcutta can be imagined. He made up his mind that the robber had stopped somewhere along the route and taken refuge in the southern provinces. For twenty-four hours Fix watched the station with feverish anxiety; at last he was rewarded by seeing Mr. Fogg and Passepartout arrive, accompanied by a young woman whose presence he was wholly at a loss to explain. He hurried for a policeman; and this was how the party came to be arrested and brought before Judge Obadiah.

15.56.oldText: Judge Obadiah had unfortunately caught Passepartout's rash exclamation, which the poor fellow would have given the world to take back.

15.57.oldText: "The facts are admitted?" asked the judge.

15.59.oldText: "Inasmuch," the judge went on, "as the English law protects equally and sternly the religions of the Indian people, and as the man Passepartout has admitted that he violated the sacred pagoda of Malabar Hill, at Bombay, on the 20th of October, I condemn the said Passepartout to imprisonment for fifteen days and a fine of three hundred pounds."

15.60.oldText: "Three hundred pounds!" cried Passepartout, startled by the size of the sum.

15.62.oldText: "And inasmuch," the judge continued, "as it is not proved that the act was not done in connivance between the master and his servant, and as the master must in any case be held responsible for the acts of his paid servant, I condemn Phileas Fogg to a week's imprisonment and a fine of one hundred and fifty pounds."

15.64.oldText: Phileas Fogg, as self-composed as if the judgment did not concern him in the least, did not even raise his eyebrows while it was being pronounced. Just as the clerk was calling the next case, he rose and said, "I offer bail."

15.65.oldText: "You have that right," returned the judge.

15.66.oldText: Fix's blood ran cold, but he regained his composure when he heard the judge announce that the bail required for each prisoner would be one thousand pounds.

15.67.oldText: "I will pay it at once," said Mr. Fogg, taking a roll of bank-bills from the carpet-bag, which Passepartout had with him, and placing them on the clerk's desk.

15.68.oldText: "This sum will be returned to you on your release from prison," said the judge. "In the meantime, you are released on bail."

15.69.oldText: "Come!" said Phileas Fogg to his servant.

15.70.oldText: "But let them at least give me back my shoes!" cried Passepartout angrily.

15.71.oldText: "Ah, these are pretty dear shoes!" he muttered as they were handed to him. "More than a thousand pounds apiece; and besides, they pinch my feet."

15.72.oldText: Mr. Fogg, offering his arm to Aouda, then walked out, followed by the crestfallen Passepartout. Fix still nourished hopes that the robber would not, after all, leave the two thousand pounds behind him, but would decide to serve out his week in jail, and he set off on Mr. Fogg's traces. That gentleman took a carriage, and the party were soon set down on one of the quays.

15.73.oldText: The "Rangoon" was moored half a mile off in the harbor, its signal of departure hoisted at the mast-head. Eleven o'clock was striking; Mr. Fogg was an hour ahead of time. Fix saw them leave the carriage and push off in a boat for the steamer, and stamped his feet with disappointment.

15.74.oldText: "The rascal is off, after all!" he exclaimed. "Two thousand pounds sacrificed! He's as prodigal as a thief! I'll follow him to the end of the world if necessary; but at the rate he is going on, the stolen money will soon be gone."

16.0.oldText: The "Rangoon"—one of the Peninsular and Oriental Company's boats plying in the Chinese and Japanese seas—was a screw steamer, built of iron, weighing about seventeen hundred and seventy tons, with engines of four hundred horse-power. She was as fast, but not as well fitted out, as the "Mongolia," and Aouda was not as comfortably provided for on board as Phileas Fogg could have wished. However, the trip from Calcutta to Hong Kong was only some three thousand five hundred miles, taking from ten to twelve days, and the young woman was not difficult to please.

16.1.oldText: During the first days of the journey Aouda became better acquainted with her protector and kept giving evidence of her deep gratitude for what he had done. The phlegmatic gentleman listened to her—outwardly, at least—with coldness, neither his voice nor his manner betraying the slightest emotion; but he seemed always on the watch to make sure that nothing should be lacking for Aouda's comfort. He called on her regularly each day at certain hours, not so much to talk himself as to sit and hear her talk. He treated her with the strictest politeness, but with the precision of an automaton whose movements had been arranged for the purpose. Aouda did not quite know what to make of him, though Passepartout had given her some hints about his master's eccentricity and made her smile by telling her of the wager that was sending him round the world. After all, she owed Phileas Fogg her life, and she always saw him through the exalting medium of her gratitude.

16.2.oldText: Aouda confirmed the Parsee guide's account of her touching history. She did indeed belong to the highest of the native races of India. Many of the Parsee merchants have made great fortunes there by dealing in cotton; and one of them, Sir Jametsee Jeejeebhoy, was made a baronet by the English government. Aouda was a relative of this great man, and it was his cousin, Jeejeeh, whom she hoped to join at Hong Kong. Whether she would find a protector in him she could not say; but Mr. Fogg tried to calm her anxieties and assure her that everything would be mathematically—he used the very word—arranged. Aouda fastened her great eyes, "clear as the sacred lakes of the Himalaya," upon him; but the intractable Fogg, as reserved as ever, did not seem at all inclined to throw himself into this lake.

16.3.oldText: The first few days of the voyage passed prosperously, amid favorable weather and propitious winds, and they soon came in sight of the great Andaman, the principal island in the Bay of Bengal, with its picturesque Saddle Peak, two thousand four hundred feet high, looming above the waters. The steamer passed close to the shores, but the savage Papuans, who are at the lowest scale of humanity, but are not, as has been claimed, cannibals, did not make their appearance.

16.4.oldText: The panorama of the islands, as they steamed by them, was superb. Vast forests of palms, arecs, bamboo, teakwood, of the gigantic mimosa and tree-like ferns, covered the foreground, while behind them the graceful outlines of the mountains were traced against the sky; and along the coasts swarmed by the thousands the precious swallows whose nests furnish a luxurious dish for the tables of the Celestial Empire. The varied landscape offered by the Andaman Islands was soon left behind, however, and the "Rangoon" was rapidly nearing the Straits of Malacca, which gave access to the China seas.

16.5.oldText: What was detective Fix, so unluckily drawn on from country to country, doing all this time? He had managed to embark on the "Rangoon" at Calcutta without being seen by Passepartout, after leaving orders that if the warrant should arrive, it should be forwarded to him at Hong Kong; and he hoped to keep his presence concealed to the end of the voyage. It would have been difficult to explain why he was on board without rousing Passepartout's suspicions, since Passepartout believed he was still at Bombay. But necessity drove him, nevertheless, to renew his acquaintance with the worthy servant, as will be seen.

16.6.oldText: All the detective's hopes and wishes now centered on Hong Kong; for the steamer's stay at Singapore would be too brief to allow him to take any steps there. The arrest must be made at Hong Kong, or the robber would probably escape him forever. Hong Kong was the last English ground on which he would set foot; beyond it, China, Japan, and America offered Fogg an almost certain refuge. If the warrant should at last turn up at Hong Kong, Fix could arrest him and hand him over to the local police, and there would be no further trouble. But beyond Hong Kong, a simple warrant would be of no use; an extradition warrant would be needed, and that would mean delays and obstacles of which the rascal would take advantage to slip away from justice.

16.7.oldText: Fix turned these probabilities over in his mind during the long hours he spent in his cabin, and kept repeating to himself, "Now, either the warrant will be at Hong Kong, in which case I shall arrest my man, or it will not be there; and this time it is absolutely necessary that I delay his departure. I have failed at Bombay, and I have failed at Calcutta; if I fail at Hong Kong, my reputation is lost. Cost what it may, I _must_ succeed! But how shall I prevent his departure, if that should turn out to be my last resource?"

16.8.oldText: Fix made up his mind that, if the worst came to the worst, he would take Passepartout into his confidence and tell him what kind of fellow his master really was. That Passepartout was not Fogg's accomplice he was quite sure. The servant, enlightened by his disclosure and afraid of being himself implicated in the crime, would no doubt become an ally of the detective. But this method was a dangerous one, only to be used when everything else had failed. A single word from Passepartout to his master would ruin everything. The detective was therefore in a tight spot. But suddenly a new idea struck him. The presence of Aouda on the "Rangoon," in the company of Phileas Fogg, gave him new material for reflection.

16.9.oldText: Who was this woman? What combination of events had made her Fogg's traveling companion? They had evidently met somewhere between Bombay and Calcutta; but where? Had they met by chance, or had Fogg gone into the interior on purpose in quest of this charming damsel? Fix was fairly puzzled. He asked himself whether there had not been a wicked elopement; and this idea so impressed itself upon his mind that he determined to make use of the supposed intrigue. Whether the young woman were married or not, he would be able to create such difficulties for Mr. Fogg at Hong Kong that he could not escape by paying any amount of money.

16.10.oldText: But could he even wait until they reached Hong Kong? Fogg had an abominable way of jumping from one boat to another, and before anything could be done he might be fully under way again for Yokohama.

16.11.oldText: Fix decided he must warn the English authorities and signal the "Rangoon" before her arrival. This was easy to do, since the steamer stopped at Singapore, from which there is a telegraph wire to Hong Kong. Moreover, before acting more decisively, he finally resolved to question Passepartout. It would not be hard to make him talk; and, as there was no time to lose, Fix prepared to make himself known.

16.12.oldText: It was now the 30th of October, and on the following day the "Rangoon" was due at Singapore.

16.13.oldText: Fix came out of his cabin and went on deck. Passepartout was strolling up and down in the forward part of the steamer. The detective rushed forward with every appearance of extreme surprise, and exclaimed, "You here, on the 'Rangoon'?"

16.14.oldText: "What, Monsieur Fix, are you on board?" replied the genuinely astonished Passepartout, recognizing his crony of the "Mongolia." "Why, I left you at Bombay, and here you are, on the way to Hong Kong! Are you going round the world too?"

16.15.oldText: "No, no," replied Fix; "I shall stop at Hong Kong—at least for some days."

16.16.oldText: "Hum!" said Passepartout, who seemed for an instant perplexed. "But how is it I haven't seen you on board since we left Calcutta?"

16.17.oldText: "Oh, a trifle of seasickness—I've been staying in my berth. The Gulf of Bengal doesn't agree with me as well as the Indian Ocean. And how is Mr. Fogg?"

16.18.oldText: "As well and as punctual as ever, not a day behind time! But, Monsieur Fix, you don't know that we have a young lady with us."

16.19.oldText: "A young lady?" replied the detective, not seeming to understand what was said.

16.20.oldText: Passepartout thereupon recounted Aouda's history—the affair at the Bombay pagoda, the purchase of the elephant for two thousand pounds, the rescue, the arrest, and the sentence of the Calcutta court, and the release of Mr. Fogg and himself on bail. Fix, who was familiar with the latter events, seemed equally ignorant of everything Passepartout related; and the latter was charmed to find so interested a listener.

16.21.oldText: "But does your master mean to take this young woman to Europe?"

16.22.oldText: "Not at all. We are simply going to place her under the protection of one of her relatives, a rich merchant at Hong Kong."

16.23.oldText: "Nothing to be done there," Fix said to himself, hiding his disappointment. "A glass of gin, Mr. Passepartout?"

16.24.oldText: "Willingly, Monsieur Fix. We must at least have a friendly glass on board the 'Rangoon.'"

17.1.oldText: Passepartout began very seriously to wonder what strange chance was keeping Fix still on the route his master was taking. It was really worth puzzling over: why this certainly very pleasant and obliging person, whom he had first met at Suez, had then encountered on board the "Mongolia," who disembarked at Bombay (which he announced as his destination), and now turned up so unexpectedly on the "Rangoon," was following Mr. Fogg's tracks step by step. What was Fix's object? Passepartout was ready to wager his Indian shoes—which he religiously preserved—that Fix would also leave Hong Kong at the same time as they did, and probably on the same steamer.

17.2.oldText: Passepartout might have racked his brain for a century without hitting on the real object the detective had in view. He could never have imagined that Phileas Fogg was being tracked as a robber around the globe. But, as it is in human nature to try to solve every mystery, Passepartout suddenly hit upon an explanation of Fix's movements that was, in truth, far from unreasonable. Fix, he thought, could only be an agent of Mr. Fogg's friends at the Reform Club, sent to follow him and to verify that he really was going round the world as agreed.

17.3.oldText: "It's clear!" the worthy servant repeated to himself, proud of his shrewdness. "He's a spy sent to keep us in view! That isn't quite the thing either, to be spying on Mr. Fogg, who is such an honorable man! Ah, gentlemen of the Reform Club, this shall cost you dear!"

17.5.oldText: On the afternoon of Wednesday, 30th October, the "Rangoon" entered the Strait of Malacca, which separates the peninsula of that name from Sumatra. The mountainous and craggy islets blocked the beauties of this noble island from the travelers' view. The "Rangoon" weighed anchor at Singapore the next day at four a.m. to take on coal, having gained half a day on the appointed time of her arrival. Phileas Fogg noted this gain in his journal and then, accompanied by Aouda, who showed a desire for a walk on shore, disembarked.

17.6.oldText: Fix, who suspected Mr. Fogg's every movement, followed them cautiously without being seen; while Passepartout, laughing up his sleeve at Fix's maneuvers, went about his usual errands.

17.8.oldText: After a drive of two hours through the country, Aouda and Mr. Fogg returned to the town, which is a vast collection of heavy-looking, irregular houses, surrounded by charming gardens rich in tropical fruits and plants; and at ten o'clock they re-embarked, closely followed by the detective, who had kept them constantly in sight.

17.10.oldText: At eleven o'clock the "Rangoon" stood out of Singapore harbor, and in a few hours the high mountains of Malacca, with their forests inhabited by the most beautifully furred tigers in the world, were lost to view. Singapore is some thirteen hundred miles from the island of Hong Kong, which is a small English colony near the Chinese coast. Phileas Fogg hoped to make the trip in six days, so as to be in time for the steamer that was to leave on the 6th of November for Yokohama, the principal Japanese port.

17.11.oldText: The "Rangoon" had a large complement of passengers, many of whom disembarked at Singapore, among them a number of Indians, Ceylonese, Chinamen, Malays, and Portuguese, mostly second-class travelers.

17.12.oldText: The weather, which had so far been fine, changed with the last quarter of the moon. The sea rolled heavily, and the wind at intervals rose almost to a storm, but it happily blew from the south-west and so helped the steamer's progress. Whenever he could, the captain put up his sails, and under the double action of steam and sail the vessel made rapid progress along the coasts of Anam and Cochin China. Owing to the defective construction of the "Rangoon," however, unusual precautions became necessary in unfavorable weather; but the loss of time that resulted from this, while it nearly drove Passepartout out of his senses, did not seem to affect his master in the least. Passepartout blamed the captain, the engineer, and the crew, and consigned everyone connected with the ship to the land where the pepper grows. Perhaps the thought of the gas, which was remorselessly burning at his expense in Saville Row, had something to do with his hot impatience.

17.13.oldText: "You are in a great hurry, then," Fix said to him one day, "to reach Hong Kong?"

17.15.oldText: "Mr. Fogg, I suppose, is anxious to catch the steamer for Yokohama?"

17.17.oldText: "You believe in this journey around the world, then?"

17.19.oldText: "I? I don't believe a word of it."

17.20.oldText: "You're a sly dog!" said Passepartout, winking at him.

17.21.oldText: This expression rather disturbed Fix, without his knowing why. Had the Frenchman guessed his real purpose? He didn't know what to think. But how could Passepartout have found out that he was a detective? And yet, in speaking as he did, the man evidently meant more than he said.

17.23.oldText: "Mr. Fix," he said in a bantering tone, "shall we be so unfortunate as to lose you when we get to Hong Kong?"

17.24.oldText: "Why," replied Fix, a little embarrassed, "I don't know; perhaps—"

17.25.oldText: "Ah, if only you would come on with us! An agent of the Peninsular Company, you know, can't stop on the way! You were only going to Bombay, and here you are in China. America isn't far off, and from America to Europe is only a step."

17.27.oldText: "Yes, and no," returned Fix; "there's good and bad luck in such things. But you must understand that I don't travel at my own expense."

17.28.oldText: "Oh, I am quite sure of that!" cried Passepartout, laughing heartily.

17.30.oldText: Nevertheless, he kept his coolness of mind and at last resolved to deal plainly with Passepartout. If he found it impractical to arrest Fogg at Hong Kong, and if Fogg made preparations to leave that last foothold of English territory, then he, Fix, would tell Passepartout everything. Either the servant was his master's accomplice—in which case the master knew of his operations and he would fail—or else the servant knew nothing about the robbery, in which case his interest would lie in abandoning the robber.

17.31.oldText: Such was the situation between Fix and Passepartout. Meanwhile Phileas Fogg moved above them in the most majestic and unconscious indifference. He was passing methodically in his orbit around the world, indifferent to the lesser stars that gravitated around him. And yet there was nearby what the astronomers would call a disturbing star, which might have produced an agitation in this gentleman's heart. But no! the charms of Aouda failed to act, to Passepartout's great surprise; and the disturbances, if any existed, would have been harder to calculate than those of Uranus that led to the discovery of Neptune.

17.32.oldText: It was an ever-growing wonder to Passepartout, who read in Aouda's eyes the depths of her gratitude to his master. Phileas Fogg, though brave and gallant, must, he thought, be quite heartless. As for any sentiment that this journey might have awakened in him, there was clearly no trace of such a thing; while poor Passepartout lived in perpetual daydreams.

17.34.oldText: "The valves are not sufficiently charged!" he exclaimed. "We're not going. Oh, these English! If this were an American craft, we might blow up, perhaps, but at all events we would go faster!"

18.0.oldText: The weather was bad during the latter days of the voyage. The wind, obstinately holding in the north-west, blew a gale and held the steamer back. The "Rangoon" rolled heavily, and the passengers grew impatient with the long, monstrous waves that the wind raised across their path. A sort of tempest came up on the 3rd of November, the squall knocking the vessel about with fury and the waves running high. The "Rangoon" reefed all her sails, and even the rigging proved too much, whistling and shaking amid the squall. The steamer was forced to move slowly, and the captain estimated that she would reach Hong Kong twenty hours behind time, and more if the storm lasted.

18.1.oldText: Phileas Fogg gazed at the tempestuous sea—which seemed to be struggling especially to delay him—with his habitual tranquility. He never changed countenance for an instant, though a delay of twenty hours, by making him too late for the Yokohama boat, would almost inevitably mean the loss of the wager. But this man of nerve showed neither impatience nor annoyance; it was as if the storm were a part of his program and had been foreseen. Aouda was amazed to find him as calm as he had been from the first time she saw him.

18.2.oldText: Fix did not view the state of things in the same light. The storm pleased him greatly. His satisfaction would have been complete had the "Rangoon" been forced to retreat before the violence of wind and waves. Each delay filled him with hope, for it was becoming more and more probable that Fogg would have to remain some days at Hong Kong; and now the heavens themselves became his allies, with the gusts and squalls. It did not matter that they made him seasick—he took no account of this inconvenience; and, while his body was writhing under their effects, his spirit bounded with hopeful exultation.

18.3.oldText: Passepartout was enraged beyond words by the unpropitious weather. Everything had gone so well till now! Earth and sea had seemed to be at his master's service; steamers and railways obeyed him; wind and steam combined to speed his journey. Had the hour of adversity come? Passepartout was as worked up as if the twenty thousand pounds were to come out of his own pocket. The storm exasperated him, the gale made him furious, and he longed to lash the stubborn sea into obedience. Poor fellow! Fix carefully concealed his own satisfaction from him, for, had he betrayed it, Passepartout could scarcely have kept himself from personal violence.

18.4.oldText: Passepartout stayed on deck as long as the tempest lasted, unable to stay quiet below, and taking it into his head to help the ship along by lending a hand with the crew. He overwhelmed the captain, officers, and sailors—who could not help laughing at his impatience—with all sorts of questions. He wanted to know exactly how long the storm was going to last; whereupon he was referred to the barometer, which seemed to have no intention of rising. Passepartout shook it, but with no perceptible effect; for neither shaking nor maledictions could prevail on it to change its mind.

18.5.oldText: On the 4th, however, the sea grew calmer and the storm let up in violence; the wind veered to the south and was once more favorable. Passepartout cleared up with the weather. Some of the sails were unfurled, and the "Rangoon" resumed its most rapid speed. The time lost could not, however, be made up. Land was not sighted until five o'clock on the morning of the 6th; the steamer was due on the 5th. Phileas Fogg was twenty-four hours behind, and the Yokohama steamer would, of course, be missed.

18.6.oldText: The pilot came on board at six and took his place on the bridge to guide the "Rangoon" through the channels into the port of Hong Kong. Passepartout longed to ask him whether the steamer had left for Yokohama; but he dared not, for he wished to preserve the spark of hope that still remained till the last moment. He had confided his anxiety to Fix, who—the sly rascal!—tried to console him by saying that Mr. Fogg would be in time if he took the next boat; but this only put Passepartout in a passion.

18.7.oldText: Mr. Fogg, bolder than his servant, did not hesitate to approach the pilot and tranquilly ask him if he knew when a steamer would leave Hong Kong for Yokohama.

18.8.oldText: "At high tide tomorrow morning," answered the pilot.

18.9.oldText: "Ah!" said Mr. Fogg, without betraying any astonishment.

18.10.oldText: Passepartout, who heard what was said, would willingly have embraced the pilot, while Fix would have been glad to twist his neck.

18.11.oldText: "What is the steamer's name?" asked Mr. Fogg.

18.14.oldText: "Yes, sir; but they had to repair one of her boilers, and so her departure was put off till tomorrow."

18.15.oldText: "Thank you," returned Mr. Fogg, going mathematically down to the saloon.

18.16.oldText: Passepartout clasped the pilot's hand and shook it heartily in his delight, exclaiming, "Pilot, you are the best of good fellows!"

18.17.oldText: The pilot probably does not know to this day why his answers earned him this enthusiastic greeting. He remounted the bridge and guided the steamer through the flotilla of junks, tankas, and fishing boats that crowd the harbor of Hong Kong.

18.18.oldText: At one o'clock the "Rangoon" was at the quay, and the passengers were going ashore.

18.19.oldText: Chance had strangely favored Phileas Fogg, for if the "Carnatic" had not been forced to lie over for the repair of her boilers, she would have left on the 6th of November, and the passengers for Japan would have had to wait a week for the sailing of the next steamer. Mr. Fogg was, it is true, twenty-four hours behind his time; but this could not seriously imperil the rest of his tour.

18.20.oldText: The steamer that crossed the Pacific from Yokohama to San Francisco made a direct connection with the one from Hong Kong, and could not sail until the latter reached Yokohama; and if Mr. Fogg were twenty-four hours late on reaching Yokohama, this time would no doubt be easily made up on the twenty-two-day voyage across the Pacific. So he found himself about twenty-four hours behind time, thirty-five days after leaving London.

18.21.oldText: The "Carnatic" was announced to leave Hong Kong at five the next morning. Mr. Fogg had sixteen hours in which to attend to his business there, which was to deposit Aouda safely with her wealthy relative.

18.22.oldText: On landing, he conducted her to a palanquin, in which they made their way to the Club Hotel. A room was engaged for the young woman, and Mr. Fogg, after seeing that she wanted for nothing, set out in search of her cousin Jeejeeh. He instructed Passepartout to remain at the hotel until his return, so that Aouda would not be left entirely alone.

18.23.oldText: Mr. Fogg went to the Exchange, where, he had no doubt, everyone would know so wealthy and considerable a personage as the Parsee merchant. Meeting a broker, he made the inquiry, only to learn that Jeejeeh had left China two years before and, having retired from business with an immense fortune, had taken up his residence in Europe—in Holland, the broker thought, since it was with the merchants of that country that he had chiefly traded. Phileas Fogg returned to the hotel, asked for a moment's conversation with Aouda, and, without more ado, informed her that Jeejeeh was no longer at Hong Kong, but probably in Holland.

18.24.oldText: At first Aouda said nothing. She passed her hand across her forehead and reflected for a few moments. Then, in her sweet, soft voice, she said, "What ought I to do, Mr. Fogg?"

18.25.oldText: "It is very simple," replied the gentleman. "Go on to Europe."

18.27.oldText: "You do not intrude, nor do you in the least embarrass my project. Passepartout!"

18.29.oldText: "Go to the 'Carnatic,' and engage three cabins."

18.30.oldText: Passepartout, delighted that the young woman, who had been so gracious to him, was going to continue the journey with them, went off at a brisk pace to obey his master's order.

19.0.oldText: Hong Kong is an island that came into the possession of the English by the Treaty of Nankin, after the war of 1842; and the colonizing genius of the English has built on it an important city and an excellent port. The island lies at the mouth of the Canton River and is separated by about sixty miles from the Portuguese town of Macao on the opposite coast. Hong Kong has beaten Macao in the struggle for the Chinese trade, and now the greater part of the transportation of Chinese goods finds its depot at the former place. Docks, hospitals, wharves, a Gothic cathedral, a government house, macadamised streets, give to Hong Kong the appearance of a town in Kent or Surrey transferred by some strange magic to the antipodes.

19.1.oldText: Passepartout wandered, with his hands in his pockets, toward the Victoria port, gazing as he went at the curious palanquins and other modes of conveyance, and at the groups of Chinese, Japanese, and Europeans who passed back and forth in the streets. Hong Kong seemed to him not unlike Bombay, Calcutta, and Singapore, since, like them, it showed everywhere the evidence of English supremacy. At the Victoria port he found a confused mass of ships of all nations: English, French, American, and Dutch, men-of-war and trading vessels, Japanese and Chinese junks, sempas, tankas, and flower-boats, which made up so many floating parterres. Passepartout noticed in the crowd a number of natives who looked very old and were dressed in yellow. On going into a barber's to get a shave, he learned that these ancient men were all at least eighty years old, at which age they are permitted to wear yellow, which is the Imperial color. Passepartout, without exactly knowing why, thought this very funny.

19.2.oldText: On reaching the quay where they were to embark on the "Carnatic," he was not surprised to find Fix walking up and down. The detective seemed very much disturbed and disappointed.

19.3.oldText: "This is bad," muttered Passepartout, "for the gentlemen of the Reform Club!" He accosted Fix with a merry smile, as if he had not noticed that gentleman's chagrin. The detective did, indeed, have good reason to rail against the bad luck that pursued him. The warrant had not come! It was certainly on the way, but just as certainly it could not now reach Hong Kong for several days; and, this being the last English territory on Mr. Fogg's route, the robber would escape unless he could manage to detain him.

19.4.oldText: "Well, Monsieur Fix," said Passepartout, "have you decided to come with us as far as America?"

19.5.oldText: "Yes," returned Fix through his set teeth.

19.6.oldText: "Good!" exclaimed Passepartout, laughing heartily. "I knew you couldn't bring yourself to part with us. Come and engage your berth."

19.7.oldText: They went into the steamer office and secured cabins for four. The clerk, as he gave them the tickets, informed them that, the repairs on the "Carnatic" having been completed, the steamer would leave that very evening, and not next morning, as had been announced.

19.8.oldText: "That will suit my master all the better," said Passepartout. "I will go and let him know."

19.9.oldText: Fix now decided to make a bold move; he resolved to tell Passepartout everything. It seemed to be the only possible means of keeping Phileas Fogg several days longer at Hong Kong. He accordingly invited his companion into a tavern that caught his eye on the quay. On entering, they found themselves in a large, handsomely decorated room, at the end of which was a large camp-bed furnished with cushions. Several persons lay on this bed in a deep sleep. At the small tables arranged about the room some thirty customers were drinking English beer, porter, gin, and brandy, while smoking long red clay pipes stuffed with little balls of opium mingled with essence of rose. From time to time one of the smokers, overcome by the narcotic, would slip under the table, whereupon the waiters, taking him by the head and feet, carried him over and laid him on the bed. The bed already supported twenty of these stupefied sots.

19.10.oldText: Fix and Passepartout saw that they were in a smoking-house haunted by those wretched, cadaverous, idiotic creatures to whom the English merchants sell each year the miserable drug called opium, to the amount of one million four hundred thousand pounds—thousands devoted to one of the most despicable vices that afflict humanity! The Chinese government has tried in vain to deal with the evil through stringent laws. It passed gradually from the rich, to whom it was at first exclusively reserved, to the lower classes, and then its ravages could not be stopped. Opium is smoked everywhere, at all times, by men and women, in the Celestial Empire; and, once accustomed to it, the victims cannot do without it, except by enduring horrible bodily contortions and agonies. A great smoker can smoke as many as eight pipes a day; but he dies in five years. It was in one of these dens that Fix and Passepartout, in search of a friendly glass, found themselves. Passepartout had no money, but willingly accepted Fix's invitation in the hope of returning the favor at some future time.

19.11.oldText: They ordered two bottles of port, to which the Frenchman did ample justice, while Fix watched him with close attention. They chatted about the journey, and Passepartout was especially merry at the idea that Fix was going to continue it with them. When the bottles were empty, however, he rose to go and tell his master about the change in the time of the "Carnatic's" sailing.

19.12.oldText: Fix caught him by the arm and said, "Wait a moment."

19.14.oldText: "I want to have a serious talk with you."

19.15.oldText: "A serious talk!" cried Passepartout, draining the little wine that was left in the bottom of his glass. "Well, we'll talk about it tomorrow; I haven't time now."

19.16.oldText: "Stay! What I have to say concerns your master."

19.17.oldText: At this, Passepartout looked attentively at his companion. Fix's face seemed to have a peculiar expression. He sat back down.

19.18.oldText: "What is it that you have to say?"

19.19.oldText: Fix placed his hand on Passepartout's arm, and, lowering his voice, said, "You have guessed who I am?"

19.21.oldText: "Then I'm going to tell you everything—"

19.22.oldText: "Now that I know everything, my friend! Ah! that's very good. But go on, go on. First, though, let me tell you that those gentlemen have put themselves to a useless expense."

19.23.oldText: "Useless!" said Fix. "You speak confidently. It's clear you don't know how large the sum is."

19.24.oldText: "Of course I do," returned Passepartout. "Twenty thousand pounds."

19.25.oldText: "Fifty-five thousand!" answered Fix, pressing his companion's hand.

19.26.oldText: "What!" cried the Frenchman. "Has Monsieur Fogg dared—fifty-five thousand pounds! Well, there's all the more reason for not losing an instant," he continued, getting up hastily.

19.27.oldText: Fix pushed Passepartout back into his chair and went on: "Fifty-five thousand pounds; and if I succeed, I get two thousand pounds. If you'll help me, I'll let you have five hundred of them."

19.28.oldText: "Help you?" cried Passepartout, whose eyes were standing wide open.

19.29.oldText: "Yes; help me keep Mr. Fogg here for two or three days."

19.30.oldText: "Why, what are you saying? Those gentlemen are not satisfied with following my master and suspecting his honor; they must also try to put obstacles in his way! I blush for them!"

19.32.oldText: "I mean that it is a piece of shameful trickery. They might as well waylay Mr. Fogg and put his money in their pockets!"

19.33.oldText: "That's just what we count on doing."

19.34.oldText: "It's a conspiracy, then," cried Passepartout, who grew more and more excited as the liquor mounted to his head—for he drank without noticing it. "A real conspiracy! And gentlemen, too. Bah!"

19.36.oldText: "Members of the Reform Club!" Passepartout went on. "You must know, Monsieur Fix, that my master is an honest man, and that when he makes a wager, he tries to win it fairly!"

19.37.oldText: "But who do you think I am?" asked Fix, looking at him intently.

19.38.oldText: "Parbleu! An agent of the members of the Reform Club, sent out here to interrupt my master's journey. But, though I found you out some time ago, I've taken good care to say nothing about it to Mr. Fogg."

19.40.oldText: "Nothing," replied Passepartout, again draining his glass.

19.41.oldText: The detective passed his hand across his forehead, hesitating before speaking again. What should he do? Passepartout's mistake seemed sincere, but it made his design more difficult. It was clear that the servant was not the master's accomplice, as Fix had been inclined to suspect.

19.42.oldText: "Well," said the detective to himself, "as he is not an accomplice, he will help me."

19.43.oldText: He had no time to lose: Fogg must be detained at Hong Kong, so he resolved to make a clean breast of it.

19.44.oldText: "Listen to me," said Fix abruptly. "I am not, as you think, an agent of the members of the Reform Club—"

19.45.oldText: "Bah!" retorted Passepartout, with an air of raillery.

19.46.oldText: "I am a police detective, sent out here by the London office."

19.48.oldText: "I will prove it. Here is my commission."

19.49.oldText: Passepartout was speechless with astonishment when Fix displayed this document, whose genuineness could not be doubted.

19.50.oldText: "Mr. Fogg's wager," Fix went on, "is only a pretext, of which you and the gentlemen of the Reform Club are dupes. He had a motive for securing your innocent complicity."

19.52.oldText: "Listen. On the 28th of last September a robbery of fifty-five thousand pounds was committed at the Bank of England by a person whose description was fortunately obtained. Here is his description; it matches exactly that of Mr. Phileas Fogg."

19.53.oldText: "What nonsense!" cried Passepartout, striking the table with his fist. "My master is the most honorable of men!"

19.54.oldText: "How can you tell? You know scarcely anything about him. You entered his service the day he left; and he left on a foolish pretext, without trunks, and carrying a large sum in banknotes. And yet you are bold enough to maintain that he is an honest man!"

19.55.oldText: "Yes, yes," the poor fellow repeated mechanically.

19.56.oldText: "Would you like to be arrested as his accomplice?"

19.57.oldText: Passepartout, overcome by what he had heard, held his head between his hands and did not dare to look at the detective. Phileas Fogg, the savior of Aouda, that brave and generous man, a robber! And yet how many presumptions there were against him! Passepartout tried to reject the suspicions that forced themselves upon his mind; he did not want to believe his master was guilty.

19.58.oldText: "Well, what do you want of me?" he said at last, with an effort.

19.59.oldText: "See here," replied Fix; "I have tracked Mr. Fogg to this place, but I have not yet received the warrant of arrest for which I sent to London. You must help me keep him here in Hong Kong—"

19.61.oldText: "I will share with you the two thousand pounds reward offered by the Bank of England."

19.62.oldText: "Never!" replied Passepartout, who tried to rise but fell back, exhausted in mind and body.

19.63.oldText: "Mr. Fix," he stammered, "even should what you say be true—if my master is really the robber you are seeking—which I deny—I have been, and am, in his service; I have seen his generosity and goodness; and I will never betray him—not for all the gold in the world. I come from a village where they don't eat that kind of bread!"

19.66.oldText: "Consider that I've said nothing," said Fix; "and let us drink."

19.68.oldText: Passepartout felt himself yielding more and more to the effects of the liquor. Fix, seeing that he must at all hazards be separated from his master, wished to overcome him entirely. Some pipes full of opium lay on the table. Fix slipped one into Passepartout's hand. He took it, put it between his lips, lit it, drew several puffs, and his head, growing heavy under the influence of the narcotic, fell upon the table.

19.69.oldText: "At last!" said Fix, seeing Passepartout unconscious. "Mr. Fogg will not be informed of the 'Carnatic's' departure; and, if he is, he will have to go without this cursed Frenchman!"

19.70.oldText: And, after paying his bill, Fix left the tavern.

20.1.oldText: "It is in the interest of my journey—part of my programme."

20.2.oldText: Their purchases made, they returned to the hotel, where they dined at a lavishly served table-d'hôte. Afterward Aouda, shaking hands with her protector in the English fashion, retired to her room to rest. Mr. Fogg spent the rest of the evening absorbed in the Times and the Illustrated London News.

20.3.oldText: If he had been capable of being surprised by anything, it would have been the failure of his servant to return by bedtime. But, knowing that the steamer would not leave for Yokohama until the next morning, he did not trouble himself about it. When Passepartout failed to answer his master's bell the following morning, Mr. Fogg betrayed not the slightest annoyance. He simply picked up his carpet-bag, called for Aouda, and sent for a palanquin.

20.4.oldText: It was now eight o'clock; at half-past nine, when the tide would be high, the "Carnatic" was due to leave the harbor. Mr. Fogg and Aouda climbed into the palanquin, their luggage following behind on a wheelbarrow, and half an hour later they stepped onto the quay from which they were to embark. There Mr. Fogg learned that the "Carnatic" had sailed the previous evening. He had expected to find both the steamer and his servant waiting, and was forced to give up both; yet no sign of disappointment appeared on his face, and he merely remarked to Aouda, "It is an accident, madam; nothing more."

20.5.oldText: At that moment a man who had been watching him closely approached. It was Fix, who bowed and addressed Mr. Fogg: "Weren't you, like me, sir, a passenger on the 'Rangoon' that arrived yesterday?"

20.6.oldText: "I was, sir," replied Mr. Fogg coldly. "But I have not the honor—"

20.7.oldText: "Forgive me; I thought I would find your servant here."

20.8.oldText: "Do you know where he is, sir?" Aouda asked anxiously.

20.9.oldText: "What!" Fix exclaimed, feigning surprise. "Isn't he with you?"

20.10.oldText: "No," said Aouda. "He has not appeared since yesterday. Could he have boarded the 'Carnatic' without us?"

20.11.oldText: "Without you, madam?" answered the detective. "Excuse me, but did you intend to sail on the 'Carnatic'?"

20.13.oldText: "So did I, madam, and I am terribly disappointed. The 'Carnatic', her repairs completed, left Hong Kong twelve hours ahead of schedule without giving any notice; and now we must wait a week for another steamer."

20.14.oldText: As he said "a week," Fix felt his heart leap with joy. Fogg held up in Hong Kong for a week! There would be time for the warrant to arrive, and fortune was at last smiling on the representative of the law. His horror can be imagined when he heard Mr. Fogg say, in his unruffled voice, "But there are other vessels besides the 'Carnatic,' it seems to me, in the harbor of Hong Kong."

20.17.oldText: "Is your honor looking for a boat?"

20.18.oldText: "Do you have a boat ready to sail?"

20.19.oldText: "Yes, your honor; a pilot-boat—No. 43—the best in the harbor."

20.21.oldText: "Eight to nine knots an hour. Would you like to look at her?"

20.23.oldText: "Your honor will be pleased with her. Is it for a sea outing?"

20.26.oldText: "Yes. Will you agree to take me to Yokohama?"

20.27.oldText: The sailor leaned on the railing, opened his eyes wide, and said, "Is your honor joking?"

20.28.oldText: "No. I have missed the 'Carnatic,' and I must reach Yokohama by the 14th at the latest to catch the boat for San Francisco."

20.29.oldText: "I am sorry," said the sailor, "but it's impossible."

20.30.oldText: "I offer you a hundred pounds a day, and an additional reward of two hundred pounds if I reach Yokohama on time."

20.34.oldText: Mr. Fogg turned to Aouda and asked, "You would not be afraid, would you, madam?"

20.35.oldText: "Not with you, Mr. Fogg," she answered.

20.38.oldText: "Well, your honor," he replied, "I couldn't risk myself, my men, or my little boat of barely twenty tons on so long a voyage at this time of year. Besides, we couldn't reach Yokohama in time, for it's sixteen hundred and sixty miles from Hong Kong."

20.42.oldText: "But," added the pilot, "it might be arranged another way."

20.45.oldText: "By going to Nagasaki, at the southern tip of Japan, or even to Shanghai, which is only eight hundred miles from here. By heading for Shanghai we wouldn't have to sail wide of the Chinese coast, which would be a great advantage, since the currents run northward and would help us."

20.46.oldText: "Pilot," said Mr. Fogg, "I must catch the American steamer at Yokohama, not at Shanghai or Nagasaki."

20.47.oldText: "Why not?" returned the pilot. "The San Francisco steamer does not start from Yokohama. It calls at Yokohama and Nagasaki, but it sails from Shanghai."

20.50.oldText: "And when does the boat leave Shanghai?"

20.51.oldText: "On the 11th, at seven in the evening. We have, then, four days ahead of us—that is, ninety-six hours; and in that time, with good luck and a south-west wind, and a calm sea, we could make those eight hundred miles to Shanghai."

20.53.oldText: "In an hour; as soon as provisions could be got on board and the sails set."

20.54.oldText: "It's a bargain. Are you the master of the boat?"

20.57.oldText: "If it would not inconvenience your honor—"

20.58.oldText: "Here are two hundred pounds on account." Then, turning to Fix, Phileas Fogg added, "sir, if you would like to take advantage—"

20.59.oldText: "Thank you, sir; I was about to ask the favor."

20.60.oldText: "Very well. In half an hour we shall go on board."

20.61.oldText: "But poor Passepartout?" Aouda pressed, deeply troubled by the servant's disappearance.

20.62.oldText: "I shall do all I can to find him," Phileas Fogg replied.

20.63.oldText: While Fix, in a feverish, anxious state, headed for the pilot-boat, the others made their way to the police-station at Hong Kong. There Phileas Fogg gave Passepartout's description and left a sum of money to be spent searching for him. After the same formalities had been carried out at the French consulate, and after the palanquin had stopped at the hotel to collect the luggage that had been sent back there, they returned to the wharf.

20.64.oldText: It was now three o'clock; and pilot-boat No. 43, with its crew on board and its provisions stowed away, was ready to depart.

20.65.oldText: The "Tankadere" was a neat little craft of twenty tons, as gracefully built as a racing yacht. Her gleaming copper sheathing, her galvanized iron-work, her deck white as ivory, all bore witness to the pride John Bunsby took in keeping her presentable. Her two masts leaned a little backward; she carried a brigantine, foresail, storm-jib, and standing-jib, and was well rigged for running before the wind; and she seemed capable of brisk speed, which, in fact, she had already proved by winning several prizes in pilot-boat races. The crew of the "Tankadere" was made up of John Bunsby, the master, and four tough sailors familiar with the Chinese seas. John Bunsby himself, a man of about forty-five, vigorous, sun-burned, with a lively expression in his eye and an energetic, self-reliant countenance, would have inspired confidence in the most timid passenger.

20.67.oldText: "I am sorry to have nothing better to offer you," said Mr. Fogg to Fix, who bowed without replying.

20.68.oldText: The detective felt something close to humiliation at benefiting from Mr. Fogg's kindness.

20.69.oldText: "It's certain," he thought, "that scoundrel as he is, he is a polite one!"

20.71.oldText: John Bunsby, the master, at last gave the order to depart, and the "Tankadere," catching the wind in her brigantine, foresail, and standing-jib, bounded briskly forward over the waves.

21.1.oldText: It would clearly have been to the master's advantage to carry his passengers all the way to Yokohama, since he was paid a fixed sum per day; but to attempt such a voyage would have been reckless, and it was imprudent even to try for Shanghai. Still, John Bunsby believed in the "Tankadere," which rode the waves like a seagull; and perhaps he was not mistaken.

21.2.oldText: Late in the day they passed through the capricious channels of Hong Kong, and the "Tankadere," driven by favourable winds, behaved admirably.

21.3.oldText: "I do not need, pilot," said Phileas Fogg, once they had reached the open sea, "to tell you to use every ounce of speed."

21.4.oldText: "Trust me, your honour. We are carrying every sail the wind will allow. The topmasts would add nothing, and are only used when entering port."

21.5.oldText: "It's your trade, not mine, pilot, and I leave it to you."

21.9.oldText: Fix, seated in the bow, gave himself up to his thoughts. He kept apart from his fellow-passengers, knowing Mr. Fogg's preference for silence; besides, he was not eager to talk to the man whose favours he had accepted. He was also thinking about what came next. It seemed certain that Fogg would not stop at Yokohama, but would board the next boat for San Francisco; and the vast expanse of America would guarantee him impunity and safety. Fogg's plan struck Fix as the simplest in the world. Instead of sailing directly from England to the United States, like a common criminal, he had crossed three-quarters of the globe, so as to reach the American continent more surely; and there, after shaking off the police, he would quietly enjoy himself on the fortune stolen from the bank. But once in the United States, what would he, Fix, do? Should he abandon the chase? No, a hundred times no! Until he had secured the extradition warrant, he would not let his man out of sight for an hour. It was his duty, and he would see it through. At least there was one thing to be thankful for: Passepartout was not with his master; and it was crucial, after the confidences Fix had let slip to him, that the servant should never get a chance to speak with his master.

21.10.oldText: Phileas Fogg was also thinking about Passepartout, who had so strangely disappeared. Looking at the matter from every angle, it did not seem impossible to him that, by some mistake, the man might have boarded the "Carnatic" at the last minute; and this was Aouda's opinion too, who deeply regretted the loss of the good fellow to whom she owed so much. They might still find him at Yokohama; for if the "Carnatic" had carried him there, it would be easy to check whether he had been on board.

21.11.oldText: A brisk breeze rose around ten o'clock; but, though it might have been prudent to reef the sails, the pilot, after carefully examining the sky, left the rigging as it was. The "Tankadere" handled the sails admirably, as she drew a great deal of water, and everything was prepared for high speed in case of a gale.

21.13.oldText: At sunrise the next day, which was the 8th of November, the boat had covered more than a hundred miles. The log showed an average speed of between eight and nine miles an hour. The "Tankadere" still carried all sail, and was achieving her greatest possible speed. If the wind held, the odds were in her favour. During the day she kept close to the coast, where the currents were favourable; the coastline, irregular in profile and visible at times through the gaps in the haze, was at most five miles distant. The sea was less rough, since the wind was coming off the land — a lucky circumstance for the boat, which, given her small tonnage, would have suffered in a heavy swell.

21.15.oldText: Mr. Fogg and Aouda, happily unaffected by the rough sea, ate with good appetite, and Fix was invited to share their meal, which he accepted with secret chagrin. To travel at this man's expense and live off his provisions was distasteful to him. Still, he had to eat, and so he ate.

21.16.oldText: When the meal was over, he drew Mr. Fogg aside and said, "Sir" — this "sir" scorched his lips, and he had to hold himself back from grabbing this "gentleman" by the collar — "sir, you have been very kind to give me a passage on this boat. But although my means will not let me spend as freely as you do, I must insist on paying my share —"

21.17.oldText: "Let us not speak of it, sir," replied Mr. Fogg.

21.19.oldText: "No, sir," repeated Mr. Fogg in a tone that left no room for reply. "This is part of my general expenses."

21.23.oldText: The "Tankadere" entered the Straits of Fo-Kien, which separate the island of Formosa from the Chinese coast, in the small hours of the night, and crossed the Tropic of Cancer. The sea was very rough in the straits, full of eddies formed by the counter-currents, and the choppy waves broke her course, while it became very difficult to stand on deck.

21.25.oldText: John Bunsby studied the threatening sky for a long time, muttering between his teeth. At last he said in a low voice to Mr. Fogg, "Shall I speak plainly to your honour?"

21.27.oldText: "Well, we are going to have a squall."

21.28.oldText: "Is the wind from the north or the south?" Mr. Fogg asked quietly.

21.29.oldText: "From the south. Look! A typhoon is rising."

21.30.oldText: "Glad it's a typhoon from the south, since it will carry us forward."

21.31.oldText: "Oh, if you take it that way," said John Bunsby, "I've nothing more to say." John Bunsby's hunch was right. At a less advanced season of the year the typhoon, according to a famous meteorologist, would have passed by like a glowing cascade of electric flame; but in the winter equinox, there was every reason to fear it would burst on them with great violence.

21.34.oldText: The storm of rain and wind came down on them around eight o'clock. With only its scrap of sail, the "Tankadere" was lifted like a feather by a wind whose violence can scarcely be described. To compare her speed to four times that of a locomotive at full steam would be an understatement.

21.35.oldText: The boat ran northward like this all day long, carried by monstrous waves, fortunately always keeping a speed equal to theirs. Twenty times she seemed about to be swallowed by these mountains of water rising behind her; but the pilot's skilful handling saved her. The passengers were often drenched in spray, but they bore it stoically. Fix cursed under his breath, no doubt; but Aouda, her eyes fixed on her protector, whose coolness astonished her, proved herself worthy of him, and weathered the storm bravely. As for Phileas Fogg, it seemed as if the typhoon were a scheduled part of his programme.

21.36.oldText: Up to this point the "Tankadere" had held her northward course; but towards evening the wind, shifting three points, blew down from the north-west. The boat, now lying in the trough of the waves, shook and rolled terribly; the sea struck her with fearful violence. At night the tempest grew worse. John Bunsby watched the dark coming on and the storm rising with grim foreboding. He thought a while, then asked his crew whether it was not time to slacken speed. After a consultation he went up to Mr. Fogg and said, "I think, your honour, we should do well to make for one of the ports along the coast."

21.39.oldText: "I know of only one," answered Mr. Fogg calmly.

21.42.oldText: At first the pilot did not seem to grasp it; he could scarcely take in such determination and tenacity. Then he cried, "Well — yes! Your honour is right. To Shanghai!"

21.43.oldText: So the "Tankadere" kept steadily on her northward course.

21.45.oldText: Day returned. The tempest still raged with undiminished fury; but the wind had now shifted back to the south-east.
