It was a favourable change, and the "Tankadere" again surged forward over this mountainous sea, though the waves crossed one another and sent shocks and counter-shocks through her that would have broken a less solidly built craft. From time to time the coast was visible through the broken mist, but no other vessel was in sight. The "Tankadere" was alone on the sea.

21.48.oldText: The wind grew decidedly calmer, and happily the sea fell with it. Every sail was now hoisted, and by noon the "Tankadere" was within forty-five miles of Shanghai. Six hours remained to cover that distance. Everyone on board feared it could not be done, and every man — Phileas Fogg excepted, no doubt — felt his heart pound with impatience. The boat would have to keep up an average of nine miles an hour, and the wind was slackening every moment! It was a fickle breeze, coming off the coast, and after it passed the sea grew smooth. Still, the "Tankadere" was so light, and her fine sails caught the inconstant breezes so well, that, with the help of the currents, John Bunsby found himself at six o'clock no more than ten miles from the mouth of the Shanghai River. Shanghai itself lies at least twelve miles up the river. At seven they were still three miles from Shanghai. The pilot swore an angry oath; the two-hundred-pound reward was clearly slipping out of his grasp. He looked at Mr. Fogg. Mr. Fogg was perfectly calm; and yet at this moment his whole fortune was on the line.

21.50.oldText: "Confound her!" cried John Bunsby, shoving back the rudder with a desperate jerk.

21.52.oldText: A small brass cannon stood on the forward deck of the "Tankadere," used for signalling in the fogs. It was loaded to the muzzle; but just as the pilot was about to touch a red-hot coal to the touchhole, Mr. Fogg said, "Hoist your flag!"

21.53.oldText: The flag was run up at half-mast, this being the signal of distress, in the hope that the American steamer, seeing it, would alter her course a little, so as to come to the pilot-boat's aid.

21.54.oldText: "Fire!" said Mr. Fogg. And the boom of the little cannon rang out through the air.

22.0.oldText: The "Carnatic," setting sail from Hong Kong at half-past six on the 7th of November, headed at full steam towards Japan. She carried a large cargo and a cabin crowded with passengers. Two staterooms aft, however, stood empty — the ones engaged by Phileas Fogg.

22.2.oldText: It was Passepartout; and what had happened to him was this. Shortly after Fix left the opium den, two waiters had lifted the unconscious Passepartout and carried him to the bed reserved for the smokers. Three hours later, haunted even in his dreams by one fixed idea, the poor fellow woke and struggled against the stupefying grip of the narcotic. The thought of an unfulfilled duty shook off his torpor, and he hurried out of this den of drunkenness. Staggering and propping himself up against the walls, falling and crawling back to his feet, driven on irresistibly by a kind of instinct, he kept crying out, "The 'Carnatic!' the 'Carnatic!'"

22.3.oldText: The steamer lay puffing alongside the quay, on the point of departure. Passepartout had only a few steps to take; and, throwing himself onto the gangplank, he crossed it and collapsed unconscious on the deck just as the "Carnatic" was casting off. Several sailors, evidently used to this kind of scene, carried the poor Frenchman down to the second cabin, and Passepartout did not wake until they were a hundred and fifty miles out from China. So he found himself the next morning on the deck of the "Carnatic," eagerly breathing in the invigorating sea air. The fresh breeze sobered him. He began to gather his wits — a difficult task — but at last he remembered the events of the previous evening: Fix's confession, the opium house.

22.4.oldText: "Clearly," he said to himself, "I was abominably drunk! What will Mr. Fogg say? At least I haven't missed the steamer, which is the main thing."

22.5.oldText: Then, thinking of Fix: "As for that scoundrel, I hope we've seen the last of him, and that he didn't dare, as he threatened, to follow us on board the 'Carnatic.' A detective on the trail of Mr. Fogg, accused of robbing the Bank of England! Nonsense! Mr. Fogg is no more a robber than I am a murderer."

22.6.oldText: Should he tell his master about Fix's real mission? Would it be right to reveal the part the detective was playing? Or would it be better to wait until Mr. Fogg reached London again, and then let him know that an agent of the metropolitan police had been chasing him around the world, and have a good laugh over it? No doubt about it; or at least, it was worth thinking through. The first thing to do was to find Mr. Fogg and apologise for his strange behaviour.

22.7.oldText: Passepartout got up and made his way, as best he could against the rolling of the steamer, to the after-deck. He saw no one resembling either his master or Aouda. "All right!" he muttered. "Aouda isn't up yet, and Mr. Fogg has probably found some whist partners."

22.8.oldText: He went down to the saloon. Mr. Fogg was not there. Passepartout only had to ask the purser for the number of his master's stateroom. The purser replied that he knew of no passenger by the name of Fogg.

22.9.oldText: "I beg your pardon," said Passepartout, pressing on. "He is a tall gentleman, quiet, not very talkative, and has with him a young lady —"

22.10.oldText: "There is no young lady on board," the purser interrupted. "Here is the passenger list; see for yourself."

22.11.oldText: Passepartout scanned the list, but his master's name was not on it. All at once an idea struck him.

22.16.oldText: For an instant Passepartout had feared he was on the wrong boat; but although he really was on the "Carnatic," his master was not.

22.17.oldText: He dropped onto a seat as if struck by lightning. Now he saw it all. He remembered that the time of sailing had been changed, that he was supposed to have told his master, and that he had failed to do so. It was his fault, then, that Mr. Fogg and Aouda had missed the steamer. Yes — but it was even more the fault of the traitor who, in order to separate him from his master and detain Mr. Fogg at Hong Kong, had tricked him into getting drunk! He saw the detective's scheme clearly now; and at this moment Mr. Fogg was surely ruined, his wager lost, and perhaps Passepartout himself arrested and jailed! At this thought Passepartout tore at his hair. Ah, if Fix ever fell within his reach, what a reckoning there would be!

22.19.oldText: At dawn on the 13th the "Carnatic" entered the port of Yokohama. This is a major port of call in the Pacific, where all the mail-steamers, and those carrying travellers between North America, China, Japan, and the Oriental islands, put in. It is situated in the Bay of Yeddo, only a short distance from that second capital of the Japanese Empire and seat of the Tycoon — the civil Emperor, before the Mikado, the spiritual Emperor, absorbed his office into his own. The "Carnatic" anchored at the quay near the custom-house, amid a crowd of ships flying the flags of every nation.

22.20.oldText: Passepartout went timidly ashore on this so curious territory of the Sons of the Sun. He had nothing better to do than let chance be his guide and wander aimlessly through the streets of Yokohama. He found himself at first in a thoroughly European quarter, the houses with low fronts and adorned with verandas under which he caught glimpses of neat porticoes. This quarter, with its streets, squares, docks, and warehouses, filled all the space between the "promontory of the Treaty" and the river. Here, as in Hong Kong and Calcutta, swarmed mixed crowds of every race: Americans and English, Chinese and Dutch, mostly merchants ready to buy or sell anything. The Frenchman felt himself as much alone among them as if he had dropped into a tribe of Hottentots.

22.21.oldText: He had at least one resource: to call on the French and English consuls at Yokohama for help. But he balked at telling the story of his adventures, bound up as it was with his master's; and before doing so, he resolved to exhaust every other option. As chance did not favour him in the European quarter, he ventured into the part inhabited by the native Japanese, determined, if need be, to push on as far as Yeddo.

22.23.oldText: The streets were crowded with people. Priests were passing in processions, beating their dreary tambourines; police and custom-house officers in pointed hats lacquered hard and wearing two sabres at their waists; soldiers in blue cotton with white stripes and carrying guns; the Mikado's guards, wrapped in silken doublets, hauberks, and chain mail; and numbers of military men of every rank — for the military profession is as honoured in Japan as it is despised in China — went to and fro in groups and pairs. Passepartout also saw begging friars, long-robed pilgrims, and ordinary civilians, with their stiff, jet-black hair, big heads, long torsos, slim legs, short stature, and complexions ranging from copper to chalky white, but never the yellow of the Chinese, from whom the Japanese differ markedly. He did not fail to notice the curious vehicles — carriages and palanquins, sail-rigged barrows, and litters of bamboo; nor the women, whom he found not particularly handsome, taking little steps on their little feet, wearing canvas shoes, straw sandals, or clogs of carved wood, and showing narrow-looking eyes, flat chests, teeth fashionably blackened, and gowns crossed with silken scarves tied in a huge knot behind — an ornament which modern Parisian ladies seem to have borrowed from the women of Japan.

22.24.oldText: Passepartout wandered for several hours through this motley crowd, peering into the windows of the rich and curious shops, the jewellery houses gleaming with quaint Japanese ornaments, the restaurants hung with streamers and banners (which he was not allowed to enter), the tea-houses where the fragrant brew was drunk along with "saki," a liquor distilled from fermented rice, and the comfortable smoking-houses where they were puffing not opium — which is almost unknown in Japan — but a very fine, stringy tobacco. He went on until he found himself in the fields, in the middle of vast rice plantations. There he saw dazzling camellias in full bloom, with flowers giving off their last colours and scents, not on bushes but on trees; and within bamboo enclosures, cherry, plum, and apple trees that the Japanese cultivate more for their blossoms than their fruit, and that grotesquely grinning scarecrows protected from sparrows, pigeons, ravens, and other voracious birds. Large eagles perched in the branches of the cedars; herons stood solemnly on one leg amid the foliage of the weeping willows; and on every side were crows, ducks, hawks, wild birds, and a multitude of cranes — which the Japanese hold sacred, taking them as symbols of long life and prosperity.

22.29.oldText: The good fellow had taken care, of course, to eat as hearty a breakfast as possible before leaving the "Carnatic"; but after walking about all day, the demands of hunger were becoming impossible to ignore. He noticed that the butchers' stalls held neither mutton, goat, nor pork; and, knowing too that it is a sacrilege to kill cattle, which are kept solely for farming, he concluded that meat was anything but plentiful in Yokohama — and he was not wrong. For lack of butcher's meat, he could have wished for a haunch of wild boar or venison, a partridge, some quail, or some game or fish, which, along with rice, the Japanese eat almost exclusively. But he had to keep his spirits up and put off the meal he longed for until the next morning. Night came, and Passepartout went back into the native quarter, where he wandered through streets lit by lanterns of many colours, watching the dancers performing skilful steps and leaps, and the astrologers standing out in the open with their telescopes. Then he came to the harbour, lit up by the resin torches of the fishermen plying their trade from their boats.

22.30.oldText: At last the streets grew quiet, and the patrol — whose officers, in their splendid costumes and surrounded by their retinues, struck Passepartout as looking like ambassadors — replaced the bustling crowd. Every time a company passed, Passepartout chuckled and said to himself: "Good! another Japanese embassy off to Europe!"

23.1.oldText: It was perhaps a little early in the morning to mount a concert, and the audience, prematurely roused from their sleep, might well decline to pay their entertainer with coins bearing the Mikado's features. So Passepartout decided to wait several hours; and as he sauntered along, it occurred to him that he was rather too well dressed for a wandering artist. The idea struck him to swap his clothes for outfits more in keeping with his plan; and in the bargain he might get a little money to satisfy the immediate pangs of hunger. With his mind made up, it only remained to put it into action.

23.3.oldText: "Good!" he thought. "I'll pretend I'm at Carnival!"

23.4.oldText: His first concern, having thus been "Japanesed," was to step into a modest-looking tea-house, where, over half a bird and a little rice, he breakfasted like a man for whom dinner was still an open question.

23.5.oldText: "Now," he thought, when he had eaten his fill, "I mustn't lose my head. I can't trade this outfit for one even more Japanese. I must figure out how to leave this country of the Sun — of which I shall not keep the most delightful memories — as quickly as possible."

23.10.oldText: "The United States!" said Passepartout. "That's just what I want!"

23.12.oldText: This was the Honourable William Batulcar's establishment. That gentleman was a kind of Barnum, the director of a troupe of mountebanks, jugglers, clowns, acrobats, tightrope-walkers, and gymnasts who, according to the placard, was giving his last performances before leaving the Empire of the Sun for the States of the Union.

23.14.oldText: "What do you want?" he said to Passepartout, taking him at first for a native.

23.15.oldText: "Would you like a servant, sir?" asked Passepartout.

23.16.oldText: "A servant!" cried Mr. Batulcar, stroking the thick grey beard that hung from his chin. "I already have two who are obedient and faithful, who have never left me, and who serve me for their food — and here they are," he added, holding out his two robust arms, ridged with veins as thick as the strings of a bass-viol.

23.17.oldText: "So I can be of no use to you?"

23.19.oldText: "Confound it! I should so like to cross the Pacific with you!"

23.20.oldText: "Ah!" said the Honourable Mr. Batulcar. "You are no more Japanese than I am a monkey! Why are you dressed up like that?"

23.22.oldText: "True enough. You're a Frenchman, aren't you?"

23.24.oldText: "Then you must know how to pull faces?"

23.25.oldText: "Well," replied Passepartout, a little put out that his nationality should prompt the question, "we Frenchmen do know how to pull faces, that's true — but no better than the Americans do."

23.26.oldText: "True. Well, if I can't take you on as a servant, I can take you on as a clown. You see, my friend, in France they show off foreign clowns, and in foreign parts they show off French ones."

23.31.oldText: "Yes," replied Passepartout, who had once been in the habit of singing in the streets.

23.32.oldText: "But can you sing standing on your head, with a top spinning on your left foot and a sabre balanced on your right?"

23.33.oldText: "Hmph! I think so," answered Passepartout, recalling the exercises of his younger days.

23.34.oldText: "Well, that's enough," said the Honourable William Batulcar.

23.37.oldText: The performance, so noisily advertised by the Honourable Mr. Batulcar, was to begin at three o'clock, and soon the deafening instruments of a Japanese orchestra were sounding at the door. Passepartout, though he had had no chance to study or rehearse a part, was assigned to lend his sturdy shoulders to the great act of the "human pyramid," performed by the Long Noses of the god Tingou. This "great attraction" was to close the show.

23.38.oldText: Before three o'clock the large shed was invaded by spectators — Europeans and natives, Chinese and Japanese, men, women, and children — who rushed onto the narrow benches and into the boxes facing the stage. The musicians took their place inside, and were vigorously playing on their gongs, tam-tams, flutes, clappers, tambourines, and huge drums.

23.44.oldText: For the closing scene, a "human pyramid" had been announced, in which fifty Long Noses were to represent the Car of Juggernaut. But instead of forming a pyramid by climbing on one another's shoulders, the performers were to arrange themselves on top of the noses. As it happened, the performer who had until now formed the base of the Car had left the troupe, and since strength and skill were all that was needed for the role, Passepartout had been picked to take his place.

23.47.oldText: It was Passepartout's fault. Abandoning his position, vaulting the footlights without the help of his wings, and clambering up to the right-hand gallery, he fell at the feet of one of the spectators, crying, "Ah, my master! my master!"

23.50.oldText: "Very well; then let us go to the steamer, young man!"

23.51.oldText: Mr. Fogg, Aouda, and Passepartout passed through the lobby of the theatre to the outside, where they ran into the Honourable Mr. Batulcar, furious with rage. He demanded damages for the "breakage" of the pyramid; and Phileas Fogg pacified him by handing him a fistful of banknotes.

24.0.oldText: What happened when the pilot-boat came in sight of Shanghai is easily guessed. The signals made by the "Tankadere" had been spotted by the captain of the Yokohama steamer, who, seeing the flag at half-mast, had turned his course towards the little craft. Phileas Fogg, after paying John Bunsby the agreed price for his passage, and rewarding the good fellow with an extra sum of five hundred and fifty pounds, climbed aboard the steamer with Aouda and Fix; and they set off at once for Nagasaki and Yokohama.

24.1.oldText: They reached their destination on the morning of the 14th of November. Phileas Fogg lost no time in going aboard the "Carnatic," where he learned, to Aouda's great delight — and perhaps to his own, though he betrayed no emotion — that Passepartout, a Frenchman, had indeed arrived on her the day before.

24.2.oldText: The San Francisco steamer was due to leave that very evening, and it became necessary to find Passepartout, if at all possible, without delay. Mr. Fogg appealed in vain to the French and English consuls, and after wandering the streets a long time, began to despair of finding his missing servant. Chance, or perhaps a kind of premonition, at last led him into the Honourable Mr. Batulcar's theatre. He would certainly not have recognised Passepartout in the eccentric mountebank's costume; but the latter, lying on his back, spotted his master up in the gallery. He could not help giving a start, which so shifted the angle of his nose that the "pyramid" came tumbling down on the stage.

24.3.oldText: All this Passepartout learned from Aouda, who recounted to him what had happened on the voyage from Hong Kong to Shanghai aboard the "Tankadere," in the company of one Mr. Fix.

24.6.oldText: The steamer about to depart from Yokohama for San Francisco belonged to the Pacific Mail Steamship Company and was called the "General Grant." She was a large paddle-wheel steamer of two thousand five hundred tons; well equipped and very fast. The massive walking-beam rose and fell above the deck; at one end a piston-rod worked up and down; at the other a connecting-rod, transforming the straight-line motion into a circular one, drove directly the shaft of the paddles. The "General Grant" was rigged with three masts, giving her a large sail area, and so giving substantial help to her steam power. By making twelve miles an hour, she would cross the ocean in twenty-one days. Phileas Fogg was therefore justified in hoping that he would reach San Francisco on the 2nd of December, New York on the 11th, and London on the 20th — gaining several hours on the fatal date of the 21st of December.

24.7.oldText: There was a full complement of passengers on board: among them English, many Americans, a large number of coolies on their way to California, and several East Indian officers spending their leave on a tour of the world. Nothing of consequence happened during the voyage; the steamer, carried steadily on her large paddles, rolled little, and the "Pacific" almost lived up to its name. Mr. Fogg was as calm and taciturn as ever. His young companion felt herself drawn to him by ties other than gratitude; his silent but generous nature impressed her more than she realised; and it was almost unconsciously that she gave way to feelings which seemed not to affect her protector in the least. Aouda took the keenest interest in his plans, and grew impatient at any incident that threatened to delay the journey.

24.8.oldText: She often chatted with Passepartout, who could not fail to see the state of the lady's heart; and being the most loyal of servants, he was tireless in his praise of Phileas Fogg's honesty, generosity, and devotion. He took pains to ease Aouda's doubts about a successful outcome to the journey, telling her that the most difficult part of it was past, that they were now beyond the fantastic countries of Japan and China and well on their way back to civilised places. A railway train from San Francisco to New York, and a transatlantic steamer from New York to Liverpool, would surely bring them to the end of this impossible journey round the world within the agreed time.

24.9.oldText: On the ninth day after leaving Yokohama, Phileas Fogg had covered exactly half the globe. On the 23rd of November the "General Grant" crossed the one hundred and eightieth meridian, putting them at the antipodes of London. Mr. Fogg had, it is true, used up fifty-two of the eighty days in which he was to complete the tour, and only twenty-eight were left. But although he was only halfway in terms of difference in meridians, he had really covered two-thirds of the whole journey; for he had been forced to make long detours from London to Aden, from Aden to Bombay, from Calcutta to Singapore, and from Singapore to Yokohama. Had he been able to follow the fiftieth parallel — London's latitude — straight through, the whole distance would have been only about twelve thousand miles; whereas by the haphazard means of travel available, he would have to cover twenty-six thousand, of which on the 23rd of November he had already done seventeen thousand five hundred. And now the course ran straight, and Fix was no longer there to throw obstacles in their way!

24.10.oldText: It also happened, on the 23rd of November, that Passepartout made a joyful discovery. As will be remembered, the stubborn fellow had insisted on keeping his famous family watch on London time, and on treating that of the countries he passed through as quite false and unreliable. Now, on this day, although he had not moved the hands, he found that his watch agreed exactly with the ship's chronometers. His triumph was hilarious. He would have loved to know what Fix would say if he were on board!

24.11.oldText: "That rogue told me all sorts of stories," Passepartout kept saying, "about meridians, the sun, the moon! The moon, indeed — moonshine, more like! If you listened to that lot, a fine sort of time you'd be keeping! I always knew the sun would one day fall in line with my watch!"

24.12.oldText: Passepartout did not know that, if the face of his watch had been divided into twenty-four hours, like the Italian clocks, he would have had no reason for triumph; for the hands of his watch would then, instead of indicating nine o'clock in the morning as they did, have shown nine o'clock in the evening — that is, the twenty-first hour after midnight, precisely the difference between London time and that of the one hundred and eightieth meridian. But even if Fix had been able to explain this purely physical fact, Passepartout would not have accepted it — even if he had understood it. What was more, had the detective been aboard at that moment, Passepartout would have taken him up on a very different subject, and in a very different manner.

24.14.oldText: He was, in fact, on board the "General Grant."

24.15.oldText: On reaching Yokohama, the detective, leaving Mr. Fogg, whom he expected to run into again during the day, had gone straight to the English consulate, where he at last found the warrant of arrest. It had followed him from Bombay, and had come by way of the "Carnatic," on which steamer he himself was supposed to have been. Fix's disappointment can be imagined when he realised that the warrant was now useless. Mr. Fogg had left English ground, and it would now be necessary to obtain his extradition!

24.16.oldText: "Well," thought Fix after a moment's anger, "my warrant is no good here, but it will be in England. The rogue clearly means to return home, thinking he has shaken off the police. Good! I'll follow him across the Atlantic. As for the money — heaven grant there may be some left! But the fellow has already spent more than five thousand pounds on travel, rewards, trials, bail, elephants, and all sorts of expenses. Still, after all, the Bank is rich!"

24.17.oldText: His course decided, he went aboard the "General Grant," and was there when Mr. Fogg and Aouda arrived. To his utter amazement, he recognised Passepartout in spite of his theatrical disguise. He quickly hid himself in his cabin to avoid an awkward scene, and hoped — given the number of passengers — to remain unnoticed by Mr. Fogg's servant.

24.19.oldText: When Passepartout had finished, he felt relieved and comforted. Fix got up in a somewhat rumpled condition, and, looking at his adversary, said coldly, "Are you done?"

24.21.oldText: "Then let me have a word with you."

24.24.oldText: Passepartout seemed disarmed by Fix's coolness, for he quietly followed him, and they sat down apart from the other passengers.

24.25.oldText: "You've given me a thrashing," said Fix. "Good — I expected it. Now listen. Up to now I have been Mr. Fogg's adversary. From this moment I am in his game."

24.26.oldText: "Aha!" cried Passepartout. "You are convinced he is an honest man?"

24.27.oldText: "No," Fix replied coldly. "I take him for a rascal. Hush! Don't budge, and let me finish. As long as Mr. Fogg was on English ground, it was in my interest to hold him there until my warrant of arrest arrived. I did everything I could to detain him. I set the Bombay priests on his trail, I got you drunk at Hong Kong, I separated you from him, and I made him miss the Yokohama steamer."

24.29.oldText: "Now," Fix went on, "Mr. Fogg seems to be heading back to England. Well, I'll follow him there. But from here on, I'll do as much to clear obstacles out of his way as I've done up to now to put them in it. I've changed my game, you see, simply because it suits me to change it. Your interest is the same as mine; for it is only in England that you'll find out whether you are in the service of a criminal or an honest man."

24.32.oldText: "Friends? — no," replied Passepartout. "Allies, perhaps. But at the slightest sign of treachery, I'll wring your neck for you."

24.34.oldText: Eleven days later, on the 3rd of December, the "General Grant" entered the bay of the Golden Gate, and reached San Francisco.

25.1.oldText: Passepartout, in his joy at having reached the American continent at last, thought he would mark the moment by executing a perilous somersault in fine style; but, landing on some worm-eaten planks, he crashed straight through them. Embarrassed by the way in which he thus "set foot" on the New World, he let out a loud cry, which so frightened the countless cormorants and pelicans that perch on these movable quays that they flew off in a noisy panic.

25.2.oldText: Mr. Fogg, on reaching the shore, set about finding out at what hour the first train left for New York, and learned it was at six o'clock that evening; he therefore had a whole day to spend in the Californian capital. Hiring a carriage at a charge of three dollars, he and Aouda got in, while Passepartout climbed up beside the driver, and they set off for the International Hotel.

25.6.oldText: The ground floor of the hotel was taken up by a large bar — a sort of restaurant freely open to any passer-by — who could help himself to dried beef, oyster soup, biscuits, and cheese without taking out his purse. Payment was made only for the ale, porter, or sherry that was drunk. This seemed "very American" to Passepartout. The hotel's refreshment rooms were comfortable, and Mr. Fogg and Aouda, settling themselves at a table, were generously served on tiny plates by Negroes of the darkest hue.

25.8.oldText: He had not gone two hundred steps, however, when, "by the greatest chance in the world," he ran into Fix. The detective seemed entirely taken aback. What! Had Mr. Fogg and he crossed the Pacific together without ever meeting on the steamer? At least Fix said he was honoured to set eyes again on the gentleman to whom he owed so much; and, since his business was calling him back to Europe, he would be delighted to continue the journey in such pleasant company.

25.13.oldText: It was a political meeting; or so Fix guessed, who said to Mr. Fogg, "Perhaps we'd better not mix with the crowd. There may be danger in it."

25.14.oldText: "Yes," replied Mr. Fogg; "and blows, even political ones, are still blows."

25.18.oldText: "It is obviously a meeting," said Fix, "and its subject must be a heated one. I shouldn't be surprised if it were about the 'Alabama,' even though that question is settled."

25.20.oldText: "At any rate, there are two champions squaring off — the Honourable Mr. Camerfield and the Honourable Mr. Mandiboy."

25.21.oldText: Aouda, leaning on Mr. Fogg's arm, watched the tumultuous scene with surprise, while Fix asked a man near him what it was all about. Before the man could reply, a fresh agitation broke out; hurrahs and excited shouts went up; the staffs of the banners began to be used as offensive weapons; and fists flew in every direction. Blows were exchanged from the tops of the carriages and omnibuses trapped in the crowd. Boots and shoes went whirling through the air, and Mr. Fogg thought he even heard the crack of revolvers mingling with the din; the rout pushed up towards the stairway, and spilled over onto the lowest step. One of the parties had clearly been driven back; but the bystanders could not tell whether Mandiboy or Camerfield had gained the upper hand.

25.22.oldText: "It would be wise for us to retreat," said Fix, who was anxious that Mr. Fogg should come to no harm — at least until they were back in London. "If there's any question about England in all this, and we were recognised, I fear it would go badly for us."

25.24.oldText: He did not finish the sentence; for at that moment a terrific hubbub broke out on the terrace behind the flight of steps where they stood, and there were frantic shouts of, "Hurrah for Mandiboy! Hip, hip, hurrah!"

25.25.oldText: It was a band of voters coming to the rescue of their allies, attacking the Camerfield forces on the flank. Mr. Fogg, Aouda, and Fix found themselves caught between two fires; it was too late to escape. The torrent of men, armed with loaded canes and sticks, was unstoppable. Phileas Fogg and Fix were roughly buffeted as they tried to protect their fair companion; Fogg, as cool as ever, tried to defend himself with the weapons nature has placed at the end of every Englishman's arm — but in vain. A big brawny fellow with a red beard, a flushed face, and broad shoulders, who seemed to be the leader of the band, raised his clenched fist to strike Mr. Fogg and would have dealt him a crushing blow had not Fix rushed in and taken it in his place. An enormous bruise instantly appeared under the detective's silk hat, which was completely caved in.

25.26.oldText: "Yankee!" exclaimed Mr. Fogg, casting a contemptuous look at the ruffian.

25.27.oldText: "Englishman!" the other shot back. "We shall meet again!"

25.33.oldText: "Thanks," said Mr. Fogg to the detective, once they were clear of the crowd.

25.34.oldText: "No thanks needed," replied Fix; "but let's get going."

25.39.oldText: Dinner over, the coach that was to take the travellers and their luggage to the station drew up at the door. As he was getting in, Mr. Fogg said to Fix, "You haven't seen this Colonel Proctor again?"

25.41.oldText: "I shall come back to America to find him," said Phileas Fogg calmly. "It would not be right for an Englishman to allow himself to be treated like that without striking back."

25.43.oldText: At a quarter to six the travellers reached the station, and found the train ready to depart. As he was about to board, Mr. Fogg called a porter and said to him: "My friend, was there not some kind of trouble today in San Francisco?"

25.44.oldText: "It was a political meeting, sir," replied the porter.

25.45.oldText: "But I thought there was a great deal of disturbance in the streets."

25.46.oldText: "It was only a meeting called for an election."

25.47.oldText: "The election of a commander-in-chief, no doubt?" asked Mr. Fogg.

25.48.oldText: "No, sir; of a justice of the peace."

26.0.oldText: "From ocean to ocean" — so the Americans say; and these four words form the general name of the "great trunk line" that crosses the entire width of the United States. The Pacific Railroad is, however, really split into two distinct lines: the Central Pacific, between San Francisco and Ogden, and the Union Pacific, between Ogden and Omaha. Five main lines link Omaha with New York.

26.8.oldText: The train left Oakland station at six o'clock. It was already night, cold and cheerless, the sky overcast with clouds that seemed to threaten snow. The train did not move quickly; counting the stops, it averaged no more than twenty miles an hour, which was, however, fast enough to bring it to Omaha within its scheduled time.

26.9.oldText: There was little conversation in the car, and soon many of the passengers were overcome by sleep. Passepartout found himself seated beside the detective; but he did not speak to him. After the recent events, their relations had grown somewhat cold; there could no longer be any mutual sympathy or intimacy between them. Fix's manner had not changed; but Passepartout was very reserved, and ready to strangle his former friend at the slightest provocation.

26.11.oldText: At eight o'clock a steward entered the car and announced that it was time to go to bed; and within a few minutes the car was transformed into a dormitory. The backs of the seats were tilted down, neatly packed bedsteads were rolled out by an ingenious mechanism, berths were improvised in a moment, and each traveller soon had a comfortable bed at his disposal, screened from prying eyes by thick curtains. The sheets were clean and the pillows soft. It only remained to lie down and sleep — which everyone did — while the train sped on across the State of California.

26.13.oldText: The train, on leaving Sacramento, and passing the junction, Roclin, Auburn, and Colfax, entered the range of the Sierra Nevada. 'Cisco was reached at seven in the morning; and an hour later the dormitory was turned back into an ordinary car, and the travellers could take in the picturesque beauties of the mountain region they were steaming through. The track wound in and out among the passes, now hugging the mountainsides, now suspended over precipices, dodging sharp angles with bold curves, plunging into narrow defiles that seemed to have no outlet. The locomotive, its great funnel throwing a weird light, with its shrill bell and its cow-catcher thrust out like a spur, mingled its shrieks and bellowings with the noise of torrents and cascades, and wove its smoke through the branches of the gigantic pines.

26.15.oldText: The train entered the State of Nevada through the Carson Valley around nine o'clock, still moving north-east; and at noon it reached Reno, where there was a twenty-minute stop for breakfast.

26.18.oldText: This is exactly what happened to the train Mr. Fogg was on. Around twelve o'clock a herd of ten or twelve thousand head of buffalo blocked the track. The locomotive, slowing down, tried to clear a way with its cow-catcher; but the mass of animals was too great. The buffaloes plodded along at a calm pace, letting out a deafening bellow now and then. There was no point in interrupting them, for once they have set off in a particular direction, nothing can slow them down or turn them; it is a torrent of living flesh which no dam could hold back.

26.21.oldText: "What a country!" he cried. "Mere cattle stop the trains and parade across as if they weren't blocking traffic! Parbleu! I should like to know if Mr. Fogg foresaw _this_ mishap in his programme! And here's an engineer who doesn't even dare drive the locomotive into the herd!"

26.24.oldText: It was eight o'clock when the train passed through the defiles of the Humboldt Range, and half-past nine when it entered Utah, the region of the Great Salt Lake — the strange colony of the Mormons.

27.1.oldText: Around nine o'clock, Passepartout stepped out onto the platform for some air. The weather was cold, the sky grey, but it was not snowing. The sun's disc, swollen by the mist, looked like an enormous ring of gold, and Passepartout was amusing himself by calculating its value in pounds sterling, when he was distracted from this interesting study by a strange-looking figure who appeared on the platform.

27.3.oldText: Passepartout went up and read one of these notices, which announced that Elder William Hitch, a Mormon missionary, taking advantage of his presence on train No. 48, would give a lecture on Mormonism in car No. 117 from eleven to twelve o'clock; and that he invited all who wished to be instructed in the mysteries of the religion of the "Latter Day Saints" to attend.

27.4.oldText: "I'll go," Passepartout said to himself. He knew nothing of Mormonism beyond the practice of polygamy, which is its foundation.

27.6.oldText: At the appointed hour Elder William Hitch rose, and, in an irritated voice, as if he had already been contradicted, said, "I tell you that Joe Smith is a martyr, that his brother Hiram is a martyr, and that the persecutions of the United States Government against the prophets will also make a martyr of Brigham Young. Who dares to say the contrary?"

27.7.oldText: No one ventured to contradict the missionary, whose worked-up tone made a curious contrast with his naturally calm face. No doubt his anger sprang from the hardships the Mormons were actually being put through. The government had just succeeded, with some difficulty, in bringing these independent fanatics under its rule. It had made itself master of Utah, and subjected that territory to the laws of the Union, after imprisoning Brigham Young on charges of rebellion and polygamy. The prophet's disciples had since redoubled their efforts, and resisted, at least in words, the authority of Congress. Elder Hitch, as you see, was trying to win converts even on the railway trains.

27.9.oldText: Several listeners, not finding the missionary's narrative very interesting, left the car at this point; but Elder Hitch, going on with his lecture, told how Smith, junior, with his father, two brothers, and a few disciples, founded the church of the "Latter Day Saints," which, taken up not only in America but also in England, Norway, Sweden, and Germany, counts many artisans as well as men in the liberal professions among its members; how a colony was established in Ohio, a temple built there at a cost of two hundred thousand dollars, and a town founded at Kirkland; how Smith became an enterprising banker, and received from a humble mummy-showman a papyrus scroll written by Abraham and several famous Egyptians.

27.10.oldText: The Elder's story became somewhat tedious, and his audience gradually thinned until it was down to twenty passengers. But this did not faze the enthusiast, who went on to the story of Joseph Smith's bankruptcy in 1837, and how his ruined creditors gave him a coat of tar and feathers; his reappearance several years later, more honoured and more honourable than ever, at Independence, Missouri, as the head of a flourishing colony of three thousand disciples; and his pursuit from there by outraged Gentiles and retreat into the Far West.

27.13.oldText: "And this," added Elder William Hitch, "this is why the jealousy of Congress has been turned against us! Why have the soldiers of the Union invaded the soil of Utah? Why has Brigham Young, our chief, been thrown into prison, in contempt of all justice? Shall we yield to force? Never! Driven from Vermont, driven from Illinois, driven from Ohio, driven from Missouri, driven from Utah, we shall yet find some independent territory on which to pitch our tents. And you, my brother," the Elder went on, fixing his angry eyes on his last listener, "will you not pitch yours there too, under the shadow of our flag?"

27.14.oldText: "No!" answered Passepartout boldly, getting up in his turn and leaving the car, abandoning the Elder to preach to empty seats.

27.18.oldText: The train reached Ogden at two o'clock, where it stopped for six hours; Mr. Fogg and his party had time to pay a visit to Salt Lake City, connected with Ogden by a branch line; and they spent two hours in this strikingly American town, built on the pattern of other cities of the Union, like a chequerboard, "with the sombre sadness of right angles," as Victor Hugo puts it. The founder of the City of the Saints could not escape that taste for symmetry which marks the Anglo-Saxons. In this strange country, where the people are certainly not up to the level of their institutions, everything is done "squarely" — cities, houses, and follies.

27.19.oldText: At three o'clock, then, the travellers were walking about the streets of the town set between the banks of the Jordan and the spurs of the Wahsatch Range. They saw few or no churches, but the prophet's mansion, the court-house, and the arsenal — blue-brick houses with verandas and porches, surrounded by gardens bordered with acacias, palms, and locusts. A clay-and-pebble wall, built in 1853, encircled the town; and in the main street were the market and several hotels decked out with pavilions. The place did not seem heavily populated. The streets were almost deserted, except near the temple, which they only reached after passing through several quarters surrounded by palisades. There were many women, easily explained by the "peculiar institution" of the Mormons; but it should not be supposed that every Mormon is a polygamist. They are free to marry or not, as they please; but it is worth noting that it is mainly the female citizens of Utah who are eager to marry, since, according to the Mormon religion, single women are not admitted to its highest joys. These poor creatures seemed neither well off nor happy. Some — the better off, no doubt — wore short, open black silk dresses under a hood or modest shawl; others were dressed in Indian fashion.

27.20.oldText: Passepartout could not look without a certain alarm at these women charged, in groups, with making a single Mormon happy. His common sense pitied above all the husband. It struck him as a terrible thing to have to guide so many wives at once through the ups and downs of life, and to conduct them, as it were, in a body into the Mormon paradise, with the prospect of seeing them in the company of the glorious Smith — who was doubtless the chief ornament of that delightful place — for all eternity. He felt decidedly put off such a vocation, and imagined — perhaps mistakenly — that the fair ones of Salt Lake City were casting rather alarming glances at his person. Happily, his stay there was brief. At four the party were back at the station, took their places in the train, and the whistle sounded for departure. Just at the moment, however, when the locomotive wheels began to turn, cries of "Stop! stop!" were heard.

27.24.oldText: "One, sir," replied the Mormon, raising his arms to heaven — "one, and that was enough!"

28.3.oldText: At ten o'clock at night the train stopped at Fort Bridger station, and twenty minutes later it entered Wyoming Territory, following the valley of Bitter Creek all the way. The next day, the 7th of December, they stopped for a quarter of an hour at Green River station. Snow had fallen heavily during the night, but, mixed with rain, it had half melted and did not slow their progress. The bad weather, however, worried Passepartout; for a build-up of snow, by clogging the wheels of the cars, would surely have been fatal to Mr. Fogg's tour.

28.4.oldText: "What an idea!" he said to himself. "Why did my master make this journey in winter? Couldn't he have waited for the good season to improve his chances?"

28.8.oldText: "That Proctor on this train!" cried Fix. "Well, set your mind at ease, madam; before he settles with Mr. Fogg, he has to settle with me! It seems to me I was the more insulted of the two."

28.9.oldText: "And besides," added Passepartout, "I'll take charge of him, colonel or no colonel."

28.10.oldText: "Mr. Fix," Aouda went on, "Mr. Fogg will let no one avenge him. He said he would come back to America to find this man. If he were to spot Colonel Proctor, we could not prevent a collision that might have terrible consequences. He must not see him."

28.11.oldText: "You are right, madam," replied Fix; "a meeting between them might ruin everything. Whether he won or lost, Mr. Fogg would be delayed, and —"

28.12.oldText: "And," added Passepartout, "that would play right into the hands of the gentlemen of the Reform Club. In four days we shall be in New York. Well, if my master does not leave this car for those four days, we may hope that chance will not put him face to face with this confounded American. We must, if at all possible, keep him from going outside."

28.13.oldText: The conversation broke off. Mr. Fogg had just woken up and was looking out of the window. Soon afterwards Passepartout, without being overheard by his master or Aouda, whispered to the detective, "Would you really fight for him?"

28.14.oldText: "I would do anything," Fix replied, in a tone that betrayed an iron will, "to get him back to Europe alive!"

28.16.oldText: Was there any way of keeping Mr. Fogg in the car, to avoid a meeting between him and the colonel? It ought not to be difficult, since the gentleman was naturally sedentary and not very curious. The detective, at least, seemed to have hit on a way; for after a few moments he said to Mr. Fogg, "These are long, slow hours, sir, that we are spending on the railway."

28.18.oldText: "You used to play whist," Fix went on, "on the steamers."

28.19.oldText: "Yes; but it would be difficult to do so here. I have neither cards nor partners."

28.20.oldText: "Oh, we can easily buy some cards, for they are sold on all the American trains. And as for partners, if madam plays —"

28.21.oldText: "Certainly, sir," Aouda replied quickly; "I know whist. It is part of an English education."

28.22.oldText: "And I myself have some pretensions to playing a good game. Well, here are three of us, and a dummy —"

28.23.oldText: "As you please, sir," replied Phileas Fogg, heartily glad to take up his favourite pastime again, even on the railway.

28.26.oldText: "Now," Passepartout thought, "we've got him. He won't budge."

28.31.oldText: Aouda and Fix feared that Mr. Fogg might take it into his head to get out; but the gentleman contented himself with saying to his servant, "See what is the matter."

28.34.oldText: Passepartout, joining the group, heard the signalman say, "No! you can't go on. The bridge at Medicine Bow is shaky, and would not bear the weight of the train."

28.35.oldText: This was a suspension bridge thrown over some rapids, about a mile from where they now were. According to the signalman, it was in ruinous condition, several of the iron wires being broken; and it was impossible to risk crossing. He was in no way exaggerating the bridge's condition. It can be taken for granted that, reckless as Americans usually are, when they are cautious there is good reason for it.

28.37.oldText: "Hum!" cried Colonel Proctor; "but we're not going to stay here, I suppose, and take root in the snow?"

28.38.oldText: "Colonel," replied the conductor, "we have telegraphed to Omaha for a train, but it is unlikely to reach Medicine Bow in less than six hours."

28.40.oldText: "Certainly," returned the conductor; "besides, it will take us that long to reach Medicine Bow on foot."

28.41.oldText: "But it's only a mile from here," said one of the passengers.

28.42.oldText: "Yes, but it's on the other side of the river."

28.43.oldText: "And can't we cross it in a boat?" asked the colonel.

28.44.oldText: "Impossible. The creek is swollen by the rains. It's a rapid, and we shall have to make a ten-mile detour to the north to find a ford."

28.45.oldText: The colonel let out a volley of oaths, cursing the railway company and the conductor; and Passepartout, who was furious, was not unwilling to make common cause with him. Here was an obstacle that all his master's banknotes could not remove.

28.46.oldText: There was general dismay among the passengers, who, leaving the delay aside, saw themselves forced to trudge fifteen miles over a plain covered with snow. They grumbled and protested, and would surely have drawn Phileas Fogg's attention had he not been entirely absorbed in his game.

28.47.oldText: Passepartout found he could not avoid telling his master what had happened, and, with his head down, he was turning back towards the car when the engineer, a true Yankee named Forster, called out, "Gentlemen, perhaps there is a way to get across after all."

28.53.oldText: "But the bridge is unsafe," urged the conductor.

28.54.oldText: "No matter," replied Forster; "I think that by putting on the very highest speed we might have a chance of getting across."

28.56.oldText: But a number of the passengers were immediately won over by the engineer's proposal, and Colonel Proctor especially was delighted, finding the plan perfectly feasible. He told stories of engineers leaping their trains over rivers without bridges by putting on full steam; and many of those present declared themselves of the engineer's mind.

28.57.oldText: "We've got fifty chances out of a hundred of making it," said one.

28.59.oldText: Passepartout was astounded, and, though ready to try anything to get over Medicine Creek, thought the proposed experiment a little too American. "Besides," he thought, "there's a simpler way, and it doesn't even occur to any of these people! Sir," he said aloud to one of the passengers, "the engineer's plan seems to me a little dangerous, but —"

28.60.oldText: "Eighty chances!" replied the passenger, turning his back on him.

28.61.oldText: "I know that," said Passepartout, turning to another passenger, "but a simple idea —"

28.62.oldText: "Ideas are no use," returned the American, shrugging his shoulders, "when the engineer assures us we can get across."

28.63.oldText: "No doubt," pressed Passepartout, "we can get across, but perhaps it would be more prudent —"

28.64.oldText: "What! Prudent!" cried Colonel Proctor, whom the word seemed to set off prodigiously. "At full speed, don't you see, at full speed!"

28.65.oldText: "I know — I see," Passepartout went on; "but it would be, if not more prudent — since that word displeases you — at least more natural —"

28.66.oldText: "Who! What! What's the matter with this fellow?" several voices cried.

28.69.oldText: "I, afraid? Very well; I will show these people that a Frenchman can be as American as any of them!"

28.71.oldText: "Yes, all aboard!" Passepartout repeated, and at once. "But they can't keep me from thinking it would be more natural for us to cross the bridge on foot, and let the train come after!"

29.0.oldText: The train continued on its way that evening without interruption, passing Fort Saunders, crossing Cheyne Pass, and reaching Evans Pass. Here the road reached the highest elevation of the journey, eight thousand and ninety-two feet above sea level. The travellers now had only to descend to the Atlantic by boundless plains, levelled by nature. A branch of the "grand trunk" line ran off southward to Denver, the capital of Colorado. The surrounding country is rich in gold and silver, and more than fifty thousand inhabitants have already settled there.

29.3.oldText: It was here that the Union Pacific Railroad was inaugurated on the 23rd of October, 1867, by the chief engineer, General Dodge. Two powerful locomotives, carrying nine cars of invited guests — among them Thomas C. Durant, vice-president of the road — stopped at this point; cheers were given, the Sioux and Pawnees performed a mock Indian battle, fireworks were let off, and the first issue of the _Railway Pioneer_ was printed by a press brought along on the train. Thus was celebrated the inauguration of this great railroad, a mighty instrument of progress and civilisation, flung across the desert, and destined to link up cities and towns that do not yet exist. The whistle of the locomotive, more powerful than Amphion's lyre, was about to bid them rise from American soil.

29.7.oldText: Once, having decided on a bold stroke, he was about to play a spade when a voice behind him said, "I should play a diamond."

29.10.oldText: "Ah! it's you, is it, Englishman?" cried the colonel. "It's you who are about to play a spade!"

29.11.oldText: "And who plays it," replied Phileas Fogg coolly, throwing down the ten of spades.

29.12.oldText: "Well, I'd rather have it diamonds," Colonel Proctor returned in an insolent tone.

29.13.oldText: He made a movement as if to seize the card that had just been played, adding, "You don't understand the first thing about whist."

29.14.oldText: "Perhaps I do — as well as any other man," said Phileas Fogg, rising.

29.15.oldText: "You have only to try, son of John Bull," replied the colonel.

29.16.oldText: Aouda turned pale, and her blood ran cold. She seized Mr. Fogg's arm and gently pulled him back. Passepartout was ready to fling himself on the American, who was glaring insolently at his opponent. But Fix got up, went to Colonel Proctor, and said, "You forget that it is I you have to deal with, sir; for it was I you not only insulted but struck!"

29.17.oldText: "Mr. Fix," said Mr. Fogg, "forgive me, but this affair is mine, and mine alone. The colonel has just insulted me again, by saying I should not play a spade, and he shall give me satisfaction for it."

29.18.oldText: "When and where you like," replied the American, "and with whatever weapon you choose."

29.19.oldText: Aouda tried in vain to hold Mr. Fogg back; in vain did the detective try to make the quarrel his own. Passepartout wanted to throw the colonel out of the window, but a sign from his master checked him. Phileas Fogg left the car, and the American followed him onto the platform. "Sir," said Mr. Fogg to his adversary, "I am in a great hurry to get back to Europe, and any delay whatever will be very much to my disadvantage."

29.20.oldText: "Well, what's that to me?" replied Colonel Proctor.

29.21.oldText: "Sir," said Mr. Fogg, very politely, "after our meeting in San Francisco I resolved to return to America and find you, as soon as I had finished the business that called me back to England."

29.23.oldText: "Will you set a meeting for six months from now?"

29.25.oldText: "I say six months," returned Phileas Fogg; "and I shall be at the appointed place on time."

29.26.oldText: "This is all just an evasion," cried Stamp Proctor. "Now or never!"

29.27.oldText: "Very well. You are going to New York?"

29.32.oldText: "What difference does it make to you? Do you know Plum Creek?"

29.34.oldText: "It's the next station. The train will be there in an hour, and will stop for ten minutes. In ten minutes a fair number of revolver-shots can be exchanged."

29.35.oldText: "Very well," said Mr. Fogg. "I will stop at Plum Creek."

29.36.oldText: "And I reckon you'll stay there too," added the American insolently.

29.37.oldText: "Who knows?" Mr. Fogg replied, returning to the car as cool as ever. He set about reassuring Aouda, telling her that blusterers were never to be feared, and asked Fix to be his second at the coming duel — a request the detective could not refuse. Mr. Fogg took up the interrupted game again with perfect calm.

29.38.oldText: At eleven o'clock the locomotive's whistle announced that they were nearing Plum Creek station. Mr. Fogg rose, and, followed by Fix, went out onto the platform. Passepartout went with him, carrying a pair of revolvers. Aouda stayed in the car, pale as death.

29.39.oldText: The door of the next car opened, and Colonel Proctor appeared on the platform, attended by a Yankee of his own stamp as his second. But just as the combatants were about to step down from the train, the conductor hurried up and shouted, "You can't get off, gentlemen!"

29.41.oldText: "We are twenty minutes late, and we shall not stop."

29.42.oldText: "But I am going to fight a duel with this gentleman."

29.43.oldText: "I am sorry," said the conductor; "but we shall be off at once. There's the bell ringing now."

29.45.oldText: "I'm really very sorry, gentlemen," said the conductor. "In any other circumstances I should have been happy to oblige you. But after all, since you haven't had time to fight here, why not fight as we go along?"

29.46.oldText: "That mightn't be convenient — for this gentleman," said the colonel, in a jeering tone.

29.47.oldText: "It would be perfectly convenient," replied Phileas Fogg.

29.48.oldText: "Well, we really are in America," thought Passepartout, "and the conductor is a gentleman of the first order!"

29.59.oldText: An end had to be put to the struggle, which had now lasted ten minutes, and which would end in the Sioux's triumph if the train was not stopped. Fort Kearney station, where there was a garrison, was only two miles off; but once past it, the Sioux would be masters of the train between Fort Kearney and the next station.

29.60.oldText: The conductor was fighting beside Mr. Fogg when he was shot and fell. At the same moment he cried, "Unless the train is stopped within five minutes, we are lost!"

29.61.oldText: "It shall be stopped," said Phileas Fogg, getting ready to rush out of the car.

30.2.oldText: Aouda was safe; and Phileas Fogg, who had been in the thick of the fight, had not got a scratch. Fix was lightly wounded in the arm. But Passepartout was nowhere to be found, and tears ran down Aouda's cheeks.

30.4.oldText: Mr. Fogg, arms folded, stood motionless. He had a serious decision to make. Aouda, standing near him, looked at him without speaking, and he understood her look. If his servant was a prisoner, ought he not to risk everything to snatch him from the Indians? "I will find him, living or dead," he said quietly to Aouda.

30.5.oldText: "Ah, Mr. — Mr. Fogg!" she cried, clasping his hands and covering them with tears.

30.6.oldText: "Living," Mr. Fogg added, "if we do not lose a moment."

30.7.oldText: By this resolution, Phileas Fogg was inevitably sacrificing himself; he was pronouncing his own doom. The delay of a single day would make him miss the steamer at New York, and his wager would surely be lost. But, as he thought, "It is my duty," and so he did not hesitate.

30.9.oldText: "Sir," said Mr. Fogg to the captain, "three passengers have disappeared."

30.11.oldText: "Dead or prisoners; that is the uncertainty which must be cleared up. Do you intend to pursue the Sioux?"

30.12.oldText: "That's a serious matter, sir," returned the captain. "These Indians may retreat beyond the Arkansas, and I cannot leave the fort unprotected."

30.13.oldText: "Three men's lives are at stake, sir," said Phileas Fogg.

30.14.oldText: "No doubt; but can I risk the lives of fifty men to save three?"

30.15.oldText: "I don't know whether you can, sir; but you ought to."

30.16.oldText: "No one here," returned the other, "has the right to lecture me on my duty."

30.17.oldText: "Very well," said Mr. Fogg coldly. "I will go alone."

30.18.oldText: "You, sir!" cried Fix, coming up; "you go alone in pursuit of the Indians?"

30.19.oldText: "Would you have me leave that poor fellow to perish — him to whom every man here owes his life? I shall go."

30.20.oldText: "No, sir, you shall not go alone," cried the captain, touched in spite of himself. "No! you are a brave man. Thirty volunteers!" he added, turning to the soldiers.

30.23.oldText: "Will you let me come with you?" asked Fix.

30.24.oldText: "Do as you please, sir. But if you wish to do me a favour, you will stay with Aouda. In case anything should happen to me —"

30.25.oldText: A sudden pallor spread over the detective's face. Separate himself from the man he had so doggedly followed step by step! Leave him to wander off into this desert! Fix gazed intently at Mr. Fogg, and, in spite of his suspicions and the struggle going on within him, he lowered his eyes before that calm and frank look.

30.27.oldText: A few moments later, Mr. Fogg pressed the young woman's hand, and, having entrusted to her his precious carpet-bag, went off with the sergeant and his little squad. But before going, he had said to the soldiers, "My friends, I will divide five thousand dollars among you, if we save the prisoners."

30.31.oldText: "I've been an idiot!" he thought. "And this man will see it. He has gone, and he won't come back! But how is it that I, Fix, who have a warrant for his arrest in my pocket, have been so taken in by him? Decidedly, I am nothing but an ass!"

30.34.oldText: Around two o'clock in the afternoon, while the snow was falling heavily, long whistles were heard approaching from the east. A great shadow, preceded by a wild light, slowly advanced, looking even larger through the mist, which gave it a fantastical look. No train was expected from the east, nor had there been time for the help requested by telegraph to arrive; the train from Omaha to San Francisco was not due till the next day. The mystery was soon explained.

30.38.oldText: Aouda, on seeing the locomotive come up, hurried out of the station, and asked the conductor, "Are you about to leave?"

30.41.oldText: "I cannot break off the trip," replied the conductor. "We are already three hours behind time."

30.42.oldText: "And when will another train pass through from San Francisco?"

30.44.oldText: "Tomorrow evening! But then it will be too late! We must wait —"

30.45.oldText: "Impossible," replied the conductor. "If you wish to travel, please get in."

30.54.oldText: So the night passed. At dawn the half-extinguished disc of the sun rose above a misty horizon; but it was now possible to make out objects two miles off. Phileas Fogg and the squad had gone southward; in the south all was still empty. It was then seven o'clock.

30.59.oldText: All were welcomed with joyful cries. Phileas Fogg distributed the reward he had promised to the soldiers, while Passepartout, not without reason, muttered to himself, "It really must be admitted that I cost my master dear!"

30.60.oldText: Fix, without saying a word, looked at Mr. Fogg, and it would have been hard to make out the thoughts struggling within him. As for Aouda, she took her protector's hand and pressed it in her own, too moved to speak.

30.64.oldText: "And when does the next train come through here?" asked Phileas Fogg.

31.0.oldText: Phileas Fogg found himself twenty hours behind schedule. Passepartout, the unwitting cause of this delay, was distraught. He had ruined his master!

31.1.oldText: At this moment the detective approached Mr. Fogg, looked him intently in the face, and said:

31.2.oldText: “Seriously, sir, are you in great haste?”

31.4.oldText: “I have a purpose in asking,” Fix went on. “Is it absolutely necessary that you reach New York on the 11th, before nine o’clock in the evening, when the steamer leaves for Liverpool?”

31.6.oldText: “And if your journey had not been interrupted by these Indians, you would have reached New York on the morning of the 11th?”

31.7.oldText: “Yes; with eleven hours to spare before the steamer sailed.”

31.8.oldText: “Good—so you are twenty hours behind. Twelve from twenty leaves eight. You need to make up eight hours. Do you wish to try?”

31.10.oldText: “No; on a sledge,” replied Fix. “On a sledge with sails. A man has proposed such a method to me.”

31.11.oldText: It was the same man who had spoken to Fix during the night, and whose offer he had refused.

31.12.oldText: Phileas Fogg did not reply at once; but when Fix pointed out the man, who was pacing up and down in front of the station, Mr. Fogg walked over to him. A moment later Mr. Fogg and the American, whose name was Mudge, entered a hut built just below the fort.

31.13.oldText: There Mr. Fogg examined a curious vehicle—a kind of frame on two long beams, slightly raised in front like the runners of a sledge, on which there was room for five or six people. A tall mast was fixed to the frame, held firmly by metal stays, and a large brigantine sail was attached to it. The mast carried an iron stay on which to hoist a jib-sail. Behind, a sort of rudder served to steer the vehicle. It was, in short, a sledge rigged like a sloop. During the winter, when the trains are blocked by snow, these sledges make extremely rapid journeys across the frozen plains from one station to another. Carrying more sails than a cutter, and with the wind behind them, they skim over the surface of the prairies at a speed equal to, if not greater than, that of the express trains.

31.14.oldText: Mr. Fogg quickly struck a bargain with the owner of this land-craft. The wind was favourable—fresh, and blowing from the west. The snow had hardened, and Mudge was very confident he could carry Mr. Fogg to Omaha in a few hours. From there, trains run eastward frequently to Chicago and New York. It was not impossible that the lost time might yet be recovered; and such an opportunity was not to be turned down.

31.15.oldText: Not wishing to expose Aouda to the discomforts of travelling in the open air, Mr. Fogg proposed to leave her with Passepartout at Fort Kearney, the servant undertaking to escort her on to Europe by a better route and under more favourable conditions. But Aouda refused to be parted from Mr. Fogg, and Passepartout was delighted with her decision—for nothing could have made him leave his master while Fix was with him.

31.16.oldText: It would be hard to guess the detective’s thoughts. Was his conviction shaken by Phileas Fogg’s return, or did he still regard him as an exceedingly cunning rascal who, once his journey round the world was complete, would think himself absolutely safe in England? Perhaps Fix’s opinion of Phileas Fogg was somewhat softened; but he was nevertheless resolved to do his duty and to hasten the return of the whole party to England as quickly as possible.

31.17.oldText: At eight o’clock the sledge was ready to set off. The passengers took their places on it and wrapped themselves up tightly in their travelling-cloaks. The two great sails were hoisted, and under the pressure of the wind the sledge slid over the hardened snow at a speed of forty miles an hour.

31.18.oldText: The distance between Fort Kearney and Omaha, as the crow flies, is at most two hundred miles. If the wind held, the distance could be covered in five hours; if no accident occurred, the sledge might reach Omaha by one o’clock.

31.19.oldText: What a journey! The travellers, huddled close together, could not speak for the cold, which was made sharper by the rapidity at which they were moving. The sledge skimmed along as lightly as a boat over the waves. When the breeze swept low over the earth, the sledge seemed to be lifted off the ground by its sails. Mudge, at the rudder, kept it on a straight line and corrected, with a turn of his hand, the lurches the vehicle tended to make. All the sails were up, and the jib was arranged so as not to blanket the brigantine. A topmast was hoisted, and another jib, set into the wind, added its force to the rest. The exact speed could not be measured, but the sledge could not be going at less than forty miles an hour.

31.20.oldText: “If nothing breaks,” said Mudge, “we shall get there!”

31.21.oldText: Mr. Fogg had given Mudge a real stake in reaching Omaha within the agreed time, by the offer of a handsome reward.

31.22.oldText: The prairie across which the sledge was racing in a straight line was as flat as a sea. It looked like a vast frozen lake. The railroad that ran through this section climbed from the south-west to the north-west by way of Great Island, Columbus—an important Nebraska town—Schuyler, and Fremont, on to Omaha. It followed the right bank of the Platte River throughout. The sledge, shortening that route, cut a chord of the arc described by the railway. Mudge was not worried about being stopped by the Platte River, since it was frozen. The route, then, was quite clear of obstacles, and Phileas Fogg had only two things to fear—an accident to the sledge, and a shift or lull in the wind.

31.23.oldText: But the breeze, far from slackening, blew as though to bend the mast, which the metal stays nevertheless held firm. Those stays, like the strings of an instrument, resounded as if vibrated by a violin bow. The sledge slid along in the midst of a plaintively intense melody.

31.24.oldText: “Those chords give the fifth and the octave,” said Mr. Fogg.

31.25.oldText: These were the only words he uttered during the journey. Aouda, cosily wrapped in furs and cloaks, was shielded as much as possible from the assaults of the freezing wind. As for Passepartout, his face was as red as the sun’s disc when it sets in the mist, and he laboriously drew in the biting air. With his natural buoyancy of spirits, he began to hope again. They would reach New York on the evening, if not the morning, of the 11th, and there were still chances it would be before the steamer sailed for Liverpool.

31.26.oldText: Passepartout even felt a strong urge to seize his ally, Fix, by the hand. He remembered that it was the detective who had procured the sledge, the only means of reaching Omaha in time; but, held back by some presentiment, he kept his usual reserve. One thing, however, Passepartout would never forget, and that was the sacrifice Mr. Fogg had made, without hesitation, to rescue him from the Sioux. Mr. Fogg had risked his fortune and his life. No! His servant would never forget that!

31.27.oldText: While each of the party was absorbed in such different thoughts, the sledge flew on over the vast carpet of snow. The creeks it crossed were not even noticed. Fields and streams disappeared under the uniform whiteness. The plain was absolutely deserted. Between the Union Pacific railroad and the branch that links Kearney with Saint Joseph, it formed a great uninhabited island. Neither village, station, nor fort appeared. From time to time they shot past some phantom-like tree, whose white skeleton twisted and rattled in the wind. Sometimes flocks of wild birds rose, or bands of gaunt, famished, ferocious prairie-wolves ran howling after the sledge. Passepartout, revolver in hand, held himself ready to fire on any that came too close. Had an accident happened to the sledge then, the travellers, set upon by these beasts, would have been in the most terrible danger; but it held its steady course, soon outdistanced the wolves, and before long left the howling pack at a safe distance behind.

31.28.oldText: About noon Mudge saw by certain landmarks that he was crossing the Platte River. He said nothing, but he was certain he was now within twenty miles of Omaha. In less than an hour he left the rudder and furled his sails, while the sledge, carried forward by the great impetus the wind had given it, went on for another half-mile with its sails struck.

31.29.oldText: It stopped at last, and Mudge, pointing to a cluster of roofs white with snow, said: “We’ve got there!”

31.30.oldText: Arrived! Arrived at the station that is in daily communication, by numerous trains, with the Atlantic seaboard!

31.31.oldText: Passepartout and Fix jumped down, stretched their stiffened limbs, and helped Mr. Fogg and the young woman to step down from the sledge. Phileas Fogg generously rewarded Mudge, whose hand Passepartout warmly grasped, and the party set out for the Omaha railway station.

31.32.oldText: The Pacific Railroad proper has its terminus at this important Nebraska town. Omaha is connected with Chicago by the Chicago and Rock Island Railroad, which runs straight east and passes fifty stations.

31.33.oldText: A train was about to leave when Mr. Fogg and his party reached the station, and they had only just enough time to climb into the cars. They had seen nothing of Omaha; but Passepartout admitted to himself that this was no great loss, since they were not travelling to see the sights.

31.34.oldText: The train passed rapidly across the State of Iowa, by Council Bluffs, Des Moines, and Iowa City. During the night it crossed the Mississippi at Davenport, and by way of Rock Island entered Illinois. The next day, which was the 10th, at four o’clock in the evening, it reached Chicago, already risen from its ruins and seated more proudly than ever on the shores of its beautiful Lake Michigan.

31.35.oldText: Nine hundred miles separated Chicago from New York; but trains are not lacking at Chicago. Mr. Fogg passed at once from one to another, and the locomotive of the Pittsburgh, Fort Wayne, and Chicago Railway pulled out at full speed, as if it fully understood that this gentleman had no time to lose. It tore across Indiana, Ohio, Pennsylvania, and New Jersey like a flash, rushing through towns with antique names, some of which had streets and tram-tracks but as yet no houses. At last the Hudson came into view; and at a quarter-past eleven on the evening of the 11th, the train pulled in at the station on the right bank of the river, in front of the very pier of the Cunard line.

31.36.oldText: The “China,” for Liverpool, had sailed three-quarters of an hour before!

32.0.oldText: The “China,” in leaving, seemed to have carried off Phileas Fogg’s last hope. None of the other steamers could serve his plans. The “Pereire,” of the French Transatlantic Company, whose admirable steamers are equal to any in speed and comfort, did not leave until the 14th; the Hamburg boats did not run directly to Liverpool or London, but to Havre, and the extra leg from Havre to Southampton would render Phileas Fogg’s last efforts pointless. The Inman steamer did not sail until the next day, and could not cross the Atlantic in time to save the wager.

32.1.oldText: Mr. Fogg learned all this by consulting his “Bradshaw,” which listed the daily movements of the transatlantic steamers.

32.2.oldText: Passepartout was crushed; missing the boat by three-quarters of an hour overwhelmed him. It was his fault, for instead of helping his master he had done nothing but throw obstacles in his path! And when he recalled every incident of the tour, when he counted up all the sums spent in sheer loss and on his own account, when he thought how the immense stake, added to the heavy charges of this useless journey, would completely ruin Mr. Fogg, he loaded himself with bitter self-reproach. Mr. Fogg, however, did not reproach him; and as he left the Cunard pier he said only: “We will consult about what is best tomorrow. Come.”

32.3.oldText: The party crossed the Hudson on the Jersey City ferryboat, and drove in a carriage to the St. Nicholas Hotel on Broadway. Rooms were taken, and the night passed briefly for Phileas Fogg, who slept soundly, but very long for Aouda and the others, whose agitation would not let them rest.

32.4.oldText: The next day was the 12th of December. From seven in the morning of the 12th to a quarter before nine in the evening of the 21st was nine days, thirteen hours, and forty-five minutes. If Phileas Fogg had left in the “China,” one of the fastest steamers on the Atlantic, he would have reached Liverpool, and then London, within the period agreed upon.

32.5.oldText: Mr. Fogg left the hotel alone, after giving Passepartout instructions to wait for his return and to tell Aouda to be ready at a moment’s notice. He went down to the banks of the Hudson and looked about among the vessels moored or anchored in the river, for any that were about to depart. Several had departure signals up and were preparing to put to sea on the morning tide; for in this immense and admirable port there is not one day in a hundred when vessels do not set out for every quarter of the globe. But they were mostly sailing vessels, which were, of course, of no use to Phileas Fogg.

32.6.oldText: He was about to give up all hope when he spotted, anchored at the Battery, a cable’s length off at most, a trading vessel with a screw, well shaped, whose funnel, puffing out a cloud of smoke, indicated that she was getting ready for departure.

32.7.oldText: Phileas Fogg hailed a boat, got into it, and soon found himself on board the “Henrietta,” iron-hulled and wood-built above. He climbed up to the deck and asked for the captain, who promptly appeared. He was a man of fifty, a sort of sea-wolf, with big eyes, a complexion of oxidised copper, red hair and a thick neck, and a growling voice.

32.11.oldText: “And I am Andrew Speedy, of Cardiff.”

32.12.oldText: “You are going to put to sea?”

32.19.oldText: “No passengers. Never have passengers. Too much in the way.”

32.21.oldText: “Between eleven and twelve knots. The “Henrietta,” well known.”

32.22.oldText: “Will you take me and three other persons to Liverpool?”

32.27.oldText: “No. I am setting out for Bordeaux, and I shall go to Bordeaux.”

32.30.oldText: The captain spoke in a tone that admitted no reply.

32.31.oldText: “But the owners of the ‘Henrietta’—” resumed Phileas Fogg.

32.32.oldText: “The owners are myself,” replied the captain. “The vessel belongs to me.”

32.37.oldText: Phileas Fogg did not betray the slightest disappointment; but the situation was a grave one. It was not at New York as it had been at Hong Kong, nor was the captain of the “Henrietta” the captain of the “Tankadere.” Until now, money had smoothed away every obstacle. Now money failed.

32.38.oldText: Still, some way had to be found to cross the Atlantic by boat—unless by balloon, which would have been reckless and was, besides, not practicable. Phileas Fogg seemed to have an idea, for he said to the captain: “Well, will you take me to Bordeaux?”

32.39.oldText: “No, not if you paid me two hundred dollars.”

32.45.oldText: Captain Speedy began to scratch his head. There were eight thousand dollars to be earned without changing his route—worth, surely, overcoming the repugnance he had for all kinds of passengers. Besides, passengers at two thousand dollars are no longer passengers, but valuable merchandise. “I start at nine o’clock,” said Captain Speedy, simply. “Are you and your party ready?”

32.46.oldText: “We will be on board at nine o’clock,” replied Mr. Fogg, no less simply.

32.47.oldText: It was half-past eight.
